members.dotPoint: investigate the causes and effects of non-infectious diseases in humans, including but not limited to:
members.title: Non-Infectious Disease: Causes and Patterns
members.exam: Students often incorrectly classify diseases like type 2 diabetes as purely genetic when examiners expect recognition of multiple interacting factors including diet, exercise and genetic predisposition.
members.summary: Non-infectious diseases result from genetic mutations, environmental exposures, nutritional deficiencies or lifestyle choices rather than pathogens, and have become the leading cause of death globally.

members.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain how proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes work together, and students often forget that multiple mutations are required, not just one.
members.summary: Cancer results from accumulated mutations that disable genes controlling cell division, causing cells to replicate uncontrollably and evade normal death pathways.

members.summary: Non-infectious diseases arise from genetic inheritance, nutritional deficiencies or excesses, or environmental exposures, with each category having distinct patterns of incidence and prevalence in populations.

cells.bigIdea: Non-infectious disease has no single germ to blame — so the topic runs on cause versus correlation, and on how the same disease breaks the body two ways: the mechanism at the cell, and the pattern across the population. Every question asks you to hold both, and to prove the link isn't just coincidence.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: investigate the work of Robert Koch and Louis Pasteur, to explain the causes and transmission of infectious diseases, including:
members.title: Koch, Pasteur and Germ Theory
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can state all four Koch's postulates in order and explain why they cannot be applied to viruses or obligate parasites.
members.summary: Germ theory replaced miasma explanations by demonstrating that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases through Pasteur's experiments disproving spontaneous generation and Koch's rigorous postulates.

members.dotPoint: investigate modes of transmission of infectious diseases, including direct contact, indirect contact and vector transmission
members.title: Modes of Transmission: Direct, Indirect, Vector
members.exam: Students confuse direct contact with droplet transmission, or fail to match appropriate control measures to the correct transmission mode in outbreak scenarios.
members.summary: Pathogens spread through direct contact, indirect contact via fomites or contaminated substances, airborne droplets, or biological vectors, with each route requiring different prevention strategies.

members.dotPoint: compare the adaptations of different pathogens that facilitate their entry into and transmission between hosts
members.title: Pathogens: Types and Adaptations
members.exam: Examiners frequently ask students to link pathogen characteristics to their treatment, such as why antibiotics fail against viruses or why prions resist standard sterilisation methods.
members.summary: The six pathogen types—viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, prions and parasites—each have distinct structural features, replication strategies and mechanisms for evading host immune responses.

cells.bigIdea: Disease is a broken relationship between a host and something else — a microbe, a deficiency, an inherited fault. For infection specifically, the something else is alive: a pathogen that has to get in, survive, and spread, and every question here traces one of those three jobs. Prove it's the cause and you've done what Koch and Pasteur did.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to:
members.title: Meiosis and Genetic Variation
members.exam: Students frequently confuse when crossing over occurs, incorrectly placing it in meiosis II or mitosis, or fail to explain that independent assortment refers to random orientation of homologous pairs not sister chromatids.
members.summary: Meiosis reduces chromosome number from diploid to haploid through two divisions while creating genetic variation via crossing over between homologous chromosomes in prophase I and independent assortment of chromosomes at metaphase I.

members.dotPoint: model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to:
members.title: Mitosis and the Continuity of Species
members.exam: Students often incorrectly state that mitosis produces genetic variation or confuse it with meiosis; examiners test whether students can explain why genetic identity is essential for tissue repair and growth.
members.summary: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells from one parent cell, preserving the chromosome number and genetic information across generations of cells for growth, tissue repair and asexual reproduction.

members.dotPoint: model the processes involved in cell replication, including but not limited to:
members.title: DNA Structure and Replication
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain why replication is semiconservative and often trap students by asking them to identify the direction of synthesis on leading versus lagging strands, expecting students to know that DNA polymerase only synthesizes in the 5' to 3' direction.
members.summary: DNA is a double helix with two antiparallel strands where adenine pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds and guanine pairs with cytosine via three hydrogen bonds, and semiconservative replication produces two identical molecules each containing one original and one new strand.

members.dotPoint: assess the effect of the cell replication processes on the continuity of species

cells.bigIdea: Two jobs pulling opposite ways, and the same molecule does both. Mitosis copies: two cells identical to the parent, which is what growth and repair need. Meiosis shuffles: four gametes, none alike, which is what a species needs to survive change.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: investigate the structure and function of proteins in living things
members.title: Protein Structure and the Proteome
members.exam: Questions ask students to predict mutation effects on protein function, and many don't explain the link between changed amino acid, altered shape, and lost function.
members.summary: Amino acid sequence determines how a protein folds into its three-dimensional structure, which directly determines its function, so mutations changing amino acids can alter or destroy protein activity.

members.dotPoint: model the process of polypeptide synthesis, including:
members.title: The Genetic Code and Codons
members.exam: Students frequently miscount nucleotides when converting DNA to amino acids, forgetting that 12 nucleotides code for only 4 amino acids, not 12.
members.summary: The genetic code is a triplet code where each three-nucleotide codon specifies one amino acid, and this code is nearly universal across all living organisms and includes start and stop signals.

members.dotPoint: model the process of polypeptide synthesis, including:
members.title: Gene Expression and Protein Synthesis
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can correctly identify which DNA strand is the template strand and trap students by asking them to predict the mRNA sequence, where students often forget that uracil replaces thymine and may incorrectly use the coding strand instead of the template strand.
members.summary: Gene expression involves transcription where RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3' to 5' to synthesize mRNA 5' to 3' in the nucleus, followed by translation where ribosomes read mRNA codons and tRNA molecules deliver corresponding amino acids to build polypeptide chains.

members.dotPoint: construct appropriate representations to model and compare the forms in which DNA exists in eukaryotes and prokaryotes
members.title: How DNA Is Packaged: Eukaryotes and Prokaryotes
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish that prokaryotes lack histones and a true nucleus, not just that their DNA is circular; students often incorrectly state prokaryotes have no DNA organization.
members.summary: Prokaryotes have circular DNA in a nucleoid region without histones, while eukaryotes have linear DNA wrapped around histone proteins forming nucleosomes, further coiled into chromatin and packaged in a membrane-bound nucleus.

members.dotPoint: evaluate, using examples, the benefits of engaging in an epidemiological study
members.title: Epidemiological Studies and Their Value
members.exam: Students often confuse correlation with causation or fail to identify which study type is appropriate for a given research question about disease patterns.
members.summary: Epidemiological studies identify disease causes and risk factors by analysing patterns in populations through descriptive studies (what/where/when), analytical studies (comparing groups) and intervention studies (testing preventions).

members.dotPoint: evaluate the method used in an example of an epidemiological study
members.title: Judging an Epidemiological Study
members.exam: Students frequently confuse correlation with causation when interpreting epidemiological data, failing to recognise that an association between variables does not prove one causes the other.
members.summary: Epidemiological studies investigate patterns of disease in populations to identify risk factors and correlations, but the design of the study determines whether conclusions are valid or misleading.

cells.bigIdea: You can't run the experiment — you can't give people cancer to prove a cause. So epidemiology reads the population instead: patterns, rates, and correlations across whole groups, then argues from strength, consistency, and dose whether the link is causal. Every study is that same argument, built without a lab.

members.dotPoint: investigate and assess the effectiveness of cloning, including but not limited to:
members.title: Cloning Organisms and Genes
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between reproductive cloning (whole organism) and therapeutic cloning (cells/tissues), and many students incorrectly claim all cloning produces perfect copies without acknowledging epigenetic differences.
members.summary: Cloning produces genetically identical copies at the organism, cell, or gene level, with gene cloning used routinely in research while reproductive cloning like Dolly the sheep remains controversial.

members.dotPoint: evaluate the effect on biodiversity of using biotechnology in agriculture
members.title: Applications of Biotechnology
members.exam: Students often fail to explain why genetically engineered insulin is superior to animal-sourced insulin, forgetting to mention reduced immune reactions and unlimited supply advantages.
members.summary: Biotechnology applies genetic modification to organisms to produce useful products like human insulin from bacteria or to enhance nutritional content of crops like beta-carotene enriched Golden Rice.

members.dotPoint: describe techniques and applications used in recombinant DNA technology, for example:
members.title: Recombinant DNA Technology and Transgenic Organisms
members.exam: Students commonly lose marks by failing to name the specific enzymes (restriction endonuclease cuts, DNA ligase joins) or forgetting that the host organism must transcribe and translate the foreign gene using the universal genetic code.
members.summary: Recombinant DNA technology uses restriction enzymes and ligase to insert foreign genes into host organisms, creating transgenic organisms that express the new gene as demonstrated by insulin-producing bacteria and herbicide-resistant crops.

members.dotPoint: compare the processes and outcomes of reproductive technologies, including but not limited to:
members.title: Reproductive Technologies: IVF and Artificial Insemination
members.exam: Examiners frequently test the distinction that artificial insemination involves fertilisation in vivo whereas IVF occurs in vitro, and students often confuse which procedure requires hormone treatment for multiple egg production.
members.summary: Artificial insemination introduces sperm directly into the reproductive tract while IVF fertilises egg and sperm externally before implanting the embryo, both overcoming infertility in humans and accelerating selective breeding in livestock.

cells.bigIdea: Every technique in here does one of two things: it moves a gene between organisms that would never share it, or it makes a copy where variation would normally creep in. Recombinant DNA, cloning, IVF, artificial insemination — all of them override what inheritance does on its own. The exam asks what you gained and what you traded for that control.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: conduct practical investigations to predict variations in the genotype of offspring by modelling meiosis, including the crossing over of homologous chromosomes, fertilisation and mutations
members.title: Meiosis and Genetic Variation
members.exam: Students frequently confuse when crossing over occurs, incorrectly placing it in meiosis II or mitosis, or fail to explain that independent assortment refers to random orientation of homologous pairs not sister chromatids.
members.summary: Meiosis reduces chromosome number from diploid to haploid through two divisions while creating genetic variation via crossing over between homologous chromosomes in prophase I and independent assortment of chromosomes at metaphase I.

members.dotPoint: interpreting examples of autosomal, sex-linkage, co-dominance, incomplete dominance and multiple alleles
members.title: Inheritance Beyond Dominant and Recessive
members.exam: Examiners trap students who apply 3:1 ratios to incomplete dominance crosses which actually produce 1:2:1 phenotypic ratios, or who forget that X-linked recessive conditions appear predominantly in males because they lack a second X chromosome to mask the allele.
members.summary: Beyond simple dominant-recessive inheritance, traits can show co-dominance where both alleles express equally, incomplete dominance producing blended phenotypes, multiple alleles creating more than two variants, and sex-linkage where genes on X chromosomes show male-biased expression.

members.dotPoint: constructing and interpreting information and data from pedigrees and Punnett squares
members.title: Punnett Squares and Pedigrees
members.exam: Students commonly misread pedigree symbols or incorrectly assign genotypes to carriers, and examiners test whether you can distinguish autosomal recessive from X-linked patterns by analyzing affected individuals across generations.
members.summary: Punnett squares predict offspring genotype ratios from parental crosses while pedigrees trace inheritance patterns across generations, both revealing how alleles segregate and combine according to Mendel's laws.

cells.bigIdea: Variation isn't an accident that happens to sex cells — it's the whole point of them. Meiosis is a machine built to shuffle: crossing over swaps pieces, independent assortment deals the chromosomes at random, and fertilisation stacks two shuffled hands. Every question here asks where a given difference was manufactured.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: construct and interpret negative feedback loops that show homeostasis by using a range of sources, including but not limited to: (ACSBL101, ACSBL110, ACSBL111)
members.title: Blood Glucose Regulation
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain the specific antagonistic actions of both hormones including target organs like the liver, not just naming the hormones.
members.summary: Insulin from beta cells promotes glucose uptake and glycogen storage when blood glucose is high, while glucagon from alpha cells stimulates glycogen breakdown when blood glucose is low.

members.dotPoint: construct and interpret negative feedback loops that show homeostasis by using a range of sources, including but not limited to: (ACSBL101, ACSBL110, ACSBL111)
members.title: Negative Feedback Mechanisms
members.exam: Students commonly confuse negative feedback with positive feedback or fail to identify all three components: receptor, coordination centre, and effector in their response pathways.
members.summary: Negative feedback systems maintain homeostasis by detecting deviations from set points, then triggering responses that counteract the original change and restore normal conditions.

members.dotPoint: investigate the various mechanisms used by organisms to maintain their internal environment within tolerance limits, including:
members.title: Thermoregulation in Endotherms
members.exam: Examiners expect students to distinguish between behavioral and physiological responses and to explain vasodilation versus vasoconstriction mechanisms in blood vessels near the skin surface.
members.summary: The hypothalamus receives temperature information from peripheral and central thermoreceptors, then activates appropriate effectors like sweat glands, arterioles, or skeletal muscles to adjust heat production or loss.

members.dotPoint: internal coordination systems that allow homeostasis to be maintained, including hormones and neural pathways (ACSBL112, ACSBL113, ACSBL114)
members.title: Hormonal and Neural Coordination
members.exam: Students often fail to explain that both systems use negative feedback loops but differ in speed and duration of response, or incorrectly state that only one system is involved in thermoregulation.
members.summary: The nervous system detects and responds to temperature changes within milliseconds via electrical signals, while the endocrine system responds more slowly over hours via hormones like thyroxine, both using negative feedback to maintain homeostasis.

cells.bigIdea: Your body keeps about forty things almost perfectly steady while the world does whatever it likes. Same trick every time: notice the drift, push back, repeat forever.

members.dotPoint: investigate the use of data analysis from a large-scale collaborative project to identify trends, patterns and relationships,  for example: (ACSBL064, ACSBL073)
members.title: Population Genetics and Large-Scale Studies
members.exam: Students frequently confuse allele frequency with genotype frequency or fail to apply Hardy-Weinberg assumptions correctly, especially forgetting that the equation only holds when mating is random and no selection, mutation, migration or drift occurs.
members.summary: Population genetics tracks allele frequencies across groups rather than individual pedigrees, using statistics to measure genetic drift, founder effects, and allele-disease associations in biobank cohorts containing hundreds of thousands of genomes.

members.dotPoint: investigate the use of technologies to determine inheritance patterns in a population using, for example: (ACSBL064, ACSBL085)
members.title: DNA Sequencing and Profiling
members.exam: Students often confuse sequencing with profiling - examiners test whether you know sequencing reads entire base sequences while profiling only examines specific variable regions, not whole genomes.
members.summary: DNA sequencing determines the exact order of nucleotide bases in a genome, while DNA profiling identifies variable regions like STRs to create unique genetic fingerprints for comparing individuals or populations.

cells.bigIdea: Stop watching the individual and watch the pool. Inheritance in a population isn't about one cross — it's about how allele frequencies shift across thousands of genomes, and the whole topic is measuring that drift, selection, and flow at scale. The single organism is a data point; the population is the thing that evolves.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: compare the causes, processes and effects of different types of mutation, including but not limited to:
members.title: Types of Mutation: Point to Chromosomal
members.exam: Students often misclassify frameshift severity, forgetting that insertions or deletions not divisible by three disrupt every codon downstream, whereas in-frame indels affect only local amino acids, and they confuse point mutation types with their phenotypic effects.
members.summary: Mutations span single nucleotide changes—substitutions that may be silent, missense or nonsense—through insertions/deletions causing frameshifts, up to chromosomal-scale events like duplications, inversions, translocations and aneuploidy.

members.dotPoint: explain how a range of mutagens operate, including but not limited to:
members.title: Mutagens and How They Operate
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish mechanism from outcome—for example, UV radiation causes thymine dimers that distort the helix, not direct base substitutions, and students often confuse the mutagen's action with the repair error that follows.
members.summary: Mutagens increase mutation rates above background by physically damaging DNA strands through ionising radiation, chemically mimicking bases to cause mispairing during replication, or inserting viral sequences that disrupt normal genes.

members.dotPoint: assess the significance of ‘coding’ and ‘non-coding’ DNA segments in the process of mutation
members.title: Gene Structure: Exons, Introns and Promoters
members.exam: Examiners ask students to calculate final mRNA or protein length after intron removal, and many incorrectly include intron sequences in their answers.
members.summary: Eukaryotic genes contain exons that code for protein separated by introns that are removed during RNA processing, plus upstream promoter regions where transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind.

members.dotPoint: distinguish between somatic mutations and germ-line mutations and their effect on an organism   (ACSBL082, ACSBL083)
members.title: Somatic vs Germ-Line Mutations
members.exam: Examiners set traps asking whether cancer mutations are inherited—students must recognise that most cancers arise from somatic mutations so they are not passed on, unless the question specifies a germ-line mutation in a tumour suppressor gene.
members.summary: Somatic mutations affect only body tissues and disappear when the organism dies, while germ-line mutations occur in gametes and transmit to offspring, appearing in every cell of the next generation.

runnersUp.title: Gene Structure: Exons, Introns and Promoters

runnersUp.title: Somatic vs Germ-Line Mutations

cells.bigIdea: Every mutation is one question asked twice: did the DNA change reach the sequence that codes, and did it land in a cell that gets passed on? Where in the gene decides whether the protein breaks; somatic versus germ line decides whether it dies with you or travels to the next generation.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: interpret data relating to the incidence and prevalence of infectious disease in populations, for example:
members.title: Epidemiological Studies and Their Value
members.exam: Students often confuse correlation with causation or fail to identify which study type is appropriate for a given research question about disease patterns.
members.summary: Epidemiological studies identify disease causes and risk factors by analysing patterns in populations through descriptive studies (what/where/when), analytical studies (comparing groups) and intervention studies (testing preventions).

members.dotPoint: investigate and analyse the wide range of interrelated factors involved in limiting local, regional and global spread of a named infectious disease
members.title: Controlling Spread: Quarantine, Hygiene and Public Health
members.exam: Students often fail to explain why layered defences are necessary, or cannot identify which specific control measure suits a given transmission mode in a scenario question.
members.summary: Disease control relies on multiple overlapping strategies including hygiene, quarantine, contact tracing, vaccination and border controls, because no single measure is perfect.

members.dotPoint: vaccination, including passive and active immunity (ACSBL100, ACSBL123)
members.title: Vaccination and Herd Protection
members.exam: Examiners test whether students confuse herd immunity thresholds with 100% coverage, or whether they incorrectly claim vaccines directly protect non-vaccinated people rather than reducing pathogen circulation.
members.summary: Vaccination stimulates immune memory cells without causing disease, and when vaccination rates exceed critical thresholds, unvaccinated individuals gain indirect protection because transmission chains break.

pick.title: Epidemiological Studies and Their Value

runnersUp.title: Controlling Spread: Quarantine, Hygiene and Public Health

runnersUp.title: Vaccination and Herd Protection

cells.bigIdea: You never see the disease directly — you see patterns in who gets sick, then act on the pattern before you know the mechanism. Epidemiology finds the link; quarantine, hygiene and public health break it. Every measure is a bet placed on a pattern, and it works whether or not you've named the pathogen.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: explain the mechanisms of reproduction that ensure the continuity of a species, by analysing sexual and asexual methods of reproduction in a variety of organisms, including but not limited to:
members.title: Sexual and Asexual Reproduction
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can link reproduction type to environmental stability, with many incorrectly claiming asexual reproduction is always disadvantageous or failing to recognise that stable environments favour asexual while changing environments favour sexual reproduction.
members.summary: Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring rapidly without a mate, while sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two parents creating variation at the cost of time and energy investment.

members.dotPoint: analyse the features of fertilisation, implantation and hormonal control of pregnancy and birth in mammals
members.title: Fertilisation, Pregnancy and Hormonal Control
members.exam: Examiners commonly test whether students can sequence the hormonal changes across the menstrual cycle and pregnancy, or students incorrectly state that oestrogen rather than progesterone maintains the endometrium during pregnancy.
members.summary: Reproduction from fertilisation to birth is orchestrated by a hormonal sequence where FSH and LH trigger ovulation, hCG signals implantation, progesterone maintains the uterine lining throughout pregnancy, and oxytocin initiates labour contractions.

members.dotPoint: evaluate the impact of scientific knowledge on the manipulation of plant and animal reproduction in agriculture
members.title: Manipulating Reproduction in Agriculture
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between different reproductive technologies and explain their specific advantages, with common errors including confusing cloning with genetic modification or failing to link techniques to actual genetic outcomes.
members.summary: Agricultural reproduction techniques allow farmers to control genetic outcomes through artificial insemination, selective breeding, cloning and controlled pollination to improve yield, disease resistance and desirable traits in crops and livestock.

pick.dotPoint: explain the mechanisms of reproduction that ensure the continuity of a species, by analysing sexual and asexual methods of reproduction in a variety of organisms, including but not limited to:
pick.title: Sexual and Asexual Reproduction
pick.exam: Examiners test whether students can link reproduction type to environmental stability, with many incorrectly claiming asexual reproduction is always disadvantageous or failing to recognise that stable environments favour asexual while changing environments favour sexual reproduction.

runnersUp.title: Fertilisation, Pregnancy and Hormonal Control

runnersUp.title: Manipulating Reproduction in Agriculture
runnersUp.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between different reproductive technologies and explain their specific advantages, with common errors including confusing cloning with genetic modification or failing to link techniques to actual genetic outcomes.
runnersUp.summary: Agricultural reproduction techniques allow farmers to control genetic outcomes through artificial insemination, selective breeding, cloning and controlled pollination to improve yield, disease resistance and desirable traits in crops and livestock.

cells.bigIdea: Every reproductive strategy is one answer to a single trade-off: copy yourself cheaply and stay identical, or mix with another and buy variation at the cost of effort. Fertilisation, pregnancy, and the hormones running them are all the machinery for paying that price — the exam asks how each species banks the return.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: investigate the response of a named Australian plant to a named pathogen through practical and/or secondary-sourced investigation, for example:
members.title: Plant Defence Responses to Pathogens
members.exam: Students often incorrectly apply animal immune concepts to plants by describing antibodies or phagocytes instead of explaining hypersensitive response, systemic acquired resistance, or recognition via pattern recognition receptors.
members.summary: Plants use physical barriers like waxy cuticles and cell walls, plus chemical defences including antimicrobial compounds and enzymes, while infected cells can self-destruct to prevent pathogen spread and release airborne signals warning nearby plants.

members.dotPoint: investigate and model the innate and adaptive immune systems in the human body
members.title: Innate and Adaptive Immunity
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between primary and secondary immune responses, particularly expecting explanations of why secondary responses produce antibodies faster and in greater quantities due to memory cells.
members.summary: Innate immunity provides immediate, non-specific defense responses within hours, while adaptive immunity develops over days but creates immunological memory for faster responses upon re-exposure to the same pathogen.

members.dotPoint: analyse responses to the presence of pathogens by assessing the physical and chemical changes that occur in the host animals cells and tissues (ACSBL119, ACSBL120, ACSBL121, ACSBL122)
members.title: How Animal Hosts Fight Back
members.exam: Students commonly lose marks by failing to identify fever and inflammation as innate responses or by incorrectly categorizing antibody production as part of innate rather than adaptive immunity.
members.summary: Physical barriers like skin and mucous membranes, chemical defenses including stomach acid and lysozymes, and cellular responses such as phagocytosis and inflammation all operate before adaptive immunity activates.

pick.dotPoint: investigate the response of a named Australian plant to a named pathogen through practical and/or secondary-sourced investigation, for example:
pick.title: Plant Defence Responses to Pathogens
pick.exam: Students often incorrectly apply animal immune concepts to plants by describing antibodies or phagocytes instead of explaining hypersensitive response, systemic acquired resistance, or recognition via pattern recognition receptors.
pick.summary: Plants use physical barriers like waxy cuticles and cell walls, plus chemical defences including antimicrobial compounds and enzymes, while infected cells can self-destruct to prevent pathogen spread and release airborne signals warning nearby plants.

runnersUp.title: Innate and Adaptive Immunity

runnersUp.summary: Innate immunity provides immediate, non-specific defense responses within hours, while adaptive immunity develops over days but creates immunological memory for faster responses upon re-exposure to the same pathogen.

runnersUp.title: How Animal Hosts Fight Back

runnersUp.summary: Physical barriers like skin and mucous membranes, chemical defenses including stomach acid and lysozymes, and cellular responses such as phagocytosis and inflammation all operate before adaptive immunity activates.

cells.bigIdea: A plant can't run, can't make antibodies, can't call in a cell to eat the invader — so it defends with what it can't move: barriers it built before the attack, and chemistry it triggers the instant a cell is breached. Every plant defence is either the wall or the alarm.

cells.subject: Biology

members.dotPoint: explain a range of causes of disorders by investigating the structures and functions of the relevant organs, for example:
members.title: Kidney Failure and Dialysis
members.exam: Students often fail to explain that dialysis relies on concentration gradients and diffusion, not active transport, or cannot compare limitations like inability to regulate hormones (erythropoietin, renin) that kidneys normally produce beyond just filtration.
members.summary: Kidneys maintain homeostasis through nephron filtration of blood, reabsorption of useful materials and waste removal, but when damaged beyond repair dialysis machines artificially filter blood using diffusion across a semipermeable membrane though less efficiently than healthy kidneys.

members.dotPoint: investigate technologies that are used to assist with the effects of a disorder, including but not limited to:
members.title: Disorders of Organs and Assistive Technologies
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain the specific biological function being replaced and how the technology achieves this, not just name devices.
members.summary: Assistive technologies like cochlear implants, dialysis machines and pacemakers replace or support failing organ function by mimicking biological processes through engineered devices.

members.dotPoint: explain a range of causes of disorders by investigating the structures and functions of the relevant organs, for example:
members.title: How Sense Organs Fail: Hearing and Vision
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish conductive hearing loss (outer/middle ear blockage, fixed by amplification) from sensorineural loss (damaged hair cells/neurons, requiring cochlear implants), and similarly cataracts (lens replacement) versus retinal damage (no current cure for photoreceptor loss).
members.summary: Sensory organs convert stimuli into electrical signals at specific sites where damage occurs: in hearing, hair cells in the cochlea transduce sound vibrations while in vision photoreceptors in the retina transduce light, with different assistive technologies targeting conductive versus sensorineural problems.

pick.title: Kidney Failure and Dialysis
pick.exam: Students often fail to explain that dialysis relies on concentration gradients and diffusion, not active transport, or cannot compare limitations like inability to regulate hormones (erythropoietin, renin) that kidneys normally produce beyond just filtration.

runnersUp.title: Disorders of Organs and Assistive Technologies

cells.bigIdea: Every disorder here is a job an organ can't finish, and every technology is something else stepping in to finish it. Name the lost function, then name what restores it — the pairing is the whole topic. A cochlear implant isn't magic; it's the job the cochlea stopped doing.

cells.subject: Business Studies

members.dotPoint: efficiency – expense ratio (total expenses ÷ sales), accounts receivable turnover ratio (sales ÷ accounts receivable)
members.title: Efficiency Ratios
members.exam: Students often confuse inventory turnover days with inventory turnover times, or fail to use cost of goods sold instead of sales when calculating inventory turnover ratio.
members.summary: Efficiency ratios measure how quickly a business converts assets like inventory and receivables into cash, with higher turnover rates indicating better asset management.

members.dotPoint: financial institutions – banks, investment banks, finance companies, superannuation funds, life insurance companies, unit trusts and the Australian Securities Exchange
members.title: Financial Institutions and Regulation
members.exam: Students often confuse the roles of different institutions or fail to link ASIC's regulatory powers to specific business financing scenarios in case studies.
members.summary: Financial institutions provide capital to businesses while regulatory bodies like ASIC enforce legal compliance and protect stakeholders within Australia's financial system.

members.dotPoint: planning and implementing – financial needs, budgets, record systems, financial risks, financial controls
members.title: Financial Planning and Controls
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can recommend specific control procedures for given scenarios rather than just listing generic controls like "separation of duties".
members.summary: Financial planning converts strategic objectives into budgets and forecasts while internal controls safeguard assets through procedures that prevent fraud, theft and accounting errors.

members.dotPoint: limitations of financial reports – normalised earnings, capitalising expenses, valuing assets, timing issues, debt repayments, notes to the financial statements
members.title: The Limits of Ratios
members.exam: Students lose marks by recommending decisions based solely on ratio analysis without acknowledging limitations like different accounting policies, one-off events, or non-financial factors affecting business performance.
members.summary: Financial ratios are useful analytical tools but have significant limitations because they only capture historical quantitative data and ignore qualitative factors that drive future business success.

members.dotPoint: methods of international payment – payment in advance, letter of credit, clean payment, bill of exchange
members.title: Global Financial Management and International Payments
members.exam: Students commonly forget to calculate the actual financial impact of exchange rate movements on profits or confuse when different payment methods are appropriate.
members.summary: International trade exposes businesses to fluctuating exchange rates and payment risks requiring hedging strategies and secure payment methods like letters of credit.

members.dotPoint: internal sources of finance – retained profits
members.title: Sources of Finance: Debt and Equity
members.exam: Examiners expect students to evaluate suitability of finance sources for specific situations and accurately calculate gearing ratios rather than just defining terms.
members.summary: Businesses fund operations through retained earnings, debt from lenders or equity from shareholders with each source creating different obligations and affecting financial leverage.

members.dotPoint: strategic role of financial management
members.title: The Role and Objectives of Financial Management
members.exam: Students often fail to explain trade-offs between competing objectives or cannot identify which financial objective is most threatened in a case study.
members.summary: Financial management ensures businesses have sufficient funds to operate while balancing liquidity needs, profitability goals, solvency requirements and operational efficiency.

members.dotPoint: distribution of payments, discounts for early payment, factoring
members.title: Working Capital Management
members.exam: Examiners test calculation of working capital ratios and whether students can diagnose cash flow problems despite paper profits in financial statements.
members.summary: Working capital management controls the cash conversion cycle by optimising stock levels, collecting receivables quickly and delaying payables to maintain daily operational liquidity.

runnersUp.summary: Financial planning converts strategic objectives into budgets and forecasts while internal controls safeguard assets through procedures that prevent fraud, theft and accounting errors.

runnersUp.dotPoint: limitations of financial reports – normalised earnings, capitalising expenses, valuing assets, timing issues, debt repayments, notes to the financial statements
runnersUp.title: The Limits of Ratios
runnersUp.exam: Students lose marks by recommending decisions based solely on ratio analysis without acknowledging limitations like different accounting policies, one-off events, or non-financial factors affecting business performance.
runnersUp.summary: Financial ratios are useful analytical tools but have significant limitations because they only capture historical quantitative data and ignore qualitative factors that drive future business success.

cells.bigIdea: Finance is one question asked in every section: can the business get the money it needs, when it needs it, without giving away more control or paying more than the money earns? Ratios, debt versus equity, working capital, global payments — all of it measures whether cash is in the right place at the right time.

cells.subject: Business Studies

members.dotPoint: explain how businesses exhibit corporate social responsibility in the management of human resources
members.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Business
members.exam: Students often describe CSR as purely voluntary when examiners expect recognition that stakeholder pressure, reputational risk and social license to operate make CSR increasingly essential for long-term business viability.
members.summary: Corporate social responsibility is the expectation that businesses actively contribute to social good and minimise harm beyond meeting minimum legal requirements through their operations, supply chains and stakeholder relationships.

members.dotPoint: discuss the influence of government on the process of determining employment contracts
members.title: Industrial Relations and Dispute Resolution
members.exam: Students commonly confuse the hierarchy of industrial instruments (awards provide minimum standards, enterprise agreements override awards, individual contracts must meet National Employment Standards) or cannot correctly sequence the dispute resolution process from negotiation through to arbitration.
members.summary: Industrial relations involves the formal system where employee wages and conditions are set through awards, enterprise agreements or individual contracts, with disputes resolved through a process escalating from workplace discussion to conciliation, mediation, arbitration and potentially Fair Work Commission intervention.

members.dotPoint: antidiscrimination and equal employment opportunity
members.title: Employment Relations and Legal Framework
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly order the hierarchy from NES as minimum, to modern awards, to enterprise agreements, to individual contracts, with each able to exceed but not undercut the previous level.
members.summary: The Fair Work Act 2009 sets the National Employment Standards as the safety net of ten minimum entitlements, while modern awards and enterprise agreements provide industry-specific or workplace-specific conditions above this floor.

members.dotPoint: examine the advantages of a diverse, culturally competent workforce for a global business
members.title: Global Human Resources, Outsourcing and Workforce Diversity
members.exam: Students often fail to distinguish between outsourcing (contracting external providers, often offshore) and offshoring (relocating company operations overseas), or cannot explain how diversity creates competitive advantage beyond stating it improves company image.
members.summary: Global HR manages employees across different countries through outsourcing, embraces diverse cultural backgrounds and identities, and leverages this diversity to improve innovation and business performance rather than just meeting legal requirements.

members.dotPoint: stakeholders – employers, employees, employer associations, unions, government organisations, society
members.title: Stakeholders and Their Conflicts
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify specific stakeholder conflicts in case studies and propose realistic management responses; the trap is suggesting win-win solutions that ignore genuine resource scarcity or claiming conflicts don't exist.
members.summary: Stakeholders have conflicting interests because resources are finite—when owners extract more profit, less remains for employee wages; when customers demand lower prices, profit margins shrink; when suppliers want higher prices, costs increase and squeeze profitability or customer value.

members.dotPoint: rewards – monetary and non-monetary, individual or group, performance pay
members.title: Maintenance and Separation
members.exam: Students often treat all separations as negative when voluntary retirement or resignation can be positive, or forget that redundancy requires consultation and compensation unlike dismissal for serious misconduct.
members.summary: Maintenance uses monetary rewards like salaries and bonuses plus non-monetary benefits like flexibility and recognition to retain staff, while separation manages voluntary departures like resignations and involuntary exits like redundancies or dismissals.

pick.dotPoint: explain how businesses exhibit corporate social responsibility in the management of human resources
pick.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Business
pick.exam: Students often describe CSR as purely voluntary when examiners expect recognition that stakeholder pressure, reputational risk and social license to operate make CSR increasingly essential for long-term business viability.
pick.summary: Corporate social responsibility is the expectation that businesses actively contribute to social good and minimise harm beyond meeting minimum legal requirements through their operations, supply chains and stakeholder relationships.

runnersUp.title: Industrial Relations and Dispute Resolution
runnersUp.exam: Students commonly confuse the hierarchy of industrial instruments (awards provide minimum standards, enterprise agreements override awards, individual contracts must meet National Employment Standards) or cannot correctly sequence the dispute resolution process from negotiation through to arbitration.
runnersUp.summary: Industrial relations involves the formal system where employee wages and conditions are set through awards, enterprise agreements or individual contracts, with disputes resolved through a process escalating from workplace discussion to conciliation, mediation, arbitration and potentially Fair Work Commission intervention.

runnersUp.dotPoint: antidiscrimination and equal employment opportunity
runnersUp.title: Employment Relations and Legal Framework
runnersUp.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly order the hierarchy from NES as minimum, to modern awards, to enterprise agreements, to individual contracts, with each able to exceed but not undercut the previous level.
runnersUp.summary: The Fair Work Act 2009 sets the National Employment Standards as the safety net of ten minimum entitlements, while modern awards and enterprise agreements provide industry-specific or workplace-specific conditions above this floor.

runnersUp.dotPoint: examine the advantages of a diverse, culturally competent workforce for a global business
runnersUp.title: Global Human Resources, Outsourcing and Workforce Diversity
runnersUp.exam: Students often fail to distinguish between outsourcing (contracting external providers, often offshore) and offshoring (relocating company operations overseas), or cannot explain how diversity creates competitive advantage beyond stating it improves company image.
runnersUp.summary: Global HR manages employees across different countries through outsourcing, embraces diverse cultural backgrounds and identities, and leverages this diversity to improve innovation and business performance rather than just meeting legal requirements.

cells.bigIdea: Every part of human resources is one negotiation: people are both the business's biggest cost and its only real capability, so managers are always balancing what workers give against what they're owed. Stakeholder conflict, awards, outsourcing, separation — each is that same tension, priced differently. The exam asks how a business holds both sides at once.

cells.subject: Business Studies

members.dotPoint: examine why ethical behaviour and government regulation are important in marketing
members.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Business
members.exam: Students often describe CSR as purely voluntary when examiners expect recognition that stakeholder pressure, reputational risk and social license to operate make CSR increasingly essential for long-term business viability.
members.summary: Corporate social responsibility is the expectation that businesses actively contribute to social good and minimise harm beyond meeting minimum legal requirements through their operations, supply chains and stakeholder relationships.

members.dotPoint: channel choice – intensive, selective, exclusive
members.title: Distribution Channels and Place Strategies
members.exam: Students often confuse distribution channel types or fail to justify why a business should choose intensive versus selective versus exclusive distribution based on product type and brand positioning.
members.summary: Distribution channels determine how products physically reach customers, involving decisions about intermediaries, market coverage intensity, and logistics like warehousing and transport to ensure availability at the right place and time.

members.dotPoint: types of markets – resource, industrial, intermediate, consumer, mass, niche
members.title: Markets and Customer Choice
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly distinguish between market types and link them to appropriate marketing approaches, or explain specific influences on consumer behaviour like reference groups or perception.
members.summary: Markets are categorised by buyer type and purpose, from industrial buyers seeking components to mass consumer markets, while customer choice within these markets is shaped by psychological, social, cultural and economic factors.

members.dotPoint: pricing strategies – skimming, penetration, loss leaders, price points
members.title: Pricing Strategies
members.exam: Students frequently select pricing strategies without justifying them against business objectives or fail to explain how price elasticity of demand should guide the choice between premium and penetration approaches.
members.summary: Pricing strategies range from skimming high early prices to penetration low prices for market share, with decisions influenced by costs, competition, demand elasticity and psychological factors like prestige or odd-number pricing.

members.dotPoint: situational analysis – SWOT, product life cycle
members.title: The Marketing Planning Process
members.exam: Examiners look for students to apply SWOT analysis correctly to real scenarios or demonstrate understanding of how product life cycle stage should inform marketing objectives and strategy selection.
members.summary: The marketing planning process follows a sequence: situational analysis assesses internal and external conditions, objectives define measurable targets, strategies outline the approach, implementation executes the plan, and monitoring evaluates performance against goals.

members.dotPoint: assess why a mix of promotional strategies is important in the marketing of goods and services
members.title: The Promotion Mix and Marketing Communication
members.exam: Students often fail to recommend the most appropriate promotion element for a given situation or neglect to explain how elements of the communication process like encoding, decoding and feedback affect message effectiveness.
members.summary: The promotion mix combines advertising, personal selling, publicity, sales promotion and relationship marketing to communicate with target markets, with effectiveness influenced by message design, media choice and factors like opinion leaders or noise.

members.dotPoint: explain how globalisation has affected marketing management
members.title: The Strategic Role of Marketing
members.exam: Examiners test whether students understand marketing as a business-wide philosophy beyond just promotion, or can explain how marketing orientation differs from production or selling orientations in achieving business objectives.
members.summary: Marketing's strategic role is to align the entire organisation around customer needs and market opportunities, shifting from a production focus to customer-centric thinking that drives competitive advantage and long-term business sustainability.

pick.dotPoint: examine why ethical behaviour and government regulation are important in marketing
pick.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Business
pick.exam: Students often describe CSR as purely voluntary when examiners expect recognition that stakeholder pressure, reputational risk and social license to operate make CSR increasingly essential for long-term business viability.
pick.summary: Corporate social responsibility is the expectation that businesses actively contribute to social good and minimise harm beyond meeting minimum legal requirements through their operations, supply chains and stakeholder relationships.

runnersUp.dotPoint: channel choice – intensive, selective, exclusive
runnersUp.title: Distribution Channels and Place Strategies
runnersUp.exam: Students often confuse distribution channel types or fail to justify why a business should choose intensive versus selective versus exclusive distribution based on product type and brand positioning.
runnersUp.summary: Distribution channels determine how products physically reach customers, involving decisions about intermediaries, market coverage intensity, and logistics like warehousing and transport to ensure availability at the right place and time.

runnersUp.dotPoint: types of markets – resource, industrial, intermediate, consumer, mass, niche
runnersUp.title: Markets and Customer Choice
runnersUp.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly distinguish between market types and link them to appropriate marketing approaches, or explain specific influences on consumer behaviour like reference groups or perception.
runnersUp.summary: Markets are categorised by buyer type and purpose, from industrial buyers seeking components to mass consumer markets, while customer choice within these markets is shaped by psychological, social, cultural and economic factors.

runnersUp.dotPoint: pricing strategies – skimming, penetration, loss leaders, price points
runnersUp.title: Pricing Strategies
runnersUp.exam: Students frequently select pricing strategies without justifying them against business objectives or fail to explain how price elasticity of demand should guide the choice between premium and penetration approaches.
runnersUp.summary: Pricing strategies range from skimming high early prices to penetration low prices for market share, with decisions influenced by costs, competition, demand elasticity and psychological factors like prestige or odd-number pricing.

cells.bigIdea: Marketing is one decision made seven ways: every element — price, promotion, place, the plan itself — is a bet about what a specific customer wants and will pay for. Get the customer wrong and every tactic misfires in the same direction. The exam hands you a business and asks whether its choices actually match the market it's chasing.

members.dotPoint: explain how operations strategy can help a business sustain its competitive advantage
members.title: Porter's Generic Strategies
members.exam: Students incorrectly claim a business can successfully pursue both strategies simultaneously, or they confuse differentiation with simply having better quality rather than distinct uniqueness customers value.
members.summary: Porter's Generic Strategies state businesses must choose between cost leadership through operational efficiency and lower prices, or differentiation through unique features that justify premium pricing, as attempting both dilutes competitive advantage.

members.dotPoint: transformed resources (materials, information, customers)
members.title: The Transformation Process
members.exam: Examiners expect students to identify where and how value is added at each transformation stage, not just describe the stages themselves.
members.summary: The transformation process adds value at each stage by converting raw inputs into increasingly finished products that customers are willing to pay more for.

members.dotPoint: examine the impact of globalisation on operations strategy
members.title: Supply Chain Management and Global Sourcing
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can evaluate trade-offs between cost savings from offshore suppliers versus risks like longer lead times, quality control issues, currency fluctuations and supply disruptions.
members.summary: Supply chain management coordinates the flow of materials, information and money from raw material suppliers through to end customers, while global sourcing involves selecting suppliers from different countries to optimise cost, quality and delivery.

members.dotPoint: technology, task design and process layout
members.title: Technology and Operations
members.exam: Students must explain specific impacts of technology on operations rather than making vague statements about technology making things "better" or "faster.
members.summary: Technology like CAD, automated production lines, and ERP systems increase efficiency, reduce errors, and enable real-time monitoring of operations across the supply chain.

members.dotPoint: goods and/or services in different industries
members.title: The Operations System
members.exam: Examiners require students to apply the input-process-output model to unfamiliar business examples, not just recite the definition.
members.summary: The operations system transforms inputs into outputs through processes, forming the core function of every business regardless of industry or size.

members.dotPoint: performance objectives – quality, speed, dependability, flexibility, customisation, cost
members.title: Operations Objectives
members.exam: Students frequently list objectives without explaining the trade-offs involved, such as how pursuing lowest cost might compromise quality or flexibility.
members.summary: Operations objectives include quality, speed, dependability, flexibility, and cost, which guide decision-making but require businesses to make strategic trade-offs between competing priorities.

Every part — objectives, strategy, technology, suppliers, ethics — is a decision about that transformation, and each one is a trade-off. The exam never asks 'what is this?' It asks 'why this choice, and what did it cost you elsewhere?'

cells.subject: Chemistry

members.dotPoint: conduct a practical investigation to measure and reliably compare the enthalpy of combustion for a range of alcohols
members.title: Heat of Combustion and Energy Efficiency
members.exam: Examiners specifically ask you to identify and explain multiple sources of heat loss rather than accepting a single generic statement about experimental error.
members.summary: Experimental combustion values are always lower than theoretical data book values because heat escapes to surroundings, the apparatus absorbs energy, and combustion is often incomplete in open systems.

members.dotPoint: compare and contrast fuels from organic sources to biofuels, including ethanol
members.title: Fossil Fuels and Biofuels Compared
members.exam: Examiners want you to compare specific properties like energy density, storage, carbon neutrality over the full cycle, and land use rather than vague statements about sustainability.
members.summary: Fossil fuels formed over millions of years so burning them adds ancient carbon to the atmosphere, while biofuels regrow in years so their carbon was recently absorbed from the atmosphere.

members.dotPoint: investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including:
members.title: Alcohols and the Hydroxyl Group
members.exam: Students incorrectly predict boiling points by forgetting that hydrogen bonding requires both a hydrogen on oxygen/nitrogen AND a lone pair acceptor; they also confuse solubility trends, missing that longer carbon chains make larger alcohols insoluble despite having -OH.
members.summary: The hydroxyl group (-OH) enables hydrogen bonding, dramatically increasing boiling points and water solubility compared to the parent hydrocarbon.

members.dotPoint: write equations, state conditions and predict products to represent the reactions of alcohols, including but not limited to (ACSCH128, ACSCH136):
members.title: Reactions and Oxidation of Alcohols
members.exam: Students lose marks by writing incorrect oxidation products (especially oxidising tertiary alcohols or stopping primary alcohols at aldehydes without specifying distillation conditions) and by failing to balance half-equations with H⁺ and H₂O in acidic oxidation reactions.
members.summary: Alcohols undergo oxidation with acidified dichromate, where primary alcohols form aldehydes then carboxylic acids, secondary alcohols form ketones, and tertiary alcohols resist oxidation.

cells.bigIdea: One –OH changes everything. It drags up boiling points, opens the door to hydrogen bonding, and hands the molecule a whole reaction map: ferment to make it, dehydrate or substitute to transform it, oxidise it up the ladder from alcohol to aldehyde to acid. Ethanol is the case study — fuel, solvent and product in one.

cells.subject: Chemistry

members.dotPoint: conduct investigations and/or process data involving:
members.title: Volumetric Analysis
members.exam: Students use incorrect stoichiometric ratios from unbalanced equations or fail to recognize why substances must be primary standards based on purity and stability.
members.summary: Volumetric analysis determines unknown concentrations through stoichiometric calculations from precise volume measurements using a standardized titrant of known concentration.

members.dotPoint: conduct investigations and/or process data to determine the concentration of coloured species and/or metal ions in aqueous solution, including but not limited to, the use of:
members.title: Calibration Curves
members.exam: Students incorrectly extrapolate beyond the calibrated range or fail to recognize that readings outside the standards are invalid and unreliable.
members.summary: Calibration curves relate instrument response to concentration using known standards, allowing unknown concentrations to be determined graphically from the linear relationship.

members.dotPoint: conduct qualitative investigations – using flame tests, precipitation and complexation reactions as appropriate – to test for the presence in aqueous solution of the following ions:
members.title: Identifying Ions: Flame Tests and Precipitation
members.exam: Students often confuse similar flame colours like sodium yellow versus calcium brick-red, or fail to clean the wire loop properly between tests causing contamination.
members.summary: Flame tests produce characteristic colours when metal ions are heated in a flame, while precipitation reactions form insoluble solids that help identify ions present in solution.

cells.bigIdea: The environment is a solution of hidden ions, and this topic is how you make them confess. Flame tests and precipitates say which ion; calibration curves and instruments say how much. Monitoring water, soil and air is just these two questions asked carefully, over and over.

cells.subject: Chemistry

members.dotPoint: investigate the processes used to analyse the structure of simple organic compounds addressed in the course, including but not limited to:
members.title: Proton NMR and the n+1 Rule
members.exam: Students misapply the n+1 rule by counting hydrogens on the same carbon instead of adjacent carbons or misread integration ratios as absolute numbers.
members.summary: Proton NMR reveals hydrogen environments through chemical shift, relative numbers through integration, and neighbouring hydrogens through splitting patterns following the n+1 rule.

members.dotPoint: investigate the processes used to analyse the structure of simple organic compounds addressed in the course, including but not limited to:
members.title: Chromatography
members.exam: Students confuse retention factor calculations or fail to explain separation in terms of polarity differences and relative attractions to each phase.
members.summary: Chromatography separates mixtures based on differential partitioning between a mobile phase and stationary phase, with retention time determined by relative affinities.

members.dotPoint: investigate the processes used to analyse the structure of simple organic compounds addressed in the course, including but not limited to:
members.title: Infrared Spectroscopy
members.exam: Students try to determine molecular structure from IR alone or misidentify broad O-H peaks versus sharp N-H peaks in interpretation questions.
members.summary: Infrared spectroscopy identifies functional groups by detecting characteristic bond vibrations at specific frequencies determined by bond strength and atomic masses.

members.dotPoint: investigate the processes used to analyse the structure of simple organic compounds addressed in the course, including but not limited to:
members.title: Putting the Spectra Together
members.exam: Students propose structures inconsistent with one technique or fail to systematically check their answer against all provided spectroscopic data before finalizing.
members.summary: Structure elucidation requires combining mass spectrometry for molecular mass, infrared for functional groups, and NMR for carbon skeleton and hydrogen connectivity.

members.dotPoint: investigate the processes used to analyse the structure of simple organic compounds addressed in the course, including but not limited to:
members.title: Carbon-13 NMR
members.exam: Students count peaks and assume that equals the number of carbons, forgetting that symmetrical molecules show fewer peaks than total carbons present.
members.summary: Carbon-13 NMR produces one peak per unique carbon environment, with molecular symmetry reducing the number of peaks below the total carbon count.

members.dotPoint: investigate the processes used to analyse the structure of simple organic compounds addressed in the course, including but not limited to:
members.title: Mass Spectrometry
members.exam: Students confuse the molecular ion peak with the base peak or fail to propose logical fragment structures that account for observed mass losses.
members.summary: Mass spectrometry determines molecular mass from the molecular ion peak and identifies structural fragments from the breakdown pattern of ionized molecules.

members.dotPoint: conduct qualitative investigations to test for the presence in organic molecules of the following functional groups:
members.title: Chemical Tests for Functional Groups
members.exam: Students often forget that tertiary alcohols will NOT oxidise with acidified dichromate, only primary and secondary alcohols produce the orange to green colour change.
members.summary: Chemical tests use simple reagents to identify functional groups in organic compounds through observable colour changes or precipitate formation.

runnersUp.exam: Students propose structures inconsistent with one technique or fail to systematically check their answer against all provided spectroscopic data before finalizing.
runnersUp.summary: Structure elucidation requires combining mass spectrometry for molecular mass, infrared for functional groups, and NMR for carbon skeleton and hydrogen connectivity.

cells.bigIdea: No single spectrum names a molecule. Mass spec gives the size, infrared the functional groups, NMR the carbon skeleton and its hydrogens — each one a partial witness. The skill is triangulation: stack the evidence until only one structure survives.

cells.subject: Chemistry

members.dotPoint: perform calculations to find the value of *K**eq* and concentrations of substances within an equilibrium system, and use these values to make predictions on the direction in which a reaction may proceed
members.title: ICE Tables
members.exam: Students fail to apply stoichiometric ratios in the change row or forget that changes are negative for reactants and positive for products.
members.summary: ICE tables track Initial concentrations, Change in concentrations using stoichiometric ratios, and final Equilibrium concentrations for calculating equilibrium constants.

members.dotPoint: deduce the equilibrium expression (in terms of* Keq*) for homogeneous reactions occurring in solution (ACSCH079, ACSCH096)
members.title: The Equilibrium Constant K
members.exam: Students include solids or pure liquids in K expressions, forget to apply coefficients as powers, or claim K changes when concentrations or pressure change at constant temperature.
members.summary: The equilibrium constant expression uses product concentrations divided by reactant concentrations each raised to stoichiometric coefficients, with K value indicating equilibrium position favouring products when large.

pick.dotPoint: perform calculations to find the value of *K**eq* and concentrations of substances within an equilibrium system, and use these values to make predictions on the direction in which a reaction may proceed
pick.title: ICE Tables
pick.exam: Students fail to apply stoichiometric ratios in the change row or forget that changes are negative for reactants and positive for products.
pick.summary: ICE tables track Initial concentrations, Change in concentrations using stoichiometric ratios, and final Equilibrium concentrations for calculating equilibrium constants.

runnersUp.title: The Equilibrium Constant K
runnersUp.exam: Students include solids or pure liquids in K expressions, forget to apply coefficients as powers, or claim K changes when concentrations or pressure change at constant temperature.
runnersUp.summary: The equilibrium constant expression uses product concentrations divided by reactant concentrations each raised to stoichiometric coefficients, with K value indicating equilibrium position favouring products when large.

cells.bigIdea: Keq is where a reaction settles, written as one number. Big K, products win; tiny K, barely started; and no amount of waiting changes it. Set up the expression, feed it an ICE table, and you can predict the mixture before you ever open the flask.

cells.subject: Chemistry

members.dotPoint: evaluate the factors that need to be considered when designing a chemical synthesis process, including but not limited to:
members.title: Green Chemistry in Drug Synthesis
members.exam: Examiners ask students to compare two synthetic routes and justify which is greener by calculating atom economy or identifying reduced solvent use and hazardous waste generation.
members.summary: Drug synthesis produces fifty to one hundred times its own mass in waste solvents and by-products, so green chemistry redesigns reactions to use safer reagents, catalytic processes, and atom-efficient pathways.

members.dotPoint: evaluate the factors that need to be considered when designing a chemical synthesis process, including but not limited to:
members.title: Percentage Yield and Atom Economy
members.exam: Students confuse the two calculations, using actual yield in atom economy formulas or claiming high atom economy guarantees high percentage yield.
members.summary: Percentage yield compares actual mass obtained to theoretical maximum, while atom economy calculates the proportion of reactant mass incorporated into desired product.

members.dotPoint: evaluate the factors that need to be considered when designing a chemical synthesis process, including but not limited to:
members.title: Reaction Pathways and Synthesis Design
members.exam: Students design synthesis pathways without considering reaction selectivity, proposing sequences where an earlier step would destroy a functional group needed for a later transformation.
members.summary: Retrosynthetic analysis works backwards from the target molecule to identify suitable starting materials and reagents, breaking the molecule conceptually at key functional groups or carbon-carbon bonds.

members.dotPoint: evaluate the factors that need to be considered when designing a chemical synthesis process, including but not limited to:
members.title: Industrial Compromise Conditions
members.exam: Students recommend extreme conditions without acknowledging the rate-yield trade-off or fail to justify why compromise conditions are economically necessary.
members.summary: Optimal equilibrium conditions often give impractically slow rates, so industry uses moderate temperatures with catalysts to balance acceptable yield with economic reaction speed.

cells.bigIdea: Making a molecule is never one reaction — it's a route. Every step trades yield, cost, energy, and purity, and the target dictates the path backwards: you start from what you want and ask what could have made it. Design is choosing the sequence the constraints allow.

cells.subject: Chemistry

members.dotPoint: explain the overall observations about equilibrium in terms of the collision theory
members.title: Collision Theory
members.exam: Students forget orientation requirements and claim all collisions above activation energy react, or they confuse increased collision frequency with increased collision energy.
members.summary: For a successful collision particles need sufficient kinetic energy to overcome activation energy and correct spatial orientation to allow bond breaking and forming.

members.dotPoint: investigate the effects of temperature, concentration, volume and/or pressure on a system at equilibrium and explain how Le Chatelier’s principle can be used to predict such effects, for example:
members.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
members.exam: Students predict the system completely reverses the stress or ignore that adding a catalyst causes no shift because it affects both directions equally.
members.summary: When equilibrium is disturbed the system shifts to partially counteract the change, establishing a new equilibrium position without fully reversing the disturbance.

members.dotPoint: investigate the effects of temperature, concentration, volume and/or pressure on a system at equilibrium and explain how Le Chatelier’s principle can be used to predict such effects, for example:
members.title: Industrial Compromise Conditions
members.exam: Students recommend extreme conditions without acknowledging the rate-yield trade-off or fail to justify why compromise conditions are economically necessary.
members.summary: Optimal equilibrium conditions often give impractically slow rates, so industry uses moderate temperatures with catalysts to balance acceptable yield with economic reaction speed.

members.dotPoint: examine how activation energy and heat of reaction affect the position of equilibrium
members.title: Energy Profile Diagrams
members.exam: Students incorrectly label activation energy as the gap from products to peak instead of reactants to peak, or think catalysts change the enthalpy change of the reaction.
members.summary: The vertical axis is enthalpy, reactants and products sit on horizontal sections, the peak is the transition state, and the difference in height between reactants and products is the enthalpy change.

pick.summary: For a successful collision particles need sufficient kinetic energy to overcome activation energy and correct spatial orientation to allow bond breaking and forming.

runnersUp.title: Le Chatelier's Principle

runnersUp.summary: Optimal equilibrium conditions often give impractically slow rates, so industry uses moderate temperatures with catalysts to balance acceptable yield with economic reaction speed.

runnersUp.title: Energy Profile Diagrams
runnersUp.exam: Students incorrectly label activation energy as the gap from products to peak instead of reactants to peak, or think catalysts change the enthalpy change of the reaction.
