members.dotPoint: derive and use the formula for the limiting sum of a geometric series with |r| < 1: $S = \frac{a}{1 - r}$ AAM [Critical and creative thinking icon]
members.title: The Limiting Sum of a Geometric Series
members.exam: Students commonly forget to check that |r| < 1 before applying the limiting sum formula, or they incorrectly use S = a/(1-r) when |r| ≥ 1 where the series actually diverges and has no finite sum.
members.summary: When the common ratio r satisfies -1 < r < 1, an infinite geometric series converges to the limiting sum S = a/(1-r), where a is the first term, allowing infinitely many terms to sum to a finite value.

members.dotPoint: know the difference between a sequence and a series
members.title: Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences and Series
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can correctly identify which type of sequence is present from a worded context, then apply the appropriate sum formula with n terms rather than confusing Sₙ formulas between arithmetic and geometric cases.
members.summary: Arithmetic sequences grow by adding a constant difference each step, geometric sequences grow by multiplying by a constant ratio, and both can be summed using formulas that depend on the first term and either the difference or ratio.

members.dotPoint: Apply the formulas for geometric sequences and series to model and solve growth and decay problems where a quantity is an exponential function of time
members.title: Geometric Growth and Compound Interest
members.exam: Examiners catch students using addition instead of multiplication for compound interest, or applying the interest rate incorrectly by forgetting to add one to the rate as the multiplier.
members.summary: When a quantity is repeatedly multiplied by the same factor greater than one it grows exponentially, and when multiplied by a factor less than one it decays exponentially.

members.dotPoint: Apply the formulas for arithmetic sequences and their partial sums to model and solve growth and decay problems involving a quantity that is a linear function of time
members.title: Linear Growth and Decay
members.exam: Students confuse simple interest with compound interest scenarios, incorrectly applying linear models to situations described with percentage growth language or missing that flat depreciation means subtraction not multiplication.
members.summary: Linear models add or subtract the same fixed amount each period producing arithmetic sequences where the balance changes by a constant value rather than a constant percentage.

cells.bigIdea: Two questions decide everything in this topic: does the pattern add the same amount each step, or multiply by the same factor? Add, and you have an arithmetic sequence — linear in n, growth that never changes pace. Multiply, and you have a geometric one — exponential in n. And if that factor is smaller than 1, infinitely many terms can still add up to a finite number.

members.dotPoint: Solve problems involving finding the mean or standard deviation of a normal random variable given the probability of an event less or more extreme than a given outcome
members.title: Inverse Normal Problems and Finding Unknown Values
members.exam: Examiners test whether students remember to use the complement when given upper tail probabilities, as tables typically show left-tail cumulative probabilities only.
members.summary: Working backwards from a given probability involves finding the z-score from tables or calculator, then using x = μ + zσ to convert back to the original variable's units.

members.dotPoint: Recognise the mean, or expected value, μ or E(X), of a discrete random variable X as a measure of centre for its distribution
members.title: Expected Value and Mean of Discrete Random Variables
members.exam: Students commonly make calculation errors by forgetting to multiply each x-value by its probability before summing, or they fail to include all possible outcomes in the summation.
members.summary: Expected value E(X) represents the long-run average outcome calculated by summing each value multiplied by its probability, providing the theoretical mean if an experiment were repeated infinitely.

members.dotPoint: Define a discrete probability distribution to be the set of values x taken by a discrete random variable X, together with the probabilities P(x) that x is the outcome of the experiment
members.title: Definition and Properties of Discrete Random Variables
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify that discrete random variables must have countable outcomes and verify that probability distributions sum to exactly 1, with students often forgetting to check this condition.
members.summary: A discrete random variable takes only specific, separate values with gaps between them, like rolling a die giving only integers 1 through 6, and each outcome has an associated probability that sums to 1.

members.dotPoint: identify the numerical and graphical properties of data that is normally distributed [Paperclip icon]
members.title: Calculating Probabilities Using the Normal Distribution
members.exam: Students often forget to subtract cumulative probabilities correctly when finding P(a < X < b), incorrectly adding them instead of subtracting the smaller from the larger.
members.summary: Converting raw scores to z-scores allows us to use standard normal tables to find areas under the curve, which represent probabilities for any normally distributed variable.

members.dotPoint: Define a probability density function (PDF), f(x), for a random variable X with cumulative b distribution function F(x) as f(x) = F'(x) and recognise that P(a < X < b) = ∫ f(x) dx a
members.title: Continuous Random Variables and PDFs
members.exam: Students incorrectly try to find P(X = a) for a continuous variable instead of recognizing they must find P(a < X < b) as an area, or they forget that the total area under any PDF must equal 1.
members.summary: Continuous random variables assign zero probability to single points, so we find probabilities by calculating areas under the probability density function curve over intervals using integration.

members.dotPoint: understand and calculate the z-score (standardised score) corresponding to a particular value in a dataset AAM [Paperclip icon]
members.title: The Standard Normal Distribution and Z-Scores
members.exam: Students frequently make sign errors when calculating z-scores for values below the mean, forgetting that these should be negative z-values.
members.summary: The formula z = (x - μ)/σ converts any normal distribution to standard normal with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, enabling comparison across different scales.

members.dotPoint: Recognise that the variance is an expected value because Var(X) = E((X ― μ)2 )
members.title: Variance and Standard Deviation of Discrete Random Variables
members.exam: A common error is calculating Var(X) as E(X²) minus E(X) instead of E(X²) minus [E(X)]², forgetting to square the expected value term.
members.summary: Variance measures the spread of a distribution by calculating the average squared deviation from the mean, while standard deviation is the square root of variance giving spread in the original units.

cells.bigIdea: Statistics is the art of turning a scatter of individual points into one shape you can reason about. Once you know a distribution's centre and spread, the z-score turns any value into a distance — how far from normal, in standard deviations — and correlation measures how tightly two shapes move together, never whether one causes the other.

members.dotPoint: Recognise and solve the first order differential equations for exponential growth and decay: dQ dQ
members.title: Differential Equations with Exponential Growth and Decay
members.exam: Students often forget to use initial conditions to find the constant A, or mix up signs when k is negative in decay problems, leading to solutions that grow instead of decrease.
members.summary: Exponential models use dy/dt = ky where k positive gives growth and k negative gives decay, leading to the solution y = Ae^(kt) that describes populations, radioactive substances, temperature change, and financial growth over time.

members.dotPoint: Solve problems involving related rates of change using the chain rule, given the required formulas for problems relating to area, surface area or volume
members.title: Implicit Differentiation and Related Rates
members.exam: Students forget to multiply by dy/dx when differentiating y terms, or they fail to substitute known values of both x and y before solving for dy/dx in related rates problems.
members.summary: Implicit differentiation treats y as a function of x without solving for it explicitly, applying the chain rule to every term involving y and then collecting dy/dx terms algebraically.

members.dotPoint: solve problems involving ∫sin ²nx dx and ∫cos²nx dx [Critical and creative thinking icon]
members.title: Integration by Substitution
members.exam: Students choose a substitution without checking whether its derivative actually appears in the integrand, or they forget to convert dx to du or to change the limits in definite integrals.
members.summary: Substitution works by recognising that an integrand contains both a function and its derivative as a factor, allowing you to replace the inner function with u and its derivative with du.

members.dotPoint: Examine the proofs of the derivatives of sin―1 x, cos―1 x and tan―1 x d f' (x)
members.title: Differentiating Inverse Circular Functions
members.exam: Students forget to include the constant 'a' in denominators when integrating to arcsin(x/a) or arctan(x/a), or they mix up which inverse function corresponds to which algebraic form.
members.summary: The derivatives of inverse trig functions produce algebraic expressions involving square roots, which means integrands with forms like 1/√(a²−x²) integrate directly to inverse trig functions.

members.dotPoint: Form a slope field for a first order differential equation using graphing applications

cells.subject: Mathematics Extension 1

members.dotPoint: prove results using mathematical induction [Critical and creative thinking icon]
members.title: Proving Summation Formulas Using Induction
members.exam: Examiners check that students correctly expand the sum up to k plus 1 by writing it as the sum up to k plus the new term, not incorrectly treating it as a separate expression.
members.summary: Mathematical induction proves summation formulas by first verifying the formula works at n equals 1, then showing if it works for n equals k it must work for n equals k plus 1, establishing truth for all positive integers.

members.dotPoint: Prove divisibility results using mathematical induction
members.title: Divisibility Proofs by Induction
members.exam: Students lose marks by writing "assume n=k works" without using it, or by failing to algebraically manipulate P(k+1) to explicitly show where the divisibility assumption P(k) gets substituted in.
members.summary: Divisibility induction rewrites the k+1 expression by extracting the k case that you assume is divisible, leaving a remainder you must show is also divisible by the target number.

members.dotPoint: Examine the nature of inductive proof, including the statement to be proved, the base case and the inductive step
members.title: The Inductive Hypothesis
members.exam: Examiners penalise students who assume the statement is true for n equals k plus 1 instead of n equals k, which is circular reasoning.
members.summary: The inductive hypothesis assumes the statement is true for some arbitrary positive integer n equals k, written explicitly as an equation you will use in the next step.

members.dotPoint: Examine the nature of inductive proof, including the statement to be proved, the base case and the inductive step
members.title: The Inductive Step
members.exam: Students often fail to clearly show where they substituted the inductive hypothesis or make algebraic errors when factorising expressions like k plus 1 from combined terms.
members.summary: The inductive step proves the statement for n equals k plus 1 by substituting the k plus 1 value into the left side, replacing parts using the inductive hypothesis, then simplifying to match the right side with k plus 1 substituted.

members.dotPoint: Examine the nature of inductive proof, including the statement to be proved, the base case and the inductive step
members.title: The Base Case
members.exam: Students lose marks by skipping the base case entirely or checking n equals 0 when the question specifies positive integers starting from n equals 1.
members.summary: The base case verifies the proposition holds for the smallest value in the domain, typically n equals 1, by substituting and confirming both sides equal the same number.

members.dotPoint: Identify errors in false ‘proofs by induction’, such as cases where only one of the two required steps of a proof by induction is true
members.title: Diagnosing a False Induction Proof
members.exam: Examiners test whether students verify the base case actually sits inside the domain where the inductive step works, catching proofs that assume k≥2 but only prove n=1.
members.summary: A false induction proof fails because the base case doesn't actually connect to the inductive step, creating a gap where the argument silently breaks down between n=1 and n=2.

pick.dotPoint: prove results using mathematical induction [Critical and creative thinking icon]
pick.title: Proving Summation Formulas Using Induction
pick.exam: Examiners check that students correctly expand the sum up to k plus 1 by writing it as the sum up to k plus the new term, not incorrectly treating it as a separate expression.
pick.summary: Mathematical induction proves summation formulas by first verifying the formula works at n equals 1, then showing if it works for n equals k it must work for n equals k plus 1, establishing truth for all positive integers.

cells.bigIdea: Induction never proves the formula outright — it proves that truth is contagious. Show it holds once, then show that whenever it holds it hands itself to the next case, and the whole infinite chain falls for free. You're not summing anything; you're building a machine that sums forever.

members.dotPoint: Define a binomial random variable, X, as the number of ‘successes’ in n independent and identically distributed Bernoulli trials, with the same probability of success p in each trial, where n is a fixed finite number
members.title: Binomial Probability Formula and Notation
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly identify n, p, and r from word problems, with common errors including confusing the number of trials with the number of successes or using p when they should use (1-p).
members.summary: The binomial probability formula P(X = r) = nCr × p^r × (1-p)^(n-r) calculates the probability of exactly r successes in n independent trials where p is the constant probability of success on each trial.

members.dotPoint: State the central limit theorem as: for a population with mean μ and variance σ2 , provided the sample size n is large enough (n ≥ 30), the sampling distribution is approximately normal with
members.title: Linear Combinations and the Central Limit Theorem
members.exam: The most common error is adding standard deviations directly instead of adding variances first then taking the square root, particularly when finding the standard deviation of differences like X minus Y.
members.summary: For independent random variables, means add for sums and subtract for differences, but variances always add in both cases; the Central Limit Theorem then guarantees sample means are approximately normal for sufficiently large samples, whatever the population distribution.

members.dotPoint: Define the sample mean for a sample X1 ,X2 ,…,Xn taken from a population as X = n ∑i=1 Xi
members.title: Point Estimation and Sampling Distributions
members.exam: Examiners test whether students understand that the standard error measures the spread of the sampling distribution and decreases as sample size increases, and that students can distinguish between population standard deviation and standard error of the mean.
members.summary: A point estimator uses a single value from sample data to estimate an unknown population parameter, while the sampling distribution describes the probability distribution of that estimator across all possible samples of the same size.

members.dotPoint: use binomial distributions and their associated probabilities to solve practical problems (ACMMM150) AAM [Critical and creative thinking icon]
members.title: Mean Variance and Standard Deviation of Binomial Distribution
members.exam: A common trap is forgetting to take the square root when finding standard deviation from variance, or substituting into the wrong formula by using p² instead of (1-p) in the variance calculation.
members.summary: For X tilde B(n,p) the mean is μ = np, the variance is σ² = np(1-p), and the standard deviation is σ = √(np(1-p)), providing measures of centre and spread without calculating individual probabilities.

members.dotPoint: use binomial distributions and their associated probabilities to solve practical problems (ACMMM150) AAM [Critical and creative thinking icon]
members.title: Conditions for Binomial Distribution
members.exam: Students often incorrectly apply binomial distribution to sampling without replacement situations where probability changes between trials, or when the number of trials is not predetermined.
members.summary: Four conditions must all hold: fixed number of trials n, each trial has only two outcomes (success or failure), trials are independent, and probability of success p remains constant across all trials.

Once you've checked those conditions hold, you don't count outcomes one by one — n and p alone hand you the mean (np) and the spread (npq). The conditions are the price of admission; the formulas are what you buy.

cells.subject: Mathematics Extension 1

members.dotPoint: Graph y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x, for ―2π ≤ x ≤ 2π using graphing applications and recognise that these three functions fail the horizontal line test
members.title: Circular Functions and Their Graphs
members.exam: Students lose marks by confusing the period formula (period equals 2π divided by the coefficient of x, not the coefficient itself) and by forgetting that tan has period π while sin and cos have period 2π.
members.summary: Sine and cosine graphs are horizontally shifted versions of each other where amplitude stretches vertically, period compresses or stretches horizontally, and phase shift plus vertical translation position the wave in the plane.

members.dotPoint: Graph the composite functions y = sin (sin―1 x), y = cos (cos―1 x) and y = tan (tan―1 x) by considering their domains and ranges
members.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions: Graphs and Properties
members.exam: Examiners test whether students correctly identify the range of inverse trigonometric functions, with a common trap being stating the range of arcsin as [0, π] instead of [-π/2, π/2], or confusing domain restrictions with range values.
members.summary: To create inverse trigonometric functions, we restrict the domains of sin, cos, and tan to intervals where they are one-to-one: sin restricted to [-π/2, π/2], cos to [0, π], and tan to (-π/2, π/2), so each output value corresponds to exactly one input angle.

members.dotPoint: Define sin―1 x or arcsin x to be the inverse function of y = sin x restricted to ― ≤ x ≤ , and 2 2 determine the domain and range of y = sin―1 x
members.title: Inverse Circular Functions
members.exam: Students lose marks by forgetting the restricted range of arcsin is [-π/2, π/2] and arccos is [0, π], giving answers outside these principal value intervals.
members.summary: Inverse trigonometric functions only exist because we restrict the domain of sine, cosine and tangent to intervals where they are one-to-one and can be reversed.

cells.bigIdea: sin, cos and tan have no inverses — they repeat, so they fail the horizontal line test. Inverse trigonometric functions exist only because we choose one stretch of each where the curve strictly rises or strictly falls, and throw the rest away. That single decision is the entire topic: the stretch you keep becomes the RANGE of the inverse, and every peculiarity that follows is that choice showing its consequences.

members.dotPoint: Model and analyse a projectile’s path where the projectile is a point and air resistance is negligible, subject to only acceleration due to gravity, assuming that the projectile is moving close to the Earth’s surface
members.title: Projectile Motion Using Vector Methods
members.exam: Students incorrectly apply the same acceleration in both directions or forget that horizontal acceleration is zero when writing the acceleration vector.
members.summary: Treating projectile motion as a vector problem means writing acceleration as a single downward vector then integrating twice with initial conditions to get velocity and position.

members.dotPoint: Solve motion problems involving constant velocity using vectors
members.title: Vector Calculus: Position, Velocity and Acceleration
members.exam: Students differentiate or integrate only the magnitude instead of differentiating each i j k component separately or they confuse speed with velocity when finding rates of change.
members.summary: Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time and acceleration is the derivative of velocity meaning you differentiate component by component.

members.dotPoint: define and use the projection of one vector onto another (ACMSM022)
members.title: Scalar Product and Applications in Three Dimensions
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can find angles between vectors using the rearranged formula cos(theta) = (a dot b)/(|a||b|), with students often forgetting to take the inverse cosine or making sign errors in component multiplication.
members.summary: The scalar product multiplies corresponding components and adds them, giving a single number that relates to the angle between vectors and tests for perpendicularity when the result equals zero.

members.dotPoint: Identify and use notation for vectors in both two dimensions and three dimensions, including a, a and AB, where AB is the vector with magnitude and direction those of the directed line
members.title: Three-Dimensional Vector Representation and Components
members.exam: Students often forget to include all three components when converting between component form and column vector notation, or incorrectly add scalars to vectors.
members.summary: A 3D vector is expressed as xi + yj + zk or as a column with three components, where i, j, k are unit vectors along the x, y, z axes respectively.

members.dotPoint: Derive the method for integration by parts
members.title: Integration by Parts
members.exam: The most common error is poor choice of u and dv leading to a harder integral, or forgetting to apply limits to the uv term when doing definite integrals.
members.summary: Integration by parts uses the formula ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du, converting a product into a boundary term minus a new integral that should be easier to evaluate.

members.dotPoint: Find indefinite integrals and evaluate definite integrals using the method of integration by substitution, where the substitution may or may not be given
members.title: Integration by Substitution
members.exam: Students choose a substitution without checking whether its derivative actually appears in the integrand, or they forget to convert dx to du or to change the limits in definite integrals.
members.summary: Substitution works by recognising that an integrand contains both a function and its derivative as a factor, allowing you to replace the inner function with u and its derivative with du.

members.dotPoint: Integrate rational functions by completing the square on a quadratic denominator
members.title: Integration Using Partial Fractions
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can set up the correct partial fraction form for repeated or irreducible quadratic factors, and whether they remember to perform polynomial division first when the numerator degree equals or exceeds the denominator.
members.summary: Partial fractions decompose a rational function into simpler fractions with linear or quadratic denominators, each of which integrates to logarithms or inverse trig functions.

members.dotPoint: Derive the identities for trigonometric products as sums and differences for $\cos A\cos B = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)]$, $\sin A\sin B = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)]$, $\sin A\cos B = \frac{1}{2}[\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)]$ and $\cos A\sin B = \frac{1}{2}[\sin(A+B)-\sin(A-B)]$
members.title: Trigonometric Products as Sums and Differences
members.exam: Students forget to halve coefficients correctly after applying identities, or fail to adjust limits when the argument changes from (A±B) form.
members.summary: Use product-to-sum identities to convert integrals like ∫sin(mx)cos(nx)dx into sums of sine or cosine terms that integrate directly.

cells.bigIdea: You can't integrate what you're handed — so you rewrite it into something you can. Partial fractions splits one hostile quotient into a sum of standard logs; product-to-sum turns a product of trig functions into terms you already know how to integrate. Every technique here is the same move: reshape the integrand until it's a form you've already beaten.

cells.subject: Mathematics Extension 2

members.dotPoint: Define and perform complex number addition, subtraction and multiplication, with and without digital tools
members.title: Operations and De Moivre's Theorem
members.exam: Students commonly forget to take all n distinct nth roots when solving equations like z to the power n equals w, missing roots by not adding 2 pi k over n to the argument for k equals 0, 1, 2, up to n minus 1.
members.summary: De Moivre's theorem states that the quantity r times the quantity cos theta plus i sin theta raised to the power n equals r to the power n times the quantity cos n theta plus i sin n theta, which is essential for finding powers and roots of complex numbers efficiently.

members.dotPoint: Graph regions associated with lines, rays and circles defined using complex numbers, giving a geometrical description of any such curves or regions, and using circle geometry theorems where necessary
members.title: Regions and Loci in the Complex Plane
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can sketch the intersection of multiple regions (like |z - 2| ≤ 3 AND arg(z - 1) = π/4) or students incorrectly forget that arg(z - a) = θ is a ray from point a, not from the origin.
members.summary: An equation or inequality involving a complex number z describes a geometric shape or region in the complex plane, such as circles from modulus conditions, rays from argument conditions, or half-planes from inequalities.

members.dotPoint: Illustrate the geometrical relationship connecting the $n$th roots of $\pm 1$
members.title: Roots of Unity
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify that the sum of all nth roots of unity equals zero and that multiplying any nth root of unity by another simply rotates around the vertices.
members.summary: The n distinct nth roots of unity are given by cis 2 pi k over n where k equals 0, 1, 2, up to n minus 1, forming a regular n-gon on the unit circle with one vertex always at 1 plus 0i.

members.dotPoint: Convert between complex numbers in Cartesian form and polar form and use complex numbers in Cartesian form and polar form to solve problems
members.title: Cartesian and Polar Forms of Complex Numbers
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students correctly identify the quadrant when converting from Cartesian to polar form, as simply using inverse tan without checking the signs of a and b leads to arguments that differ by pi radians.
members.summary: A complex number z equals a plus bi can be written in polar form as r times the quantity cos theta plus i sin theta, where r is the modulus calculated as the square root of a squared plus b squared and theta is the argument found using tan theta equals b over a with careful attention to quadrant.

members.dotPoint: Classify numbers as belonging to the set of natural numbers ($\mathbb{N}$), integers ($\mathbb{Z}$), rational numbers ($\mathbb{Q}$), real numbers ($\mathbb{R}$) or complex numbers ($\mathbb{C}$), each of which is an extension of the previous
members.title: The Complex Number System and the Imaginary Unit
members.exam: A common error is incorrectly simplifying powers of i beyond i squared, where students must remember the cycle i cubed equals negative i, i to the fourth equals 1, then the pattern repeats every four powers.
members.summary: The imaginary unit i is defined by the property that i squared equals negative one, which extends the real number system to complex numbers and allows every polynomial equation to have solutions according to the fundamental theorem of algebra.

cells.bigIdea: Inventing i doesn't break the number line — it turns it into a plane, where every number carries a length and a direction. Once that's true, multiplication becomes rotation, and the roots of unity are just a circle cut into equal slices. The whole topic is one move: numbers become geometry.

cells.subject: Mathematics Extension 2

members.dotPoint: Define simple harmonic motion as motion in which acceleration is proportional to, and in the opposite direction to, displacement, that is x = ― n2 (x ― c), where x ― c is the displacement of a particle from the centre of motion at c and x is the acceleration
members.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
members.exam: Students forget that SHM requires proving both the proportionality AND the negative sign in the acceleration equation a = -n²x, or they incorrectly identify damped motion as simple harmonic.
members.summary: Simple harmonic motion occurs when acceleration is always proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed toward it, producing sinusoidal position functions regardless of the physical system.

members.dotPoint: Derive the equations of motion for a particle travelling, without resistance, in a straight line with constant and variable acceleration and use the equations of motion to solve problems
members.title: Calculus Applied to Motion
members.exam: Students forget to add the constant of integration when finding position from velocity, or they fail to use initial conditions to determine the specific value of that constant.
members.summary: Position differentiates to velocity which differentiates to acceleration, and integration reverses the process, so velocity is the antiderivative of acceleration and position is the antiderivative of velocity.

members.dotPoint: Examine Newton’s three laws of motion, including force, acceleration, action and reaction under a constant and non-constant force
members.title: Newton's Laws in Vector Form
members.exam: Examiners expect you to resolve all forces into perpendicular components then write separate equations for each direction especially when motion is constrained to one axis.
members.summary: Because force and acceleration are vectors the equation F equals ma actually represents two or three simultaneous scalar equations one per coordinate direction.

members.dotPoint: Derive expressions for acceleration: dt , where v is a function of t, as well as v dx and dx 2 v2 , where v is a function of x
members.title: Kinematics with Variable Acceleration
members.exam: Examiners give acceleration as a function of time or velocity then ask for velocity or displacement requiring you to separate variables and integrate rather than substitute into a formula.
members.summary: When acceleration depends on time or velocity or position you must use calculus definitions directly because the suvat formulas assume constant acceleration and will give wrong answers.

members.dotPoint: Define the terminal velocity of a particle falling through a medium as the constant velocity the particle reaches when the resistance of the medium prevents further acceleration
members.title: Resisted Motion and Terminal Velocity
members.exam: Students incorrectly solve dv/dt = g - kv by separating variables as dv/(g-kv) = dt but then integrate the left side as ln(g-kv) instead of -1/k·ln(g-kv), losing the negative sign and the coefficient.
members.summary: In resisted motion, drag force increases with velocity until it balances the driving force, causing acceleration to reach zero at terminal velocity where the object moves at constant speed.

pick.dotPoint: Define simple harmonic motion as motion in which acceleration is proportional to, and in the opposite direction to, displacement, that is x = ― n2 (x ― c), where x ― c is the displacement of a particle from the centre of motion at c and x is the acceleration
pick.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
pick.exam: Students forget that SHM requires proving both the proportionality AND the negative sign in the acceleration equation a = -n²x, or they incorrectly identify damped motion as simple harmonic.
pick.summary: Simple harmonic motion occurs when acceleration is always proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed toward it, producing sinusoidal position functions regardless of the physical system.

runnersUp.dotPoint: Derive the equations of motion for a particle travelling, without resistance, in a straight line with constant and variable acceleration and use the equations of motion to solve problems
runnersUp.title: Calculus Applied to Motion
runnersUp.exam: Students forget to add the constant of integration when finding position from velocity, or they fail to use initial conditions to determine the specific value of that constant.
runnersUp.summary: Position differentiates to velocity which differentiates to acceleration, and integration reverses the process, so velocity is the antiderivative of acceleration and position is the antiderivative of velocity.

runnersUp.dotPoint: Examine Newton’s three laws of motion, including force, acceleration, action and reaction under a constant and non-constant force
runnersUp.title: Newton's Laws in Vector Form
runnersUp.exam: Examiners expect you to resolve all forces into perpendicular components then write separate equations for each direction especially when motion is constrained to one axis.
runnersUp.summary: Because force and acceleration are vectors the equation F equals ma actually represents two or three simultaneous scalar equations one per coordinate direction.

runnersUp.dotPoint: Derive expressions for acceleration: dt , where v is a function of t, as well as v dx and dx 2 v2 , where v is a function of x
runnersUp.title: Kinematics with Variable Acceleration
runnersUp.exam: Examiners give acceleration as a function of time or velocity then ask for velocity or displacement requiring you to separate variables and integrate rather than substitute into a formula.
runnersUp.summary: When acceleration depends on time or velocity or position you must use calculus definitions directly because the suvat formulas assume constant acceleration and will give wrong answers.

cells.bigIdea: Mechanics is Newton's second law and a choice. Every problem here is F = mẍ; what decides whether it is a two-line answer or an unsolvable mess is which form of acceleration you write down. Use dv/dt when the force depends on time, and v dv/dx when it depends on position. Read what the force actually depends on, choose accordingly, and the calculus does the rest.

cells.subject: Mathematics Extension 2

members.dotPoint: Prove and use the triangle inequality
members.title: Proving Inequalities
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can justify each step with valid reasoning and direction of inequality; the common trap is multiplying or dividing by negative expressions without reversing the inequality sign.
members.summary: Proving inequalities involves showing one expression exceeds another through algebraic manipulation (completing the square to show non-negativity), applying standard inequalities like AM-GM or Cauchy-Schwarz, or using calculus to establish bounds without computing exact values.

members.dotPoint: Use examples and counterexamples to test the truth of mathematical statements
members.title: Proof by Contradiction and Counterexample
members.exam: Students confuse proof by contradiction with proof by contrapositive — contradiction assumes the statement is false and derives an impossibility, while contrapositive proves "not Q implies not P" directly. They also start a contradiction proof but forget to state clearly what they assumed and what contradiction they reached.
members.summary: A single counterexample destroys a universal claim instantly, while proof by contradiction assumes the negation of what you want to prove and derives a logical impossibility to conclude the original must be true.

members.dotPoint: Explain that a recursive formula, or recurrence relation, is a formula that defines each term of a sequence using a preceding term
members.title: Recursive Formulas and Notation
members.exam: Examiners check whether students can correctly extract R and D from worded problems, particularly testing if negative D is used for withdrawals or payments and if R incorporates both principal and interest.
members.summary: The three components are the next value V(n+1), the growth multiplier R applied to current value, and the constant change D that represents deposits or payments added each period.

members.dotPoint: Define a statement or proposition as a sentence that is either true or false, but not both
members.title: Logical Connectives and Quantifiers
members.exam: The most common error is incorrectly negating quantified statements, particularly writing the negation of 'for all x, P(x)' as 'for all x, not P(x)' instead of 'there exists x such that not P(x)'.
members.summary: Connectives (and, or, not, implies) and quantifiers (for all, there exists) build precise mathematical statements, and negation rules are strict: negate 'for all' to get 'there exists' and vice versa, then negate the predicate.

cells.bigIdea: Proof isn't calculation — it's argument, where every line has to be forced by the one before it. Whether you're climbing an induction ladder or squeezing an inequality between what you know, you're never showing that something's true; you're showing it can't be false. The claim is the destination, but the reasoning is the whole mark.

members.title: Vector Equations of Lines and Planes
members.exam: Examiners test whether you can find where a line pierces a plane by substituting the parametric line equation into the Cartesian plane equation.
members.summary: A vector line needs a point and direction vector while a plane needs a point and normal vector with all intersection and distance problems solved by substitution or projection.

members.dotPoint: Define the medians, altitudes, perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors of a triangle and recognise these definitions in vector proofs
members.title: Geometric Proofs Using Vectors
members.exam: Students often forget to show that the midpoint formula applies by adding position vectors and dividing by two, or fail to prove collinearity by showing one vector is a scalar multiple of another.
members.summary: Represent geometric points as position vectors from the origin, then prove theorems by manipulating these vectors algebraically rather than relying on diagram constructions.

members.dotPoint: Establish and use the results i ⋅ i = j ⋅ j = k ⋅ k = 1 and i ⋅ j = j ⋅ k = k ⋅ i = 0
members.title: Scalar Product and Applications in Three Dimensions
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can find angles between vectors using the rearranged formula cos(theta) = (a dot b)/(|a||b|), with students often forgetting to take the inverse cosine or making sign errors in component multiplication.
members.summary: The scalar product multiplies corresponding components and adds them, giving a single number that relates to the angle between vectors and tests for perpendicularity when the result equals zero.

cells.bigIdea: A line is one point plus every scalar multiple of a direction; a plane is one point plus every combination of two. That's the whole topic: fix where you start, then say which way you're allowed to move. Every question is just asking where two of these freedoms cross, miss, or coincide.

cells.subject: Mathematics Standard 1

members.dotPoint: Graph two linear equations using a table of values or a graphing application and identify the point of intersection
members.title: Linear Relationships
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can correctly calculate gradient from two points using rise over run, and many students mix up which value is m and which is c when substituting.
members.summary: Linear relationships create straight-line graphs where the gradient m shows the rate of change and the y-intercept c shows where the line crosses the vertical axis.

members.dotPoint: construct a graph from a table of values both with and without technology [ Information and communication technology capability icon]
members.title: Graphs and Models of Practical Situations
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can match context to shape—especially distinguishing constant rate (straight line) from increasing/decreasing rate (curve), and identifying sections where a quantity stays constant (horizontal segment).
members.summary: A graph translates a real-world story into a visual relationship between two variables, where the shape (linear, curved, steep, flat) reveals how one quantity changes as the other increases.

members.dotPoint: Solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations by finding the point of intersection of their graphs, with and without graphing applications
members.title: Simultaneous Equations and the Break-Even Point
members.exam: Students often confuse which variable represents quantity and which represents dollars, or forget to interpret their solution in context by stating the break-even quantity and corresponding dollar amount.
members.summary: The break-even point occurs where total cost equals total revenue, found by solving two simultaneous linear equations representing cost and revenue as functions of quantity sold.

Read those parts back into the real thing — cost, distance, fuel — and the model tells you what you didn't measure.

cells.subject: Mathematics Standard 1

members.dotPoint: Calculate the future value, present value or interest rate of a compound interest investment using the formula FV = PV(1 + r)n where FV = future value of the investment, PV = present value of the investment, r = interest rate per time period and n = number of time periods
members.title: Compound Interest
members.exam: Students often forget to convert percentage rates to decimals or mismatch time periods with compounding frequency, such as using years when interest compounds monthly.
members.summary: Compound interest means interest earns interest because the balance grows each period, calculated using A = P(1 + r)^n where the exponent n makes growth exponential rather than linear.

members.dotPoint: Apply the straight-line depreciation method to calculate the depreciation of an asset using the formula S = V0 ― Dn where S = salvage value, V0 = initial value of the asset, D = depreciation amount per time period and n = number of time periods
members.title: Depreciation
members.exam: Students confuse which method to apply or incorrectly use the original purchase price instead of the current value when calculating reducing balance depreciation.
members.summary: Flat rate depreciation subtracts the same dollar amount each period using V = P - DN, while reducing balance depreciation applies a fixed percentage decrease each period to the remaining value.

members.dotPoint: recognise credit cards as an example of a reducing balance loan and solve practical problems relating to credit cards
members.title: Reducing Balance Loans
members.exam: Examiners test whether students subtract the payment after applying interest not before, and whether they recognise that final payments may be smaller when the remaining balance is less than the regular payment.
members.summary: The balance after each payment equals the previous balance multiplied by one plus the interest rate then decreased by the fixed payment amount, gradually reducing principal over time.

members.dotPoint: Calculate simple interest for different interest rates and time periods using the formula
members.title: Simple Interest
members.exam: Students mix up simple and compound interest formulas or fail to align time units with the rate period, such as using months when the rate is annual.
members.summary: Simple interest calculates interest only on the original principal using I = PRT, producing linear growth because the same dollar amount is added each period regardless of accumulated interest.

cells.bigIdea: Every repayment on a reducing balance loan does two jobs at once: it pays the interest charged on what you still owe, and whatever's left chips away at the debt itself. Because the balance shrinks each period, the interest shrinks too — so early payments are mostly interest and late ones are mostly principal. Track the balance line by line and the whole topic is just that step, repeated.

members.dotPoint: solve practical problems involving ratio, for example map scales, mixtures for building materials or cost per item AAM [Critical and creative thinking icon] [ Information and communication technology capability icon]
members.title: Practical Ratio Problems and Capture-Recapture
members.exam: Students commonly confuse the order of ratio terms or fail to account for tagged animals already in the second sample when calculating total population in capture-recapture problems.
members.summary: Ratios maintain constant proportional relationships and can be used to estimate unknown quantities from partial samples, whether scaling distances on maps or estimating wildlife populations from tagged-and-recaptured animals.

members.dotPoint: use, simplify and convert between units of rates, for example km/h and m/s, mL/min and L/h (ACMEM071, ACMEM072)
members.title: Rates and Unit Conversions
members.exam: Students forget to convert both parts of a rate when changing units, commonly multiplying speed in km/h by 1000 instead of dividing by 3.6 to get m/s, or failing to convert hours to minutes when calculating drip rates.
members.summary: Rates express one quantity per unit of another, and converting units requires changing both numerator and denominator separately, like converting 72 km/h to 20 m/s by dividing distance units by 1000 and time units by 3600.

members.dotPoint: solve practical problems involving angles of elevation and depression and bearings AAM [Paperclip icon] [Critical and creative thinking icon] [ Information and communication technology capability icon] [Literacy icon]
members.title: Bearings, Elevation and Compass Radial Surveys
members.exam: Students frequently subtract bearings in the wrong order when finding the angle between two directions, or forget that a back bearing differs from the forward bearing by exactly 180 degrees.
members.summary: Bearings measure direction as angles clockwise from north, elevation angles measure upward slope from horizontal, and radial surveys use distance and bearing from one central point to map surrounding locations.

members.dotPoint: use the conditions for similarity of two-dimensional figures, including similar triangles, to solve related problems
members.title: Similarity, Scale Drawings and Plans
members.exam: Examiners test whether students confuse linear and area scale factors, expecting candidates to square the scale factor when finding area ratios or to recognise that a 1:50 scale drawing means 1 cm represents 50 cm in reality.
members.summary: Similar figures have identical angles and corresponding sides in constant ratio, meaning if you know the scale factor you can find any unknown length by multiplying, and areas scale by the square of the linear scale factor.

members.dotPoint: review the application of Pythagoras’ theorem to solve practical problems in two dimensions AAM [Paperclip icon] [Critical and creative thinking icon] [Literacy icon]

members.summary: Pythagoras theorem relates the three sides of right-angled triangles through the equation a² + b² = c², while trigonometric ratios connect angles to side ratios using sine, cosine, and tangent.

cells.subject: Mathematics Standard 1

members.dotPoint: Express the probability of an event that has a finite number of equally likely outcomes, as number of favourable outcomes
members.title: Basic Probability Calculations
members.exam: Students incorrectly add probabilities when they should multiply for independent events, or forget to simplify fractions to get the final probability in simplest form.
members.summary: Probability equals the count of outcomes you want divided by the count of all possible outcomes, always expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage between 0 and 1.

members.dotPoint: Explain the difference between variables that show correlation and those that have a causal relationship
members.title: Correlation and Causation
members.exam: Students wrongly conclude "smoking causes coffee drinking" from correlation data instead of identifying a confounding variable like age or stress that influences both.
members.summary: Correlation measures association strength but never proves one variable causes another—hidden variables or pure chance can create strong relationships without causation.

members.dotPoint: construct a bivariate scatterplot to identify patterns in the data that suggest the presence of an association (ACMGM052) AAM [Paperclip icon] [ Information and communication technology capability icon]
members.title: Correlation and Scatterplots
members.exam: Examiners commonly test whether students can identify correlation strength from scatterplot patterns and trap students who confuse correlation with causation or who incorrectly claim weak scattered data shows strong correlation.
members.summary: Scatterplots display paired data as points on a graph, revealing positive correlation when both variables increase together, negative correlation when one increases as the other decreases, or no correlation when points appear randomly scattered.

members.dotPoint: Represent equally likely outcomes using arrays and tree diagrams to solve problems, involving replacement where applicable, in two-stage events
members.title: Compound Probability and Tree Diagrams
members.exam: Students add probabilities along branches instead of multiplying them, or forget to add the probabilities of different paths that lead to the same final outcome.
members.summary: Tree diagrams show sequential events as branches where you multiply probabilities along each path to find the probability of that complete sequence occurring.

members.dotPoint: Recognise that probabilities range from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) and can be represented as fractions, decimals and percentages
members.title: The Language of Chance
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly convert between forms and interpret statements like "70% chance of rain" in context, with students often confusing "odds" terminology with actual probability.
members.summary: Probability language ranges from impossible (0) through unlikely, even chance (0.5), likely, to certain (1), and can be expressed interchangeably as fractions, decimals, or percentages.

members.title: Quadratic Relationships
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can find the axis of symmetry and vertex coordinates correctly, with common errors including sign mistakes in x = -b/2a or forgetting to substitute back to find the y-coordinate.
members.summary: Quadratic relationships follow y = ax² + bx + c where the sign of a determines upward or downward opening, and the vertex formula x = -b/2a locates the turning point.

members.dotPoint: use an exponential model to solve problems AAM [Paperclip icon]
members.title: Exponential and Reciprocal Relationships
members.exam: Students often confuse exponential decay (0 < b < 1) with negative exponential growth, or incorrectly identify asymptotes in reciprocal functions when translations are applied.
members.summary: Exponential functions show constant percentage change and have equations of the form y = a × b^x, while reciprocal functions have the form y = k/x and feature asymptotes at x = 0 and y = 0.

members.dotPoint: Develop a pair of simultaneous linear equations to model a practical situation
members.title: Simultaneous Equations and the Break-Even Point
members.exam: Students often confuse which variable represents quantity and which represents dollars, or forget to interpret their solution in context by stating the break-even quantity and corresponding dollar amount.
members.summary: The break-even point occurs where total cost equals total revenue, found by solving two simultaneous linear equations representing cost and revenue as functions of quantity sold.

pick.dotPoint: Solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations using graphical and algebraic methods
pick.title: Linear Relationships

pick.summary: Linear relationships create straight-line graphs where the gradient m shows the rate of change and the y-intercept c shows where the line crosses the vertical axis.

members.dotPoint: Identify an annuity as an investment account with regular, equal contributions and interest compounding at the end of each period, or as a single sum investment from which regular equal withdrawals are made
members.title: Annuities and Perpetuities
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify that a perpetuity requires the withdrawal amount to exactly equal the interest earned each period, not exceed it.
members.summary: An annuity depletes a lump sum by making regular withdrawals that exceed the interest earned, while a perpetuity only withdraws the interest so the principal remains intact forever.

members.dotPoint: solve practical problems involving compounding, for example determine the impact of inflation on prices and wages AAM [Paperclip icon] [ Information and communication technology capability icon] [Personal and social capability icon]
members.title: Compound Interest
members.exam: Students often forget to convert percentage rates to decimals or mismatch time periods with compounding frequency, such as using years when interest compounds monthly.
members.summary: Compound interest means interest earns interest because the balance grows each period, calculated using A = P(1 + r)^n where the exponent n makes growth exponential rather than linear.

members.dotPoint: Apply the straight-line depreciation method to calculate the depreciation of an asset using the formula S = V0 ― Dn where S = salvage value, V0 = initial value of the asset, D = depreciation amount per time period and n = number of time periods
members.title: Depreciation
members.exam: Students confuse which method to apply or incorrectly use the original purchase price instead of the current value when calculating reducing balance depreciation.
members.summary: Flat rate depreciation subtracts the same dollar amount each period using V = P - DN, while reducing balance depreciation applies a fixed percentage decrease each period to the remaining value.

members.dotPoint: recognise credit cards as an example of a reducing balance loan and solve practical problems relating to credit cards AAM
members.title: Reducing Balance Loans
members.exam: Examiners test whether students subtract the payment after applying interest not before, and whether they recognise that final payments may be smaller when the remaining balance is less than the regular payment.
members.summary: The balance after each payment equals the previous balance multiplied by one plus the interest rate then decreased by the fixed payment amount, gradually reducing principal over time.

members.dotPoint: Calculate simple interest for different rates and time periods using the formula I = Prn where I
members.title: Simple Interest
members.exam: Students mix up simple and compound interest formulas or fail to align time units with the rate period, such as using months when the rate is annual.
members.summary: Simple interest calculates interest only on the original principal using I = PRT, producing linear growth because the same dollar amount is added each period regardless of accumulated interest.

members.dotPoint: work with shares and calculate the appreciated value of items, for example antiques AAM [ Information and communication technology capability icon] [Personal and social capability icon]
members.title: Shares, Dividends and Appreciated Value
members.exam: Students frequently calculate dividend yield using the purchase price instead of current market price, or forget to annualise dividends paid quarterly or half-yearly before computing yield.
members.summary: Shares represent fractional ownership of a company where dividends are periodic cash payments to shareholders and dividend yield expresses annual dividend as a percentage of the current share price, while capital appreciation measures price growth.

cells.bigIdea: Every problem here is the same machine: money left alone grows by earning on its own growth, and the only real question is which way it's pointing at you. Compound interest, a loan, a share portfolio — all of them are that engine running forward or in reverse. Find the rate, the time, and whose side the growth is on.

cells.subject: Mathematics Standard 2

members.dotPoint: solve practical problems involving ratio, for example capture-recapture, mixtures for building materials or cost per item AAM [Critical and creative thinking icon] [ Information and communication technology capability icon]
members.title: Practical Ratio Problems and Capture-Recapture
members.exam: Students commonly confuse the order of ratio terms or fail to account for tagged animals already in the second sample when calculating total population in capture-recapture problems.
members.summary: Ratios maintain constant proportional relationships and can be used to estimate unknown quantities from partial samples, whether scaling distances on maps or estimating wildlife populations from tagged-and-recaptured animals.

members.dotPoint: solve practical problems involving Pythagoras’ theorem, the trigonometry of right-angled and non-right-angled triangles, angles of elevation and depression and the use of true bearings and compass bearings AAM [Paperclip icon] [Critical and creative thinking icon]
members.title: Bearings, Elevation and Compass Radial Surveys
members.exam: Students frequently subtract bearings in the wrong order when finding the angle between two directions, or forget that a back bearing differs from the forward bearing by exactly 180 degrees.
members.summary: Bearings measure direction as angles clockwise from north, elevation angles measure upward slope from horizontal, and radial surveys use distance and bearing from one central point to map surrounding locations.

members.dotPoint: use technology to investigate the sign of sin A and cos A for 0^(∘) ≤ A ≤ 180^(∘) [Critical and creative thinking icon] [ Information and communication technology capability icon]
members.title: Trigonometry of Non-Right-Angled Triangles
members.exam: Examiners test whether students choose cosine rule when given two sides and the included angle versus sine rule when given two angles and a side, and watch for ambiguous case errors when sine of an angle could give two different triangles.
members.summary: The sine rule connects sides and their opposite angles, the cosine rule finds a side from two sides and the included angle, and both work for any triangle shape without needing a right angle.

members.dotPoint: review and use the trigonometric ratios to find the length of an unknown side or the size of an unknown angle in a right-angled triangle AAM [Paperclip icon]
members.title: Pythagoras Theorem and Trigonometric Ratios
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can identify which side is the hypotenuse correctly, as many incorrectly apply the theorem by placing a non-hypotenuse value as c in the equation.
members.summary: Pythagoras theorem relates the three sides of right-angled triangles through the equation a² + b² = c², while trigonometric ratios connect angles to side ratios using sine, cosine, and tangent.

cells.subject: Mathematics Standard 2

members.dotPoint: solve small-scale network flow problems, including the use of the ‘maximum-flow minimum-cut’ theorem, for example determining the maximum volume of oil that can flow through a network of pipes from an oil storage tank (the source) to a terminal (the sink) (ACMGM109) AAM
members.title: Network Flow and the Maximum-Flow Minimum-Cut Theorem
members.exam: Students often forget to check all possible cuts systematically or incorrectly identify cuts by only looking at obvious bottlenecks rather than calculating capacity sums for every source-sink partition.
members.summary: The maximum flow through a network from source to sink equals the minimum capacity of any cut that separates source from sink, meaning the bottleneck determines total throughput.

members.dotPoint: Construct a network diagram from a precedence table or equivalent, including those involving dummy activities, limited to 10 activities
members.title: Network Flow and Critical Path Analysis
members.exam: Students often miscalculate float time by forgetting that float equals latest start time minus earliest start time, or they identify non-critical paths as critical when multiple paths exist.
members.summary: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities from start to finish, determining minimum project completion time, with activities on this path having zero float.

members.dotPoint: determine the minimum spanning tree of a given network with weighted edges AAM
members.title: Minimum Spanning Trees
members.exam: Students frequently forget to check for cycles when applying Kruskal's algorithm, incorrectly adding an edge that would create a loop, or they miscalculate the final total weight.
members.summary: Minimum spanning trees connect all vertices with the minimum total edge weight without forming cycles, found using either Prim's algorithm (growing from one vertex) or Kruskal's algorithm (adding cheapest edges while avoiding cycles).

members.dotPoint: Calculate float times to identify critical and non-critical activities
members.title: Project Scheduling and Critical Path
members.exam: Students make arithmetic errors in backward scanning by forgetting to subtract task durations, or fail to identify all tasks on the critical path when multiple parallel paths exist.
members.summary: Critical path analysis uses forward scanning to find earliest start times and backward scanning for latest start times, with the critical path being the sequence of tasks with zero float time.

cells.bigIdea: A network is a diagram that turns a real system — roads, pipes, cables, schedules — into dots and weighted lines, and every question is about optimising one thing along those lines. Either you connect everything for the least total cost (spanning tree) or you push the most through a fixed structure (flow). The bottleneck is always the answer.

cells.subject: Mathematics Standard 2

members.dotPoint: Explain the difference between variables that show correlation and those that have a causal relationship
members.title: Correlation and Causation
members.exam: Students wrongly conclude "smoking causes coffee drinking" from correlation data instead of identifying a confounding variable like age or stress that influences both.
members.summary: Correlation measures association strength but never proves one variable causes another—hidden variables or pure chance can create strong relationships without causation.

members.dotPoint: construct a bivariate scatterplot to identify patterns in the data that suggest the presence of an association (ACMGM052) AAM [Paperclip icon] [ Information and communication technology capability icon]
members.title: Correlation and Scatterplots
members.exam: Examiners commonly test whether students can identify correlation strength from scatterplot patterns and trap students who confuse correlation with causation or who incorrectly claim weak scattered data shows strong correlation.
members.summary: Scatterplots display paired data as points on a graph, revealing positive correlation when both variables increase together, negative correlation when one increases as the other decreases, or no correlation when points appear randomly scattered.

members.dotPoint: Construct and use arrays, tree diagrams and probability trees to determine the outcomes and probabilities for multistage events
members.title: Compound Probability and Tree Diagrams
members.exam: Students add probabilities along branches instead of multiplying them, or forget to add the probabilities of different paths that lead to the same final outcome.
members.summary: Tree diagrams show sequential events as branches where you multiply probabilities along each path to find the probability of that complete sequence occurring.

members.dotPoint: Determine the equation of the least-squares regression line for a bivariate dataset using a scientific calculator
members.title: Least Squares Regression
members.exam: Students forget to interpret the slope in context—writing "the slope is 2.3" instead of "for every extra hour studied, the test score increases by 2.3 marks.
members.summary: The least squares line minimises the sum of squared residuals and its equation y = a + bx lets you predict y-values, with the slope b showing the rate of change.

members.dotPoint: Model and apply the empirical rule, where approximately 68% of data will have z-scores between −1 and 1, approximately 95% of data will have z-scores between −2 and 2, and approximately 99.7% of data will have z-scores between −3 and 3
members.title: The 68-95-99.7 Rule
members.exam: Students miscalculate percentages outside intervals—forgetting that "more than one SD above" is 16% not 32%, because they forget the distribution is symmetric and only count one tail.
members.summary: In normal distributions, approximately 68% of data sits within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three standard deviations.

members.dotPoint: calculate the z-score (standardised score) corresponding to a particular value in a dataset AAM [Paperclip icon]
members.title: The Standard Normal Distribution and Z-Scores
members.exam: Students frequently make sign errors when calculating z-scores for values below the mean, forgetting that these should be negative z-values.
members.summary: The formula z = (x - μ)/σ converts any normal distribution to standard normal with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, enabling comparison across different scales.

cells.bigIdea: Both halves of this topic ask one thing: where does a single point sit against the pattern? A scatterplot places it against the trend of the pair; a z-score places it against the spread of the group. Read the position and you've read the data — that's the whole move.

cells.subject: Modern History

members.dotPoint: differing visions and role of leadership
members.title: Organizational Structures and Leadership Models
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can compare specific organizational models like the NAACP's formal hierarchy versus SNCC's decentralized structure and explain how these affected their effectiveness during the Civil Rights Movement.
members.summary: Movements structure themselves hierarchically with designated leaders or horizontally through consensus-based collectives, with each model offering different advantages for sustaining campaigns and responding to challenges.

members.dotPoint: international responses to apartheid
members.title: International pressure and the outside world
members.exam: Students assume international pressure always mattered; examiners test whether you can assess when it was effective versus performative, and what domestic conditions made external pressure work.
members.summary: This concept tracks when external forces—UN resolutions, economic sanctions, media coverage, diaspora campaigns, or foreign governments—actually influenced domestic change versus when they were ignored or symbolic.

members.dotPoint: nature of post-Soviet Russia and Eastern Europe
members.title: Shifting centres of global power
members.exam: Students narrate events without connecting them to power shifts; examiners test whether you can explain how specific events redistributed influence and altered which nations shaped international decisions.
members.summary: This concept maps the redistribution of global influence from postwar US-Soviet bipolarity through decolonisation, Cold War proxy conflicts, Soviet collapse, and the emergence of China, the EU, and regional powers.

members.dotPoint: role and impact of state terror and repression
members.title: State power: repression, control and response
members.exam: Students often describe repression without linking it to movement responses; examiners want analysis of how state tactics changed as resistance grew, not just lists of what governments did.
members.summary: This concept examines the tools governments use to suppress dissent—surveillance, censorship, military force, detention without trial—and how these tactics evolve when movements push back or gain ground.

members.dotPoint: Permanent Revolution, competing versions of Marxism and anti-revisionism
members.title: The Cultural Revolution and How Revolutionary China Was
members.exam: Examiners look for balanced evaluation of revolutionary achievements versus human costs—students often judge the entire revolution solely through Cultural Revolution violence or ignore terror entirely.
members.summary: The Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976 saw Mao unleash Red Guards to attack the party itself, creating chaos and terror that only ended with his death.

members.dotPoint: nature of the early democracy in Burma
members.title: Origins and Catalysts of Social Movements
members.exam: Students often describe only the immediate trigger event without analyzing underlying structural conditions or why that particular moment created opportunity for mobilization rather than earlier periods.
members.summary: Social movements emerge when long-standing grievances combine with triggering events, emerging leaders, and political opportunities that convince people collective action is both necessary and potentially successful.

members.dotPoint: reaction of military leaders in response to the pro-democracy movement
members.title: Strategies and Tactics of Resistance
members.exam: Examiners look for analysis of why movements shifted tactics over time rather than just listing methods, and students frequently fail to explain strategic reasoning behind tactical choices or responses to government countermeasures.
members.summary: Movements choose between nonviolent civil disobedience, legal challenges, economic boycotts, armed resistance, or combinations thereof based on assessments of what will achieve goals while maintaining support and minimizing state repression.

members.dotPoint: the nature of social and political change
members.title: Measuring change: what actually shifted
members.exam: Students list changes without evaluating depth or permanence; examiners want evidence-based judgment on whether change was cosmetic, partial, or fundamental, with specific criteria applied.
members.summary: This concept requires distinguishing between superficial reform and structural transformation by examining legal change, power redistribution, lived experience, and whether old systems persisted under new names.

cells.bigIdea: Change is a contest, not an event. Something pushes — a movement, a superpower, a new world order — and something pushes back, usually the state. The skill examined here is measuring what shifted when the dust settled, and what only looked like it had.
