cells.subject: Modern History
cells.topic: Core Study: Power and Authority in the Modern World 1919–1946

members.dotPoint: Frame questions to guide historical inquiry and develop a coherent research plan
members.title: Running a historical investigation
members.exam: Students commonly lose marks by jumping straight to research without establishing a clear question first, or by failing to properly reference sources and acknowledge limitations in their evidence base.
members.summary: Historical investigation begins with formulating a focused research question, then systematically gathering and evaluating diverse sources while maintaining proper citations and acknowledging different perspectives throughout the inquiry process.

members.dotPoint: opposition to the Nazi regime [Critical and creative thinking icon]
members.title: Opposition and Resistance to the Nazi Regime
members.exam: Students exaggerate the scale or effectiveness of resistance movements, or list examples without explaining why opposition remained fragmented and unable to threaten Nazi power until military defeat loomed.
members.summary: Opposition to the Nazis ranged from individual acts to organised plots but was limited by terror, surveillance and lack of mass support, with most resistance coming too late or crushed immediately.

members.dotPoint: analyses and interprets different types of sources for evidence to support an historical account or argument MH12-6
members.title: Source Analysis Framework and Methodology
members.exam: Examiners assess whether students can distinguish between a source's reliability for certain purposes versus others, with students often incorrectly labelling sources as wholly reliable or unreliable rather than conditional.
members.summary: Historians systematically evaluate sources by examining origin, purpose, audience, perspective, reliability, and usefulness, combining content analysis with contextual understanding to construct evidence-based historical arguments.

members.dotPoint: an overview of the peace treaties which ended World War I and their consequences (ACHMH130)
members.title: The Post-War Peace Treaties and Their Consequences
members.exam: Students focus only on Versailles without addressing Saint-Germain, Trianon or Sevres, or assert the treaty caused World War Two without evaluating how Hitler exploited rather than merely responded to genuine grievances.
members.summary: The Paris peace treaties ending World War One imposed territorial losses, reparations and blame on defeated powers, creating resentment particularly in Germany while redrawing European borders and planting seeds for future conflict.

members.dotPoint: an overview of the search for peace and security 1919–1946:
members.title: The Search for Peace and Security 1919-1946
members.exam: Students claim the League was doomed from the start without analysing specific failures like Manchuria and Abyssinia, or assume the UN succeeded simply by existing rather than examining how Cold War paralysed it.
members.summary: The League of Nations failed to prevent aggression due to absent great powers, lack of enforcement mechanisms and unwillingness to act, leading the United Nations to incorporate compulsory membership, veto powers and clearer intervention authority.

members.dotPoint: the conditions that enabled dictators to rise to power in the interwar period (ACHMH130, ACHMH136, ACHMH138) [Critical and creative thinking icon]
members.title: The Rise of Interwar Dictatorships in Russia, Italy and Japan
members.exam: Students treat fascism and communism as identical, or list factors without explaining how each dictatorship emerged from specific national circumstances while sharing common patterns of paramilitary violence and propaganda.
members.summary: Russia, Italy and Japan developed dictatorships by exploiting post-war instability, economic crisis and nationalist resentment, each rejecting liberal democracy in favour of authoritarian control justified by ideology and leader cult.

members.dotPoint: Develop texts, particularly historical accounts and arguments, supported by relevant evidence from sources
members.title: Building a historical argument
members.exam: Examiners penalise students who merely describe events or list sources instead of using evidence to build an analytical argument that directly addresses the question with a clear position.
members.summary: Historical arguments require students to use primary and secondary sources as evidence to construct a coherent thesis that answers a specific question about the past, then present it appropriately for their intended audience.

members.dotPoint: plans and conducts historical investigations and presents reasoned conclusions, using relevant evidence from a range of sources MH12-8
members.title: Contextualization and Corroboration Techniques
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain why a source's perspective differs from modern views due to its time period, or students fail by dismissing historical sources as simply wrong instead of contextually understanding them.
members.summary: Historians must analyse sources within their original historical context rather than applying modern values, while corroboration compares multiple sources to verify information and identify bias or gaps.

members.dotPoint: the impact of the Nazi regime on life in Germany, including cultural expression, religion, workers, youth, women, minorities including Jews (ACHMH131, ACHMH132) [Critical and creative thinking icon] [Ethical understanding icon] [Intercultural understanding icon] [Literacy icon] [Difference and diversity icon] [Work and enterprise]
members.title: Life Under the Nazi Regime
members.exam: Students often describe persecution generically without showing the progression from legal exclusion (Nuremberg Laws) to Kristallnacht violence to systematic extermination, or fail to explain how gleichschaltung enforced conformity.
members.summary: The Nazi regime controlled daily life through mass organisations and propaganda while systematically persecuting Jews, Roma, disabled people and political opponents through exclusion, violence and eventually genocide.

members.dotPoint: discusses and evaluates differing interpretations and representations of the past MH12-7
members.title: Historiography and Interpretive Debates
members.exam: Students must identify how historians' arguments differ and explain why these differences exist, but commonly fail by treating one interpretation as correct rather than analysing the validity of competing perspectives.
members.summary: Different historians interpret the same historical events differently based on their time period, cultural background, available evidence, and theoretical frameworks, creating ongoing debates about historical meaning.

members.dotPoint: discusses and evaluates differing interpretations and representations of the past MH12-7
members.title: Why Historians Disagree
members.exam: Top students name specific historians and their interpretations, showing why they disagree, while weak answers pretend one narrative exists or list facts without acknowledging scholarly debate.
members.summary: Historians reach different conclusions about the same revolution because they prioritise different evidence, approach events from different eras and political perspectives, and ask different questions of the past.

members.dotPoint: the rise of the Nazi party and Hitler in Germany and the collapse of the Weimar Republic (ACHMH129, ACHMH130) [Critical and creative thinking icon]
members.title: The Collapse of the Weimar Republic and the Rise of the Nazi Party
members.exam: Students blame Versailles alone without explaining how Article 48, proportional representation, elite conservative enabling, depression unemployment and Nazi propaganda tactics combined to create Hitler's opportunity in 1933.
members.summary: The Weimar Republic collapsed under combined pressure from Treaty of Versailles resentment, economic crises, political polarisation and elite miscalculation, allowing Hitler's Nazis to gain power through legal means then dismantle democracy.

members.dotPoint: analyses and interprets different types of sources for evidence to support an historical account or argument MH12-6
members.title: Reading Primary Sources
members.exam: The fatal error is quoting sources as pure facts without analysing who created them, why, for whom, or what bias and limitations affect their usefulness as evidence.
members.summary: Primary sources are created documents with authors, audiences and agendas, not objective windows into the past, and must be interrogated for perspective and reliability.

members.dotPoint: the nature of Nazi ideology (ACHMH130, ACHMH132) [Critical and creative thinking icon] [Ethical understanding icon]
members.title: The Nature of Nazi Ideology
members.exam: Students describe Nazi racism without connecting it to Lebensraum expansionism and social Darwinism, or fail to explain how Fuhrerprinzip justified removing democratic checks and enabled radicalisation toward genocide.
members.summary: Nazi ideology centred on racial hierarchy with Aryans supreme, demanded living space through expansion, promised national community excluding outsiders, and concentrated absolute authority in the Fuhrer as embodiment of the racial will.

pick.dotPoint: Frame questions to guide historical inquiry and develop a coherent research plan
pick.title: Running a historical investigation
pick.exam: Students commonly lose marks by jumping straight to research without establishing a clear question first, or by failing to properly reference sources and acknowledge limitations in their evidence base.
pick.summary: Historical investigation begins with formulating a focused research question, then systematically gathering and evaluating diverse sources while maintaining proper citations and acknowledging different perspectives throughout the inquiry process.

runnersUp.dotPoint: opposition to the Nazi regime [Critical and creative thinking icon]
runnersUp.title: Opposition and Resistance to the Nazi Regime
runnersUp.exam: Students exaggerate the scale or effectiveness of resistance movements, or list examples without explaining why opposition remained fragmented and unable to threaten Nazi power until military defeat loomed.
runnersUp.summary: Opposition to the Nazis ranged from individual acts to organised plots but was limited by terror, surveillance and lack of mass support, with most resistance coming too late or crushed immediately.

runnersUp.dotPoint: analyses and interprets different types of sources for evidence to support an historical account or argument MH12-6
runnersUp.title: Source Analysis Framework and Methodology
runnersUp.exam: Examiners assess whether students can distinguish between a source's reliability for certain purposes versus others, with students often incorrectly labelling sources as wholly reliable or unreliable rather than conditional.
runnersUp.summary: Historians systematically evaluate sources by examining origin, purpose, audience, perspective, reliability, and usefulness, combining content analysis with contextual understanding to construct evidence-based historical arguments.

runnersUp.dotPoint: an overview of the peace treaties which ended World War I and their consequences (ACHMH130)
runnersUp.title: The Post-War Peace Treaties and Their Consequences
runnersUp.exam: Students focus only on Versailles without addressing Saint-Germain, Trianon or Sevres, or assert the treaty caused World War Two without evaluating how Hitler exploited rather than merely responded to genuine grievances.
runnersUp.summary: The Paris peace treaties ending World War One imposed territorial losses, reparations and blame on defeated powers, creating resentment particularly in Germany while redrawing European borders and planting seeds for future conflict.

cells.bigIdea: No dictator here seized power — each was handed it, step by visible step, by crisis, fear and democracies that stopped defending themselves. Learn that machinery and 1919–1946 becomes one process you can trace, source by source.
cells.bigIdeaKey: Modern History/Core Study: Power and Authority in the Modern World 1919–1946

cells.subject: Modern History

members.dotPoint: Bolshevik ideology in theory and practice
members.title: How a regime consolidates power
members.exam: Students confuse gaining power with consolidating it, or describe repressive tactics without explaining how they systematically secured the regime's survival against rivals.
members.summary: Methods regimes use after seizing power to eliminate opposition, control institutions, monopolise violence and entrench authority through legal, coercive or democratic means.

members.dotPoint: role and impact of the leadership of Mao Zedong and Chiang Kai-shek
members.title: Leadership: the leader or the moment?
members.exam: Students write biographies instead of analysing whether structural conditions or personal agency determined outcomes, failing to weigh context against individual action.
members.summary: Whether historical figures shaped their era or were elevated by circumstances already in motion, testing if individuals drive change or reflect deeper forces.

members.dotPoint: visions for India post-independence
members.title: Holding a nation together
members.exam: Students assume national unity existed naturally rather than analysing deliberate state strategies, or ignore separatist movements and internal resistance to centralisation.
members.summary: How governments use nationalism, propaganda, language policy, education and force to create unified identity against regional, ethnic, religious or class divisions.

members.dotPoint: economic transformation under Stalin and its impact on Soviet society, including collectivisation and the five-year plans
members.title: Economic transformation and who pays for it
members.exam: Students describe economic programs without analysing who funded them, or assume transformation benefited everyone equally without examining peasants, workers or regional disparities.
members.summary: How industrialisation, collectivisation, modernisation or resource booms are funded and which social groups bear the costs through taxes, labour or displacement.

members.dotPoint: social tensions, including immigration restrictions, religious fundamentalism, Prohibition, crime, racial conflict, anti-communism and anti-unionism
members.title: Society under pressure: who gains and who loses
members.exam: Students describe change generally without identifying specific winners and losers, or ignore groups deliberately excluded from benefits like women or minorities.
members.summary: How political, economic or social upheaval redistributes power, wealth and rights unevenly across classes, regions, genders and ethnic groups.

members.dotPoint: Bolshevik ideology in theory and practice
members.title: Ideology in theory and in practice
members.exam: Students only describe ideology without comparing theory to practice, or fail to explain why gaps emerged between rhetoric and reality.
members.summary: The distance between a movement's stated principles and its actual policies once in government, measuring hypocrisy, pragmatism or radicalisation.

members.dotPoint: aims and strategies of Indian foreign policy 1947–1984, including non-alignment and the Panchsheel Treaty 1954
members.title: Foreign policy: aims, ideology and effectiveness
members.exam: Students narrate events without assessing effectiveness, or separate ideology from foreign policy instead of analysing how beliefs shaped diplomatic and military choices.
members.summary: What a nation sought internationally, how much ideology versus pragmatism shaped decisions, and whether foreign policy achieved its stated goals.

members.dotPoint: Bolshevik ideology in theory and practice
members.title: Lenin, the Bolsheviks and October
members.exam: Students must distinguish between the spontaneous February Revolution and the Bolshevik-planned October coup, not treating them as a single continuous revolution.
members.summary: The Provisional Government's decision to continue World War I while delaying land reform allowed Lenin's Bolsheviks to seize power through the Military Revolutionary Committee in October 1917.

members.dotPoint: impact of crises on changing superpower relations
members.title: Turning points and crises
members.exam: Students identify turning points without explaining what actually changed afterward or why that moment mattered more than others, relying on assertion over evidence.
members.summary: Certain battles, decisions or events shifted a conflict's trajectory, though historians debate which moments were truly decisive versus merely dramatic.

members.dotPoint: emerging differences between the superpowers
members.title: Origins and escalation of conflict
members.exam: Students confuse the immediate trigger with deeper causes, or list causes without explaining how one event led to another in a chain of escalation.
members.summary: Conflicts rarely ignite suddenly; they build through underlying tensions, specific triggers and chains of escalation that historians can trace across different wars.

members.dotPoint: reasons for the end of the Cold War
members.title: How conflicts end: victory, defeat and peacemaking
members.exam: Students describe peace treaties without evaluating their effectiveness or assume formal surrender always means genuine resolution of underlying conflict.
members.summary: Wars end through military victory, negotiated settlement or exhaustion, but the manner of ending shapes whether peace is stable or merely postponed.

members.dotPoint: attempts at peacemaking and nation-building
members.title: Outside powers and international bodies
members.exam: Students narrate what outside powers did without explaining why they intervened or fail to evaluate whether intervention helped or hindered peace.
members.summary: External nations and organisations shape conflicts through intervention, economic support, peacekeeping or constraint, pursuing their own strategic interests alongside stated principles.

members.dotPoint: changing policies, strategies and responses to the Cold War
members.title: Aims, strategies and tactics in conflict
members.exam: Students describe what happened in battle without explaining the strategic intention behind it or evaluating whether tactics actually advanced stated aims.
members.summary: Each side enters conflict with objectives, develops strategies to achieve them and adapts tactics when reality forces revision of original plans.

members.dotPoint: the nature and effects of the Holocaust in the Nazi-occupied territories
members.title: Civilians and the home front
members.exam: Students describe only military events or only hardship without linking civilian experience to broader war outcomes or analysing agency and collaboration.
members.summary: War reshapes entire societies, affecting civilians through occupation, rationing, propaganda, resistance movements and long-term trauma that outlasts armistice.

members.dotPoint: influence of the ideologies of communism and capitalism on the Cold War
members.title: Ideology and identity as drivers of conflict
members.exam: Students list ideologies present without explaining how they drove specific decisions or fail to distinguish between genuine belief and cynical propaganda.
members.summary: Political ideologies and group identities motivate combatants, justify violence to populations and define who counts as enemy, ally or victim.

cells.bigIdea: Every conflict here runs the same arc: it starts, escalates, turns, reaches civilians, draws in outsiders, and ends — or half-ends. Your war fills in the names; the arc is what gets examined.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: analyse the operation of simple DC and AC generators and AC induction motors (ACSPH110)
members.title: AC Generators and Transformers
members.exam: Students often incorrectly assume transformers work with DC current or forget that maximum emf occurs when the coil is parallel to the field (maximum rate of flux change), not perpendicular.
members.summary: AC generators convert mechanical energy to electrical energy through electromagnetic induction as a rotating coil experiences continuous flux changes, while transformers transfer AC power between circuits using mutual induction with different numbers of turns to step voltage up or down.

members.dotPoint: relate Lenz's Law to the law of conservation of energy and apply the law of conservation of energy to:
members.title: Lenz's Law and Energy Conservation
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly predict current direction using the right-hand rule after identifying whether flux is increasing or decreasing through a loop.
members.summary: Lenz's Law states that induced currents always flow in a direction to create magnetic fields opposing the change in flux that produced them, which is necessary to conserve energy in the system.

members.dotPoint: investigate the operation of a simple DC motor to analyse:
members.title: Motional EMF in a Conductor
members.exam: Students often forget that the conductor must cut across field lines, not move parallel to them, or they miss that emf equals BLv only when motion is perpendicular to the field.
members.summary: A conductor cutting through field lines experiences charge separation as the magnetic force pushes electrons to one end, producing emf equal to the product of field strength, length, and velocity.

members.dotPoint: investigate the operation of a simple DC motor to analyse:
members.title: How a DC Motor Works
members.exam: Students cannot explain why the commutator is necessary or what happens without it, missing that continuous rotation requires force direction to flip.
members.summary: Opposite sides of a current loop in a magnetic field experience opposite forces creating torque, with a commutator reversing current every half turn to maintain rotation.

cells.bigIdea: A motor and a generator are the same machine run in opposite directions: current-in makes turning, turning makes current. And the machine always fights itself — every motor generates a back emf, every generator resists being turned, because Lenz's Law is conservation of energy wearing work clothes.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: model qualitatively and quantitatively the trajectories of charged particles in electric fields and compare them with the trajectories of projectiles in a gravitational field
members.title: Comparing the Three Fields
members.exam: Students forget that magnetic fields do no work because force is always perpendicular to displacement, while gravitational and electric fields can do work.
members.summary: Gravitational fields only attract, electric fields attract or repel depending on charge sign, and magnetic fields only act on moving charges or currents.

members.dotPoint: investigate and quantitatively derive and analyse the interaction between charged particles and uniform electric fields, including: (ACSPH083)
members.title: Uniform Fields Between Parallel Plates
members.exam: Students forget that uniform field means constant acceleration, so they can use kinematic equations directly for electron motion between plates.
members.summary: Parallel charged plates create a uniform electric field E equals V over d between them, meaning constant force and constant acceleration for any charge placed inside.

members.dotPoint: analyse the interaction between charged particles and uniform magnetic fields, including: (ACSPH083)
members.title: Force on a Moving Charge
members.exam: Students incorrectly claim the magnetic force does work or changes kinetic energy, forgetting that perpendicular forces never change speed.
members.summary: A charge moving through a magnetic field experiences force F equals qvB sine theta perpendicular to both velocity and field, causing circular motion at constant speed.

pick.dotPoint: analyse the interaction between charged particles and uniform magnetic fields, including: (ACSPH083)
pick.title: Force on a Moving Charge
pick.exam: Students incorrectly claim the magnetic force does work or changes kinetic energy, forgetting that perpendicular forces never change speed.
pick.summary: A charge moving through a magnetic field experiences force F equals qvB sine theta perpendicular to both velocity and field, causing circular motion at constant speed.

altPick.summary: Gravitational fields only attract, electric fields attract or repel depending on charge sign, and magnetic fields only act on moving charges or currents.

cells.bigIdea: A field is a region that pushes. Electric fields push charges along themselves and trade voltage for speed; magnetic fields only ever push sideways, turning paths into circles. Watch the trajectory: a parabola says electric, a circle says magnetic — same charge, two signatures.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: conduct investigations to explain and evaluate, for objects executing uniform circular motion, the relationships that exist between:
members.title: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force
members.exam: Students wrongly add centripetal force as an extra force on free body diagrams instead of identifying tension, friction, gravity components or normal force as the actual source.
members.summary: Centripetal force is not a new force but the name for whichever real force or force component points toward the centre of the circular path.

members.dotPoint: analyse the forces acting on an object executing uniform circular motion in a variety of situations, for example:
members.title: Vertical Circles and Inclined Planes
members.exam: Examiners test minimum speed at the top of a loop where tension can drop to zero, or ask about normal force on inclines where students forget to resolve weight perpendicular and parallel.
members.summary: In vertical circles the required centripetal force changes with position because gravity adds or subtracts from other forces depending on whether the object is at the top or bottom.

members.dotPoint: investigate the relationship between the rotation of mechanical systems and the applied torque
members.title: Torque and Rotational Systems
members.exam: Students commonly forget to use only the perpendicular component of force when calculating torque, or they incorrectly add torques without considering clockwise versus anticlockwise direction signs.
members.summary: Torque is the rotational equivalent of force, calculated as the product of force and perpendicular distance from the pivot point, and it determines whether objects rotate or remain in rotational equilibrium.

cells.bigIdea: Nothing here moves in a straight line because something is always pulling it inward — and if it spins instead of travels, that same pull becomes a twist around a point. Every question hands you a force and asks where it points: to the centre, or around it. Name the direction and the motion is solved.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: investigate the operation and role of particle accelerators in obtaining evidence that tests and/or validates aspects of theories, including the Standard Model of matter (ACSPH120, ACSPH121, ACSPH122, ACSPH146)
members.title: Particle Accelerators
members.exam: Students often confuse the roles of electric and magnetic fields, forgetting that only electric fields do work to increase kinetic energy while magnetic fields only change direction without adding energy.
members.summary: Particle accelerators use electric fields to accelerate charged particles to high speeds and magnetic fields to confine them, allowing high-energy collisions that create new particles according to mass-energy equivalence.

members.dotPoint: investigate the Standard Model of matter, including:
members.title: The Standard Model: Quarks and Leptons
members.exam: Examiners test whether students know quarks cannot exist in isolation due to confinement and often present hadron compositions requiring students to identify valid quark combinations using charge and baryon number conservation.
members.summary: Quarks are fundamental particles that combine in groups of three to form baryons like protons and neutrons, or in quark-antiquark pairs to form mesons, while leptons like electrons exist independently.

members.dotPoint: investigate the Standard Model of matter, including:
members.title: Nuclear Structure and the Strong Nuclear Force
members.exam: Students commonly confuse the relative strengths of forces or incorrectly state that the strong force operates at long ranges, and examiners test understanding that beyond the short range the electromagnetic repulsion dominates causing instability in large nuclei.
members.summary: The strong nuclear force overcomes electrostatic repulsion between protons but only operates at distances less than about 3 femtometers, being approximately 100 times stronger than electromagnetic force at this range.

cells.bigIdea: Protons and neutrons aren't the bottom — they're bags of quarks, and the Standard Model is the full parts list of matter. The rule of discovery here is brutal and simple: to see smaller, hit harder. Accelerators are microscopes made of energy, and every collision is a question put directly to the universe.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: analyse qualitatively and quantitatively, with reference to energy transfers and transformations, examples of Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt, including but not limited to: (ACSPH081, ACSPH110)
members.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
members.exam: Students frequently forget to include the number of turns N in calculations or misapply the rate of change by using final flux instead of the change per unit time.
members.summary: Faraday's Law quantifies that induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux multiplied by the number of turns, with the negative sign from Lenz's Law indicating the induced emf opposes the flux change.

members.dotPoint: analyse applications of step-up and step-down transformers, including but not limited to:
members.title: Power Transmission and Losses
members.exam: Students commonly fail to recognize that halving current reduces loss by a factor of four, or they incorrectly think voltage level directly affects power loss instead of understanding the current-squared relationship.
members.summary: Since power loss equals current squared times resistance, transmitting at high voltage with low current dramatically reduces energy wasted as heat in power lines.

members.dotPoint: analyse qualitatively and quantitatively, with reference to energy transfers and transformations, examples of Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt, including but not limited to: (ACSPH081, ACSPH110)
members.title: Lenz's Law and Energy Conservation
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly predict current direction using the right-hand rule after identifying whether flux is increasing or decreasing through a loop.
members.summary: Lenz's Law states that induced currents always flow in a direction to create magnetic fields opposing the change in flux that produced them, which is necessary to conserve energy in the system.

members.dotPoint: describe how magnetic flux can change, with reference to the relationship Φ = B_(∥)A = BAcosθ (ACSPH083, ACSPH107, ACSPH109)
members.title: Magnetic Flux and Flux Linkage
members.exam: Students commonly use the wrong angle, forgetting that θ is measured between the field and the normal to the surface, not between the field and the plane itself.
members.summary: Magnetic flux measures the total magnetic field passing through a surface and equals Φ = BAcosθ, while flux linkage is the total flux through all turns of a coil calculated as NΦ.

members.dotPoint: evaluate qualitatively the limitations of the ideal transformer model and the strategies used to improve transformer efficiency, including but not limited to:
members.title: Transformers: Ideal Models and Real Losses
members.exam: Students commonly forget that step-up transformers increase voltage but decrease current proportionally, or fail to account for energy losses in real transformers through heat in resistance and eddy currents.
members.summary: Transformers use electromagnetic induction between primary and secondary coils to change voltage levels, with the ratio Vp/Vs = Np/Ns, and in ideal transformers power is conserved so VpIp = VsIs.

pick.dotPoint: analyse qualitatively and quantitatively, with reference to energy transfers and transformations, examples of Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt, including but not limited to: (ACSPH081, ACSPH110)
pick.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
pick.exam: Students frequently forget to include the number of turns N in calculations or misapply the rate of change by using final flux instead of the change per unit time.
pick.summary: Faraday's Law quantifies that induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux multiplied by the number of turns, with the negative sign from Lenz's Law indicating the induced emf opposes the flux change.

cells.bigIdea: Nothing induces a voltage except a change in flux — a steady field does nothing, it's the changing that pays. Every device here is one trick: force flux to change and harvest the EMF, or fake a change through a shared core. Ideal models assume none of it leaks; real ones charge you for the leaks.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: conduct an investigation to examine a variety of spectra produced by discharge tubes, reflected sunlight or incandescent filaments
members.title: Spectroscopy and Spectra
members.exam: Students frequently reverse emission and absorption spectra visually (bright lines versus dark lines on continuous background), or they fail to calculate photon energy correctly using E = hf = hc/λ when given wavelength data from spectral lines.
members.summary: Each element produces unique sharp lines in emission or absorption spectra because electrons jump between fixed energy levels, releasing or absorbing photons with energies exactly matching the energy difference between levels.

members.dotPoint: conduct investigations of historical and contemporary methods used to determine the speed of light and its current relationship to the measurement of time and distance (ACSPH082)
members.title: Measuring the Speed of Light
members.exam: Students incorrectly think light speed was "discovered to be exact" rather than understanding the 1983 redefinition made the metre depend on a fixed c value, or they confuse which historical methods measured astronomical versus laboratory distances.
members.summary: From Galileo's lanterns to Rømer's Jupiter moons to Fizeau's toothed wheels and Michelson's rotating mirrors, increasingly precise experiments converged on c = 299,792,458 m/s until 1983 when the metre was redefined making light speed exact by definition.

members.dotPoint: describe the production and propagation of electromagnetic waves and relate these processes qualitatively to the predictions made by Maxwell’s electromagnetic theory (ACSPH112, ACSPH113)
members.title: Maxwell and Electromagnetic Waves
members.exam: Students often forget that electromagnetic waves require both fields perpendicular to each other AND to the direction of propagation, or incorrectly assume they need a medium like sound waves do.
members.summary: Maxwell showed that a changing electric field creates a magnetic field and vice versa, allowing electromagnetic waves to self-propagate through space at the speed of light without requiring a medium.

cells.bigIdea: Light is a travelling electromagnetic wave, and the light a thing emits or absorbs is a fingerprint of what it's made of. Maxwell tells you the wave exists and how fast it goes; spectra tell you the message it carries. Read the light, read the source — even a star you'll never reach.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: investigate the evidence, from Einstein's thought experiments and subsequent experimental validation, for time dilation t = t₀/√(1 − v²/c²) and length contraction l = l₀√(1 − v²/c²), and analyse quantitatively situations in which these are observed, for example:
members.title: Length Contraction and Relativistic Momentum
members.exam: Students often forget that length contraction only occurs in the direction parallel to motion, not perpendicular, or they incorrectly apply the formula by multiplying L_0 by gamma instead of dividing.
members.summary: Length contraction describes how objects moving at relativistic speeds appear shorter in the direction of motion, while momentum increases beyond classical predictions due to the gamma factor.

members.dotPoint: analyse and evaluate the evidence confirming or denying Einstein's two postulates:
members.title: The Two Postulates of Special Relativity
members.exam: Examiners test whether students understand that the constancy of light speed contradicts everyday intuition about relative velocities, particularly in questions asking why speeds don't simply add when approaching c.
members.summary: Special relativity rests on two postulates: all inertial frames are equivalent for physical laws, and light speed in vacuum is constant at c for all observers regardless of their motion or the source's motion.

members.dotPoint: investigate the evidence, from Einstein's thought experiments and subsequent experimental validation, for time dilation t = t₀/√(1 − v²/c²) and length contraction l = l₀√(1 − v²/c²), and analyse quantitatively situations in which these are observed, for example:
members.title: Time Dilation and the Lorentz Factor
members.exam: Students commonly confuse proper time with dilated time, applying the gamma factor incorrectly by multiplying when they should divide, or failing to identify which observer measures proper time in the rest frame.
members.summary: Time dilation means moving clocks run slower as measured by stationary observers, with the effect quantified by the Lorentz factor gamma equals one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared.

members.dotPoint: Use Einstein's mass–energy equivalence relationship E = mc² to calculate the energy released by processes in which mass is converted to energy, for example: (ACSPH134)
members.title: Mass-Energy Equivalence and Binding Energy Calculations
members.exam: Students often forget to convert mass defect from atomic mass units to kilograms using the conversion factor 1u equals 1.66 times 10 to the negative 27 kilograms before applying E equals mc squared, or they incorrectly calculate mass defect by subtracting in the wrong direction.
members.summary: The mass defect is converted to binding energy according to Einstein's equation E equals mc squared, representing the energy needed to completely separate all nucleons in a nucleus.

cells.bigIdea: The speed of light refuses to change, so everything else does. Hold c constant for every observer and time stretches, lengths shrink and mass becomes energy — not as tricks, but as the price of one stubborn constant. Muons reach the ground on borrowed time; E = mc² is the exchange rate.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: investigate the evidence from photoelectric effect investigations that demonstrated inconsistency with the wave model for light (ACSPH087, ACSPH123, ACSPH137)
members.title: The Photoelectric Effect
members.exam: Students wrongly predict that brighter low-frequency light will eventually eject electrons, missing that frequency determines whether ejection occurs at all.
members.summary: Light ejects electrons from metal surfaces instantaneously when photon energy exceeds the work function, with excess energy becoming the electron's kinetic energy.

members.dotPoint: analyse the photoelectric effect Kmax = hf − φ as it occurs in metallic elements by applying the law of conservation of energy and the photon model of light, (ACSPH119)
members.title: Photon Model of Light
members.exam: Students fail to connect photon energy to frequency rather than intensity, or confuse the conditions needed for electron ejection in the photoelectric effect.
members.summary: Light is composed of discrete packets called photons, each carrying energy directly proportional to its frequency through the relationship E equals h f.

members.dotPoint: analyse the experimental evidence gathered about black body radiation, including Wien's Law related to Planck's contribution to a changed model of light (ACSPH137)
members.title: Quantisation of Energy and Photons
members.exam: Students incorrectly assume partial photons can exist or that increasing light intensity alone can compensate for insufficient photon energy.
members.summary: Energy can only be absorbed or emitted in discrete packets called quanta, not in continuous amounts as classical physics predicted.

cells.bigIdea: Light spends its energy in whole packets or not at all. A photon's energy lives in its frequency, not the brightness of the beam — which is why dim blue light can eject electrons that a floodlight of red never will. Once you count light instead of measuring it, the classical wave quietly fails.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: conduct investigations quantitatively using the relationship of Malus’ Law I = I_(max)cos²θ for plane polarisation of light, to evaluate the significance of polarisation in developing a model for light (ACSPH050, ACSPH076, ACSPH120)
members.title: Diffraction and Polarisation (Malus' Law)
members.exam: Students often forget that Malus' Law requires the incident light to already be polarised, or they incorrectly apply it when light passes through the first polariser which simply halves the intensity.
members.summary: Diffraction shows light spreads through gaps and around edges while polarisation filters light by orientation, with Malus' Law stating transmitted intensity equals incident intensity times cosine-squared of the angle between polariser axes.

members.dotPoint: conduct investigations to analyse quantitatively the interference of light using double slit apparatus and diffraction gratings d sinθ = mλ (ACSPH116, ACSPH117, ACSPH140)
members.title: Interference and Path Difference
members.exam: Students confuse path difference with distance from slits, or incorrectly apply the conditions by mixing up when to use n-lambda versus (n+0.5)lambda for maxima and minima.
members.summary: Constructive interference occurs when path difference equals whole number multiples of wavelength, while destructive interference occurs at odd multiples of half wavelengths, creating alternating bright and dark regions.

members.dotPoint: analyse the experimental evidence that supported the models of light that were proposed by Newton and Huygens (ACSPH050, ACSPH118, ACSPH123)
members.title: Newton vs Huygens: Competing Models of Light
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify which specific phenomena each historical model successfully explained versus failed to explain, particularly that Newton's model incorrectly predicted light speeds up in denser media while Huygens predicted it slows down.
members.summary: Newton's corpuscular theory explained reflection and rectilinear propagation but failed at diffraction, while Huygens' wave theory explained diffraction and refraction but couldn't explain why light travels in straight lines or casts sharp shadows.

members.dotPoint: conduct investigations to analyse quantitatively the interference of light using double slit apparatus and diffraction gratings d sinθ = mλ (ACSPH116, ACSPH117, ACSPH140)
members.title: Young's Double-Slit Experiment
members.exam: Students misapply the formula x equals L-lambda over d by confusing which variable is which, or forget that this only works for small angles and requires coherent sources.
members.summary: Coherent light passing through two slits produces an interference pattern of bright and dark fringes on a screen, with fringe spacing proportional to wavelength and distance to screen but inversely proportional to slit separation.

pick.dotPoint: conduct investigations quantitatively using the relationship of Malus’ Law I = I_(max)cos²θ for plane polarisation of light, to evaluate the significance of polarisation in developing a model for light (ACSPH050, ACSPH076, ACSPH120)

Newton called light particles and lost this round — because only waves bend around edges and dim by cos-squared through a filter.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: derive quantitatively and apply the concepts of gravitational force and gravitational potential energy in radial gravitational fields to a variety of situations, including but not limited to:
members.title: Gravitational Potential Energy and Potential
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can distinguish between potential V (energy per kilogram, J/kg) and potential energy E (total energy, J), particularly when calculating escape velocities or orbital energies.
members.summary: Gravitational potential energy is negative because work must be done against gravity to separate masses to infinity where potential energy is defined as zero, with the system naturally moving toward lower (more negative) energy states.

members.dotPoint: apply qualitatively and quantitatively Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation to:
members.title: Gravitational Field Strength
members.exam: Students often forget that g is a vector pointing toward the mass creating the field, or incorrectly use surface gravity values when calculating field strength at orbital altitudes above Earth.
members.summary: Gravitational field strength describes the force per unit mass at any location in a gravitational field, which decreases with distance from the source mass following an inverse square relationship.

members.dotPoint: apply qualitatively and quantitatively Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation to:
members.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
members.exam: Students commonly make errors using the distance value, forgetting that r must be measured from center to center of the masses, not from surfaces, especially when dealing with planets or satellites.
members.summary: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation distance.

members.dotPoint: investigate the orbital motion of planets and artificial satellites when applying the relationships between the following quantities:
members.title: Orbital Motion and Kepler's Laws
members.exam: Students often incorrectly think gravity decreases to zero in orbit, but examiners test whether you know orbital motion requires centripetal force provided by gravity at that altitude.
members.summary: Satellites in orbit are constantly falling toward Earth but moving forward fast enough that Earth's surface curves away beneath them at the same rate they fall.

cells.bigIdea: An orbit is just falling — the object accelerates toward the mass forever but keeps missing because it's moving sideways fast enough. Kepler's laws aren't three facts to memorise; they're what falling-forever forces on any orbit: the geometry, the sweeping, and the fixed link between period and radius.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: analyse and apply Einstein’s description of the equivalence of energy and mass and relate this to the nuclear reactions that occur in stars
members.title: Nuclear Fusion and Stellar Energy
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can calculate energy released using mass defect and E=mc², and commonly trap students who forget to convert atomic mass units to kilograms before calculation.
members.summary: Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei under extreme temperature and pressure, converting a small amount of mass into enormous energy according to Einstein's mass-energy equivalence equation.

members.dotPoint: investigate the types of nucleosynthesis reactions involved in Main Sequence and Post-Main Sequence stars, including but not limited to:
members.title: Nucleosynthesis in Stars
members.exam: Students often wrongly state that iron is produced in supernovae rather than recognizing that iron is the endpoint of fusion and only elements heavier than iron require supernova conditions.
members.summary: Stars fuse light nuclei into heavier elements up to iron through nucleosynthesis, while elements heavier than iron form during supernova explosions, and all these materials are dispersed into space to form new stars and planets.

members.dotPoint: investigate the key features of stellar spectra and describe how these are used to classify stars
members.title: Stellar Spectra and Star Classification
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can link spectral class to temperature correctly, with a common error being to think M-type stars are hotter than O-type stars by reversing the sequence.
members.summary: Each chemical element absorbs specific wavelengths of light, creating dark absorption lines in a star's spectrum that identify both composition and temperature, allowing classification into spectral types O-B-A-F-G-K-M from hottest to coolest.

members.dotPoint: investigate the evidence that led to the discovery of the expansion of the Universe by Hubble
members.title: The Big Bang and the Expanding Universe (Hubble)
members.exam: Students commonly confuse the expansion of space itself with galaxies moving through space, or fail to apply Hubble's Law correctly by mixing up velocity, distance and the Hubble constant in calculations.
members.summary: Hubble discovered that galaxies are receding with velocities proportional to their distance, proving the universe is expanding uniformly from an initial hot dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago.

members.dotPoint: investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star:
members.title: The Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) Diagram
members.exam: A frequent mistake is placing stars incorrectly on the axes, especially confusing which axis represents temperature and forgetting that temperature increases leftward, or not recognizing that main sequence position correlates with stellar mass.
members.summary: The HR diagram plots luminosity versus temperature and reveals that stars occupy distinct regions—main sequence where most stars fuse hydrogen, red giants, supergiants and white dwarfs—with position indicating mass, age and evolutionary stage.

cells.bigIdea: Every atom heavier than hydrogen was cooked somewhere, and light is the receipt. Stellar spectra, the HR diagram, fusion, nucleosynthesis — they're all one story read backwards: you catch light, decode where and how it was made, and reconstruct the whole assembly line from the Big Bang to the carbon in your hand.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: analyse the motion of projectiles by resolving the motion into horizontal and vertical components, making the following assumptions:
members.title: Projectile Motion
members.exam: Students commonly use the wrong velocity component when calculating time of flight or range, or forget that initial vertical velocity is zero only when launched horizontally.
members.summary: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent—horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical motion undergoes constant downward acceleration due to gravity.

members.dotPoint: apply the modelling of projectile motion to quantitatively derive the relationships between the following variables:
members.title: Launch Angle, Range and Flight Time
members.exam: Students forget that maximum range occurs at 45 degrees only for level ground; examiners test this by asking for optimal angle when landing at different heights or by requesting time of flight comparisons between complementary angles.
members.summary: Launch angle determines the initial velocity split between horizontal and vertical components, and by solving the vertical motion for landing time then multiplying by constant horizontal velocity, you derive range which peaks at 45 degrees on flat ground.

members.dotPoint: solve problems, create models and make quantitative predictions by applying the equations of motion relationships for uniformly accelerated and constant rectilinear motion
members.title: Equations of Motion (SUVAT)
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify which equation to use when specific variables are unknown, and students often fall into the trap of using SUVAT equations when acceleration is not constant.
members.summary: The SUVAT equations are your safety net because if you know any three variables you can always calculate the other two with certainty when an object moves in a straight line with constant acceleration.

pick.dotPoint: analyse the motion of projectiles by resolving the motion into horizontal and vertical components, making the following assumptions:
pick.title: Projectile Motion
pick.exam: Students commonly use the wrong velocity component when calculating time of flight or range, or forget that initial vertical velocity is zero only when launched horizontally.
pick.summary: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent—horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical motion undergoes constant downward acceleration due to gravity.

cells.bigIdea: A projectile is two motions wearing one path: a constant horizontal glide and a vertical fall, deaf to each other. Gravity only ever touches the vertical. Split every problem into those two stories, solve each with the equations you already own, and the parabola stops being a curve and becomes two straight-line problems stapled together.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: model and explain the process of nuclear fission, including the concepts of controlled and uncontrolled chain reactions, and account for the release of energy in the process (ACSPH033, ACSPH034)
members.title: Nuclear Fission
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students understand that energy is released because products have higher binding energy per nucleon, not lower, and students must correctly identify that the mass of products is less than reactants despite having more binding energy.
members.summary: Fission releases energy because the total binding energy of the products exceeds that of uranium-235, with the released neutrons capable of triggering chain reactions in surrounding nuclei.

members.dotPoint: analyse relationships that represent conservation of mass-energy in spontaneous and artificial nuclear transmutations, including alpha decay, beta decay, nuclear fission and nuclear fusion
members.title: Nuclear Fusion and Stellar Energy
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can calculate energy released using mass defect and E=mc², and commonly trap students who forget to convert atomic mass units to kilograms before calculation.
members.summary: Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei under extreme temperature and pressure, converting a small amount of mass into enormous energy according to Einstein's mass-energy equivalence equation.

members.dotPoint: analyse relationships that represent conservation of mass-energy in spontaneous and artificial nuclear transmutations, including alpha decay, beta decay, nuclear fission and nuclear fusion (ACSPH032)
members.title: Mass-Energy Equivalence and Binding Energy Calculations
members.exam: Students often forget to convert mass defect from atomic mass units to kilograms using the conversion factor 1u equals 1.66 times 10 to the negative 27 kilograms before applying E equals mc squared, or they incorrectly calculate mass defect by subtracting in the wrong direction.
members.summary: The mass defect is converted to binding energy according to Einstein's equation E equals mc squared, representing the energy needed to completely separate all nucleons in a nucleus.

members.dotPoint: analyse the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei, and the properties of the alpha, beta and gamma radiation emitted (ACSPH028, ACSPH030)
members.title: Radioactive Decay and Half-Life Mathematics
members.exam: Students frequently confuse the number of half-lives with the fraction remaining, calculating 1 divided by n instead of 1 divided by 2 to the power of n, or they incorrectly manipulate the exponential decay equation when solving for time or initial quantity.
members.summary: Half-life represents the time for half the nuclei to decay and relates to the decay constant by the equation t half equals natural log of 2 divided by lambda, allowing prediction of activity or remaining quantity at any time.

cells.bigIdea: The nucleus is heavier than its parts should allow — except it isn't, because the missing mass left as binding energy when the thing formed. Fusion is just this run in reverse: fuse light nuclei, land somewhere more tightly bound, and the mass deficit ships out as E=mc². That's what a star burns.

cells.subject: Physics
cells.topic: Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom

members.dotPoint: relate qualitatively and quantitatively the quantised energy levels of the hydrogen atom and the law of conservation of energy to the line emission spectrum of hydrogen using:
members.title: Energy Level Transitions in Atoms
members.exam: Students incorrectly apply continuous energy formulas or forget that absorption requires photon energy to exactly match the gap, not exceed it.
members.summary: Atoms absorb or emit photons only when the photon energy matches the exact energy gap between discrete electron energy levels, producing unique spectral fingerprints for each element.

members.dotPoint: investigate de Broglie's matter waves, and the experimental evidence that developed the following formula:
members.title: De Broglie Wavelength
members.exam: Students commonly make calculation errors by forgetting to convert units (especially electron volts to joules or mass to kilograms) or incorrectly using kinetic energy formulas when given voltage instead of velocity directly.
members.summary: All matter particles have an associated wavelength inversely proportional to their momentum, given by lambda equals h divided by mv, explaining why electrons diffract through slits like light waves do.

members.dotPoint: assess the limitations of the Rutherford and Bohr atomic models
members.title: From Bohr to Schrodinger: The Quantum Atom
members.exam: Students often incorrectly claim Bohr's model works for multi-electron atoms, or they confuse orbits (fixed paths) with orbitals (probability regions); examiners test whether you know the Heisenberg uncertainty principle emerged from wave-particle duality.
members.summary: Bohr's fixed circular orbits worked only for hydrogen, so de Broglie proposed electrons behave as waves, leading Schrödinger to model electrons as three-dimensional probability clouds called orbitals where exact position and momentum cannot both be known.

pick.title: Energy Level Transitions in Atoms

pick.summary: Atoms absorb or emit photons only when the photon energy matches the exact energy gap between discrete electron energy levels, producing unique spectral fingerprints for each element.

runnersUp.title: De Broglie Wavelength

runnersUp.title: From Bohr to Schrodinger: The Quantum Atom

cells.bigIdea: Every model here is a patch on the one before it: Bohr bolts quantised orbits onto a classical atom to explain hydrogen's spectrum, de Broglie says the electron is a wave, and Schrödinger drops orbits entirely for a cloud of probability. The exam isn't asking which is right — it's asking what each fixed and what it still couldn't.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: investigate, assess and model the experimental evidence supporting the nuclear model of the atom, including:
members.title: Discovering the Nucleus
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain why small deflections were expected from the plum pudding model but large deflections require a concentrated nucleus, or students incorrectly state most alpha particles were deflected.
members.summary: Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed rare large-angle deflections of alpha particles that could only occur if positive charge and most atomic mass concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, replacing Thomson's plum pudding model.

members.dotPoint: investigate, assess and model the experimental evidence supporting the existence and properties of the electron, including:
members.title: Discovering the Electron
members.exam: Students often confuse Thomson's measurement of e/m ratio with direct measurement of electron charge, or incorrectly describe how crossed fields allow velocity selection before the magnetic deflection measurement.
members.summary: Cathode ray experiments showed negatively charged particles streaming from metal, Thomson measured their charge-to-mass ratio using crossed electric and magnetic fields, and Millikan's oil drop experiment isolated the fundamental charge unit.

pick.dotPoint: investigate, assess and model the experimental evidence supporting the nuclear model of the atom, including:
pick.title: Discovering the Nucleus
pick.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain why small deflections were expected from the plum pudding model but large deflections require a concentrated nucleus, or students incorrectly state most alpha particles were deflected.
pick.summary: Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed rare large-angle deflections of alpha particles that could only occur if positive charge and most atomic mass concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, replacing Thomson's plum pudding model.

runnersUp.dotPoint: investigate, assess and model the experimental evidence supporting the existence and properties of the electron, including:
runnersUp.title: Discovering the Electron
runnersUp.exam: Students often confuse Thomson's measurement of e/m ratio with direct measurement of electron charge, or incorrectly describe how crossed fields allow velocity selection before the magnetic deflection measurement.
runnersUp.summary: Cathode ray experiments showed negatively charged particles streaming from metal, Thomson measured their charge-to-mass ratio using crossed electric and magnetic fields, and Millikan's oil drop experiment isolated the fundamental charge unit.

cells.bigIdea: Nobody has ever seen an atom's insides — every particle was caught by the fingerprint it left in an experiment. Cathode rays gave up the electron, gold foil gave up the nucleus, and the neutron hid until the sums didn't balance. This topic is the evidence, not the diagram: know what each experiment forced physics to admit.

members.dotPoint: analyse the interaction between two parallel current-carrying wires F/l = μ₀/2π · I₁I₂/r and determine the relationship between the International System of Units (SI) definition of an ampere and Newton's Third Law of Motion (ACSPH081, ACSPH106)
members.title: Parallel Wires and the Ampere
members.exam: Students often forget to apply the right-hand rule twice—once to find the field direction from wire A at wire B's position, then again to find the force on wire B's current in that field.
members.summary: Two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other because each wire experiences a force from the magnetic field created by the other wire, while opposite currents cause repulsion.

members.dotPoint: analyse the interaction between two parallel current-carrying wires F/l = μ₀/2π · I₁I₂/r and determine the relationship between the International System of Units (SI) definition of an ampere and Newton's Third Law of Motion (ACSPH081, ACSPH106)

members.summary: A current-carrying straight wire creates concentric circular magnetic field lines around it, while a solenoid concentrates field lines inside producing a strong uniform field.

cells.subject: Accounting

members.dotPoint: the recording and reporting of balance day adjustments:
members.title: Why Balance Day Adjustments Exist
members.exam: Examiners check whether students adjust only the current period portion, not the full amount paid or owing, and whether they reverse prior period adjustments correctly.
members.summary: Balance day adjustments ensure revenue and expenses are recognised in the correct accounting period under accrual accounting, regardless of when cash is received or paid.

members.dotPoint: the recording and reporting of the disposal of a non-current depreciable asset
members.title: Carrying Value and Asset Disposal
members.exam: Students often forget to close accumulated depreciation when disposing of an asset, or they subtract sale proceeds from cost instead of carrying value when calculating gain or loss.
members.summary: Carrying value equals cost minus accumulated depreciation, and comparing it to sale proceeds determines whether a disposal results in a profit or loss.

members.dotPoint: methods of depreciation: straight-line and reducing balance
members.title: Depreciation: Straight-Line and Reducing Balance
members.exam: Examiners test whether students apply reducing balance to the diminished carrying value each year, not the original cost, and whether residual value is subtracted under straight-line only.
members.summary: Depreciation allocates asset cost over useful life using straight-line for even annual expense or reducing balance for higher early-year charges that decline over time.

members.dotPoint: prepaid expenses (asset approach), with GST being recorded at the time of payment
members.title: Prepaid and Accrued Expenses
members.exam: Students mix up the journal entry direction, debiting expense and crediting prepaid when they should debit prepaid and credit expense, or forgetting accrued expenses create a liability not a reduction in cash.
members.summary: Prepaid expenses are assets representing payments made in advance of use, while accrued expenses are liabilities representing costs incurred but not yet paid.

cells.subject: Accounting

members.dotPoint: the characteristics and use of classified accounting reports:
members.title: Preparing the Balance Sheet
members.exam: Students list items randomly without proper current versus non-current classification or forget to show subtotals for total current assets, total assets, total current liabilities and total liabilities.
members.summary: The Balance Sheet reports assets, liabilities and equity at a specific date using classified presentation, with the totals proving that assets equal liabilities plus equity.

members.dotPoint: the effects of transactions on the accounting reports
members.title: How the Reports Connect
members.exam: Students cannot trace how profit appears on the Balance Sheet, forgetting that net profit increases retained earnings rather than appearing as a separate line item in assets.
members.summary: Net profit from the Income Statement increases retained earnings in equity on the Balance Sheet, while the Cash Flow Statement reconciles opening and closing bank balances shown on consecutive Balance Sheets.

members.title: The Accounting Equation Structure
members.exam: Students incorrectly rearrange the equation as Assets minus Equity equals Liabilities, then misinterpret increases in liabilities as decreases in equity when analyzing transactions.
members.summary: Assets always equal liabilities plus equity because every resource a business owns was financed either by borrowing from creditors or by contributions and profits retained from owners.

members.title: Balance Sheet Structure and Classification
members.exam: Students incorrectly classify prepaid expenses as current assets even when the benefit extends beyond 12 months, or fail to recognize that the current portion of a long-term loan must be reclassified as a current liability.
members.summary: The balance sheet separates assets and liabilities into current (within 12 months) and non-current (beyond 12 months) to reveal how quickly a business can access cash or must pay debts.

members.title: Equity Components and Movement
members.exam: Students confuse drawings with expenses and incorrectly record them in the Income Statement rather than as direct reductions to equity in the Balance Sheet.
members.summary: Equity changes through profit or loss from the Income Statement transferred to retained earnings, plus capital contributions from owners, minus drawings withdrawn by owners.

members.title: Effect of Transactions on the Equation
members.exam: Students struggle to identify transactions that only affect assets such as purchasing inventory on credit incorrectly recording it as affecting only assets when it also increases liabilities.
members.summary: Every transaction affects at least two elements of the accounting equation while keeping it balanced, either changing items within one category or affecting multiple categories simultaneously.

cells.subject: Accounting

members.title: Budgeted Financial Statements
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between accrual-based budgeted statements and cash-based forecasts, with students commonly mistaking cash receipts timing for revenue recognition in budgeted income statements.
members.summary: Budgeted financial statements project future profit and financial position using accrual accounting, preparing an income statement from all revenue and expense budgets and a balance sheet showing expected assets, liabilities and equity.

members.title: Operating Budgets
members.exam: Examiners test the sequential dependency of budgets by asking students to calculate production budgets from sales forecasts adjusted for inventory changes, where students often forget to add desired closing stock and subtract opening stock.
members.summary: Operating budgets follow a hierarchy starting with the sales budget, which determines production requirements, then purchasing and labour budgets, and finally overhead budgets needed to support the forecast activity level.

members.title: Cash Flow Forecasts
members.exam: Students frequently fail to adjust profit figures for non-cash items when preparing cash budgets, particularly forgetting to exclude depreciation expense or to account for credit sales not yet collected.
members.summary: Cash flow forecasts track actual money inflows and outflows when cash physically changes hands, ignoring accrual accounting adjustments like depreciation, accounts receivable and accounts payable timing differences.

members.dotPoint: the use of variance reports and trends for Cash Flow Statements and Income Statements
members.title: Variance Analysis
members.exam: Students reverse favourable and unfavourable classifications, especially for expenses where spending less than budgeted is favourable, not unfavourable, despite being a negative variance mathematically.
members.summary: Variance analysis compares budgeted figures to actual results, where favourable variances exceed expectations for revenue or come under budget for expenses, while unfavourable means the opposite.

members.dotPoint: the characteristics and use of classified budgeted accounting reports:
members.title: Why Businesses Budget
members.exam: Students describe budgets only as forecasts without explaining the dual planning and control functions, or they fail to emphasize budgets are prepared in advance, not after events occur.
members.summary: Budgets translate business strategy into quantified financial plans before the period begins, then serve as benchmarks for controlling operations by measuring actual performance against planned targets.

cells.bigIdea: A budget is a plan written in numbers. Comparing it to what actually happened is how a business learns anything.

cells.subject: Accounting

members.title: DEAD CLIC Classification System
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly identify which side increases an account, particularly confusing drawings (debit, not credit despite being equity-related) or dividends declared.
members.summary: DEAD CLIC is a memory device grouping accounts by their normal balance, where DEAD accounts naturally have debit balances and CLIC accounts naturally have credit balances.

members.title: Journal Entries and Ledger Posting
members.exam: Examiners penalise missing or incorrect narrations, swapped debit/credit columns, or failure to post both sides of the entry to their respective ledger accounts.
members.summary: Journal entries record transactions chronologically in date order showing which accounts are debited and credited with explanatory narration, then posted to individual ledger accounts to show cumulative balances.

members.dotPoint: the GST Clearing account
members.title: Recording GST
members.exam: Students commonly credit GST Clearing when purchasing inventory instead of debiting it, or they include GST amounts in the expense or inventory value rather than separating it out.
members.summary: GST collected increases a liability to the ATO while GST paid on purchases creates a receivable, with the GST Clearing account netting these amounts to show the final payment or refund due.

members.dotPoint: the accounting assumptions and qualitative characteristics, as applicable
members.title: The Accounting Assumptions
members.exam: Examiners test whether students record unearned revenue as a liability or prematurely as income, and whether prepaid expenses are correctly treated as assets not immediate expenses.
members.summary: Accrual basis records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred regardless of cash timing, entity assumption separates business from owner, going concern assumes continuation, and period assumption divides activity into reporting intervals.

members.dotPoint: the accounting elements: assets, liabilities, owner’s equity, revenues and expenses
members.title: The Accounting Equation
members.exam: Students struggle with transactions affecting only one side of the equation like purchasing inventory with cash, forgetting this swaps one asset for another and still balances.
members.summary: The accounting equation Assets equals Liabilities plus Owner's Equity must always balance, with double-entry recording ensuring every transaction maintains this equality by affecting at least two accounts.

members.title: The Dual Aspect Principle
members.exam: Students often record only one side of a transaction or incorrectly double-debit or double-credit, violating the fundamental requirement that debits must equal credits.
members.summary: Every transaction affects at least two accounts because value cannot appear from nowhere or disappear into nothing, maintaining the accounting equation's balance at all times.

members.title: Debit and Credit Rules
members.exam: Students commonly reverse the rules for expenses, incorrectly crediting them to record an increase because they reduce profit, forgetting expenses themselves are debit accounts.
members.summary: Debits and credits are simply position markers where assets and expenses sit on the left side and increase with debits, while liabilities, equity and revenue sit on the right and increase with credits.

members.dotPoint: establishment of a double entry system
members.title: Debits and Credits
members.exam: Under exam pressure students reverse the treatment of drawings or returns, debiting when they should credit, especially when the transaction type is unfamiliar or worded differently.
members.summary: Debits and credits are simply the left and right sides of accounts, with every transaction requiring equal debit and credit amounts to maintain the fundamental equation balance.

pick.title: DEAD CLIC Classification System
pick.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly identify which side increases an account, particularly confusing drawings (debit, not credit despite being equity-related) or dividends declared.
pick.summary: DEAD CLIC is a memory device grouping accounts by their normal balance, where DEAD accounts naturally have debit balances and CLIC accounts naturally have credit balances.

runnersUp.title: Journal Entries and Ledger Posting
runnersUp.exam: Examiners penalise missing or incorrect narrations, swapped debit/credit columns, or failure to post both sides of the entry to their respective ledger accounts.
runnersUp.summary: Journal entries record transactions chronologically in date order showing which accounts are debited and credited with explanatory narration, then posted to individual ledger accounts to show cumulative balances.

runnersUp.dotPoint: the GST Clearing account
runnersUp.title: Recording GST
runnersUp.exam: Students commonly credit GST Clearing when purchasing inventory instead of debiting it, or they include GST amounts in the expense or inventory value rather than separating it out.
runnersUp.summary: GST collected increases a liability to the ATO while GST paid on purchases creates a receivable, with the GST Clearing account netting these amounts to show the final payment or refund due.

runnersUp.dotPoint: the accounting assumptions and qualitative characteristics, as applicable
runnersUp.title: The Accounting Assumptions
runnersUp.exam: Examiners test whether students record unearned revenue as a liability or prematurely as income, and whether prepaid expenses are correctly treated as assets not immediate expenses.
runnersUp.summary: Accrual basis records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred regardless of cash timing, entity assumption separates business from owner, going concern assumes continuation, and period assumption divides activity into reporting intervals.

cells.bigIdea: Every transaction hits two accounts and the two always balance. Everything else in accounting is that one rule applied consistently for a year.

cells.subject: Accounting

members.title: Liquidity Ratios
members.exam: Students frequently forget to subtract inventory from current assets when calculating the quick ratio, or incorrectly include non-current liabilities in the denominator.
members.summary: Liquidity ratios measure a business's ability to meet short-term debts, with the quick ratio providing a stricter test by removing inventory from current assets.

members.title: Efficiency Ratios
members.exam: Students often confuse inventory turnover days with inventory turnover times, or fail to use cost of goods sold instead of sales when calculating inventory turnover ratio.
members.summary: Efficiency ratios measure how quickly a business converts assets like inventory and receivables into cash, with higher turnover rates indicating better asset management.

members.dotPoint: indicators and other relevant information (financial and non-financial) to measure business performance
members.title: The Limits of Ratios
members.exam: Students lose marks by recommending decisions based solely on ratio analysis without acknowledging limitations like different accounting policies, one-off events, or non-financial factors affecting business performance.
members.summary: Financial ratios are useful analytical tools but have significant limitations because they only capture historical quantitative data and ignore qualitative factors that drive future business success.

members.title: Profitability Ratios
members.exam: Students commonly use the wrong profit figure in the numerator, such as using net profit instead of gross profit when calculating gross profit percentage.
members.summary: Profitability ratios express different profit levels as percentages of sales, assets or equity to evaluate how effectively a business generates returns for stakeholders.
