cells.subject: Chemistry

members.title: Empirical & Molecular Formulae
members.exam: Students often forget to divide all subscripts by the greatest common factor when finding empirical formulae, or fail to use molar mass to find the molecular formula multiplier.
members.summary: The empirical formula shows the simplest ratio of atoms while the molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms, with molar mass letting you convert between them.

members.dotPoint: determination of limiting reactants or reagents in chemical reactions
members.title: Limiting Reagents
members.exam: Students find the limiting reagent but then accidentally use the excess reagent's moles in their stoichiometry calculation, or they assume the reactant with smaller mass or moles is automatically limiting without checking the ratio.
members.summary: The limiting reagent is completely consumed and determines the maximum amount of product, while any reagent in excess has leftover material that plays no role in product calculations.

members.dotPoint: gas laws and the relationship between pressure, volume and temperature
members.title: Measuring Gases
members.exam: Students forget to convert Celsius to Kelvin or use the wrong molar volume value by applying SLC conditions when the question specifies different temperature or pressure.
members.summary: Gas volume depends on temperature and pressure so you cannot directly convert volume to moles without using the ideal gas equation or molar volume at specified conditions.

members.title: Molar Mass
members.exam: Examiners test whether students correctly calculate molar mass for compounds with brackets like calcium nitrate or hydrated salts, where students often miss multiplying the bracketed section.
members.summary: Molar mass converts between the mass of a substance you can measure and the number of moles you need for stoichiometric calculations using n equals m divided by M.

members.title: The Mole
members.exam: Students confuse the number of moles with the number of particles, forgetting to multiply or divide by Avogadro's constant when converting between them.
members.summary: The mole is a counting unit equal to 6.02 times 10 to the 23 particles that lets chemists count atoms by weighing them instead of counting individually.

members.dotPoint: calculations related to the application of stoichiometry to reactions involving the combustion of fuels, including mass-mass, mass-volume and volume-volume stoichiometry, to determine heat energy released, reactant and product amounts and net volume or mass of major greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4 and H2O), limited to standard laboratory conditions (SLC) at 25 °C and 100 kPa
members.title: Stoichiometry of Combustion
members.exam: Examiners give you the heat released and ask for volume of oxygen gas required, testing whether you can chain conversions from energy to moles of fuel to moles of oxygen to volume.
members.summary: Combustion stoichiometry uses the same mole ratio method as any other reaction, but you often start from energy released and work backwards using enthalpy of combustion to find moles of fuel.

cells.bigIdea: The mole is a counting word for things too small to count — it turns a mass you can weigh into particles you can't see. Every problem is the same move: mass to moles, follow the equation's ratio, back to what was asked. One bridge, crossed in different directions.

cells.subject: Economics

members.dotPoint: the operation of aggregate supply policies in improving supply-side conditions through their impact on the quantity and quality of the factors of production, the costs of production and productivity, and the effect on Australia’s international competitiveness, productive capacity and aggregate supply
members.title: Market-Based Supply Policies
members.exam: Students often confuse lower personal income tax (demand policy) with lower company tax (supply policy) or forget to explain the transmission mechanism from policy to productive capacity.
members.summary: Market-based supply policies use price signals and competition to improve efficiency by removing barriers, cutting taxes and opening markets to competitive pressure.

members.dotPoint: the effect of skilled immigration policy on population, productivity and participation and the subsequent effect on productive capacity, aggregate supply, international competitiveness, the achievement of domestic macroeconomic goals, and living standards
members.title: Productivity and Training Policies
members.exam: Examiners test whether students recognise the long implementation lag for training policies and that these shift LRAS rather than just aggregate demand.
members.summary: Investment in human capital through education, training and skilled migration raises labour productivity permanently but delivers results slowly compared to demand-side measures.

members.dotPoint: strengths and weaknesses of aggregate supply policies, including long implementation lags
members.title: Strengths and Weaknesses of Supply Policies
members.exam: Students mistakenly claim supply policies work quickly or forget to discuss equity concerns such as regressive impacts of consumption tax or reduced worker protections from deregulation.
members.summary: Supply policies genuinely increase potential output without inflation but require years to work and may involve short-run costs like unemployment from deregulation or reduced services from spending cuts.

members.dotPoint: the operation of aggregate supply policies in improving supply-side conditions through their impact on the quantity and quality of the factors of production, the costs of production and productivity, and the effect on Australia’s international competitiveness, productive capacity and aggregate supply
members.title: What Supply-Side Policy Does
members.exam: A common trap is claiming supply policies reduce unemployment immediately or failing to distinguish between moving along SRAS versus shifting LRAS outward permanently.
members.summary: Supply-side policies shift long-run aggregate supply rightward so the economy can grow faster at any inflation rate, unlike demand policies that only manage spending along a fixed capacity constraint.

cells.subject: Economics

members.dotPoint: the exchange rate, its meaning and measurement and the factors affecting its value, including relative interest rates, commodity prices and the terms of trade, demand for exports and imports, foreign investment, relative rates of inflation, credit ratings and speculation
members.title: Exchange Rates
members.exam: Students often confuse the direction of effects—appreciation makes Australian exports more expensive overseas (hurts competitiveness) and imports cheaper domestically, not the reverse.
members.summary: Exchange rates are the price of the Australian dollar determined by currency supply and demand, where appreciation reduces export competitiveness and depreciation does the opposite.

members.dotPoint: the balance of payments and its components
members.title: The Balance of Payments
members.exam: A common error is thinking a current account deficit is always bad, when it often reflects productive foreign investment financing growth that cannot be sustained by domestic savings alone.
members.summary: The balance of payments records all transactions between Australia and the rest of the world, divided into the current account and the capital and financial account, which must sum to zero by accounting identity.

members.title: Global Investment Flows and Financial Stability
members.exam: Examiners expect students to distinguish FDI stability from portfolio volatility with Australian examples, or students wrongly claim all foreign investment is equally risky or beneficial without recognising the contagion risk of sudden capital flight.
members.summary: Foreign direct investment involves long-term productive assets and technology transfer, while portfolio investment represents short-term financial flows that can reverse rapidly, causing currency crises and requiring IMF intervention through conditional lending programs.

members.dotPoint: international competitiveness and the factors that may affect international competitiveness, including productivity, production costs, availability of natural resources, exchange rates and relative rates of inflation
members.title: Globalisation and Competitiveness
members.exam: Students often fail to link productivity growth to unit labour costs and real wages, or cannot explain how microeconomic reform improves competitiveness beyond vague statements about efficiency.
members.summary: Globalisation integrates Australia into the world economy through flows of goods, capital, labour and technology, with international competitiveness fundamentally determined by productivity levels relative to trading partners.

members.dotPoint: the terms of trade, its meaning and measurement and the factors that may affect the terms of trade, including commodity prices and production costs in trading partners
members.title: The Terms of Trade
members.exam: Students frequently confuse terms of trade with the exchange rate or fail to explain the transmission mechanism through national income, the current account, and fiscal revenue from commodity taxation.
members.summary: The terms of trade measure export prices relative to import prices, so an improvement means Australia can purchase more imports per unit of exports, directly boosting real national income and living standards.

members.dotPoint: free trade and protection: tariffs, subsidies and quotas, and their effects
members.title: Free Trade and Protection
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish absolute advantage from comparative advantage and explain the deadweight loss of protection using supply and demand diagrams.
members.summary: Free trade allows nations to specialise according to comparative advantage and increase total output, while protection shields domestic industries using tariffs, quotas or subsidies at the expense of efficiency and consumer welfare.

members.title: Global Development and Equity
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain why GDP per capita alone is insufficient for measuring development, expecting reference to HDI components like education and life expectancy, or students incorrectly assume all developing nations have identical characteristics.
members.summary: Countries are classified by development level (LDC, developing, emerging, advanced) based on GDP per capita, human development and structural factors, with lower-income nations disproportionately vulnerable to climate change impacts despite contributing least to emissions.

pick.dotPoint: the exchange rate, its meaning and measurement and the factors affecting its value, including relative interest rates, commodity prices and the terms of trade, demand for exports and imports, foreign investment, relative rates of inflation, credit ratings and speculation
pick.title: Exchange Rates
pick.exam: Students often confuse the direction of effects—appreciation makes Australian exports more expensive overseas (hurts competitiveness) and imports cheaper domestically, not the reverse.
pick.summary: Exchange rates are the price of the Australian dollar determined by currency supply and demand, where appreciation reduces export competitiveness and depreciation does the opposite.

runnersUp.dotPoint: the balance of payments and its components
runnersUp.title: The Balance of Payments
runnersUp.exam: A common error is thinking a current account deficit is always bad, when it often reflects productive foreign investment financing growth that cannot be sustained by domestic savings alone.
runnersUp.summary: The balance of payments records all transactions between Australia and the rest of the world, divided into the current account and the capital and financial account, which must sum to zero by accounting identity.

runnersUp.title: Global Investment Flows and Financial Stability
runnersUp.exam: Examiners expect students to distinguish FDI stability from portfolio volatility with Australian examples, or students wrongly claim all foreign investment is equally risky or beneficial without recognising the contagion risk of sudden capital flight.
runnersUp.summary: Foreign direct investment involves long-term productive assets and technology transfer, while portfolio investment represents short-term financial flows that can reverse rapidly, causing currency crises and requiring IMF intervention through conditional lending programs.

runnersUp.dotPoint: international competitiveness and the factors that may affect international competitiveness, including productivity, production costs, availability of natural resources, exchange rates and relative rates of inflation
runnersUp.title: Globalisation and Competitiveness
runnersUp.exam: Students often fail to link productivity growth to unit labour costs and real wages, or cannot explain how microeconomic reform improves competitiveness beyond vague statements about efficiency.
runnersUp.summary: Globalisation integrates Australia into the world economy through flows of goods, capital, labour and technology, with international competitiveness fundamentally determined by productivity levels relative to trading partners.

cells.bigIdea: No economy is sealed. Exchange rates, trade and capital flows are how the rest of the world reaches in.

cells.subject: Economics

members.title: Cross Price Elasticity and Income Elasticity
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly interpret the sign of coefficients—students often confuse negative XED complements with negative YED inferior goods, or fail to recognise that strong substitutes have high positive XED values above 1.
members.summary: Cross price elasticity measures responsiveness of demand for one good when the price of another changes, while income elasticity measures how demand responds to changes in consumer income, revealing whether goods are substitutes, complements, normal or inferior.

members.dotPoint: factors affecting price elasticity of supply, including spare capacity, production period and durability of goods
members.title: Price Elasticity of Supply
members.exam: Students confuse supply elasticity with demand elasticity in their analysis, or fail to explain why agricultural products tend to be inelastic in the short run due to production time lags.
members.summary: Price elasticity of supply measures producer responsiveness to price changes, determined primarily by spare production capacity, availability of inputs, storage possibilities, and time period for adjustment.

members.dotPoint: factors affecting price elasticity of demand, including degree of necessity, availability of substitutes, proportion of income and time
members.title: Determinants of Price Elasticity of Demand
members.exam: Students commonly fall into the trap of claiming all necessities are perfectly inelastic or that all luxuries are elastic, when examiners expect recognition that these are tendencies along a spectrum rather than absolute rules.
members.summary: The availability of close substitutes makes demand more elastic because consumers can easily switch products when prices change, while necessities, small budget shares, and short time periods all reduce elasticity by limiting consumer flexibility to respond.

members.dotPoint: the meaning and significance of price elasticity of demand and supply
members.title: Elasticity and Total Revenue
members.exam: Students mechanically state that price rises always increase revenue, forgetting to check elasticity first, or incorrectly calculate percentage changes when determining elasticity coefficients.
members.summary: When demand is inelastic, price increases raise total revenue because quantity falls proportionally less, but when demand is elastic, price increases lower total revenue because quantity falls proportionally more.

pick.summary: Cross price elasticity measures responsiveness of demand for one good when the price of another changes, while income elasticity measures how demand responds to changes in consumer income, revealing whether goods are substitutes, complements, normal or inferior.

cells.bigIdea: Elasticity is how much people actually care. Change a price and the answer tells you whether they'll shrug or walk.

cells.subject: Economics

members.title: Environmental Policy Instruments and Their Effectiveness
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can compare instrument effectiveness using specific criteria like cost-efficiency, administrative burden, and political feasibility, not just list instruments without evaluation.
members.summary: Governments use command instruments like regulations and bans or market-based tools like carbon taxes and tradable permits to correct environmental market failures, each with different efficiency and compliance costs.

members.title: Sustainability and Intergenerational Equity
members.exam: Students often confuse sustainability with simple conservation, missing that it involves trade-offs between present and future welfare measured through intergenerational equity frameworks.
members.summary: Sustainability requires balancing current economic activity against future generations' ability to meet their needs, raising questions about discount rates and how we value costs and benefits decades away.

members.title: The Environment and the Economy
members.exam: Examiners watch for students who treat environmental degradation as an external issue rather than recognizing it as a market failure requiring economic analysis of externalities and missing markets.
members.summary: The economy depends entirely on environmental systems that provide raw materials, absorb pollution, and deliver ecosystem services like climate regulation, yet these contributions often lack market prices until scarcity or damage occurs.

pick.title: Environmental Policy Instruments and Their Effectiveness
pick.exam: Examiners test whether students can compare instrument effectiveness using specific criteria like cost-efficiency, administrative burden, and political feasibility, not just list instruments without evaluation.
pick.summary: Governments use command instruments like regulations and bans or market-based tools like carbon taxes and tradable permits to correct environmental market failures, each with different efficiency and compliance costs.

cells.bigIdea: The environment doesn't show up in prices, so the market ignores it — that's the whole problem. Judge every policy here by one question: does it make someone actually pay for the damage they'd otherwise dump on the future?

cells.subject: Economics

members.title: Policy Mix and Trade-offs
members.exam: Students often incorrectly claim the Phillips Curve trade-off exists in the long run, or fail to explain why the policy mix must balance both tools to achieve multiple macroeconomic objectives simultaneously.
members.summary: The Phillips Curve illustrates the short-run trade-off between unemployment and inflation, forcing policymakers to prioritize objectives, while fiscal policy offers precise targeting of specific sectors but creates larger budget deficits and takes longer to implement than monetary policy.

members.dotPoint: sources of government revenue, including direct and indirect taxation; progressive, regressive and proportional taxes; and revenue from government businesses and the sale of government assets
members.title: Aggregate Demand and the Budget
members.exam: Students often forget that both size and direction matter—a larger deficit stimulates AD more than a smaller one, and examiners test whether you can explain the transmission mechanism, not just state the relationship.
members.summary: The federal budget directly influences aggregate demand through government spending injections and taxation leakages, making fiscal policy a key tool for managing total economic activity.

members.dotPoint: the budget outcome: balanced, deficit or surplus
members.title: Budget Outcomes
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can distinguish cyclical factors like unemployment benefits rising in recession from deliberate policy decisions, and calculate the structural component correctly.
members.summary: Budget outcomes show whether government spending exceeds revenue in a given period, but the underlying budget balance strips out automatic stabilisers to reveal discretionary policy choices independent of the business cycle.

members.title: Fiscal Policy Mechanisms
members.exam: Students commonly confuse the size of the fiscal multiplier with the monetary multiplier, or fail to explain why the multiplier is smaller when there are leakages through savings, taxes, and imports.
members.summary: Fiscal policy works through government spending increases or tax cuts that directly inject purchasing power into the economy, which then circulates multiple times as recipients spend their additional income on other goods and services.

members.dotPoint: conventional monetary policy (cash rate target) and how it affects interest rates
members.title: Monetary Policy Transmission
members.exam: Examiners expect students to trace the full transmission mechanism from cash rate changes through to final impacts on AD components, not just state that lower rates increase spending.
members.summary: Monetary policy operates when the Reserve Bank changes the cash rate, influencing commercial bank lending rates, which then affects household borrowing for consumption and business investment decisions throughout the economy.

members.dotPoint: the stance of budgetary policy: expansionary or contractionary
members.title: Budgetary Policy Stances
members.exam: Students incorrectly think a budget surplus is always contractionary, when a shrinking surplus can still be expansionary if the government is loosening fiscal settings.
members.summary: The budget stance refers to whether policy is expansionary or contractionary based on changes in the structural balance, independent of whether the budget is actually in surplus or deficit.

members.dotPoint: the need for aggregate demand policies, including monetary policy and budgetary policy in terms of stabilising the business cycle
members.title: Strengths, Weaknesses and the Policy Mix
members.exam: Students list strengths and weaknesses mechanically without explaining why complementary policy mix is superior, or which policy should lead depending on economic circumstances.
members.summary: Monetary policy offers speed and flexibility but affects the whole economy indiscriminately, while fiscal policy can target specific sectors but faces implementation lags and political constraints.

members.title: Expansionary Fiscal Policy
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can calculate the multiplier effect accurately and explain why increased government spending has a larger total impact on GDP than the initial injection amount.
members.summary: Expansionary fiscal policy occurs when government spending exceeds tax revenue, creating a budget deficit that stimulates aggregate demand through direct injections and multiplier effects that amplify the initial spending increase.

members.title: Policy Mix and Coordination
members.exam: A common trap is failing to explain the consequences of conflicting policy stances, such as when tight monetary policy to control inflation is undermined by expansionary fiscal policy increasing demand.
members.summary: Effective policy mix requires fiscal and monetary policy working together toward the same objective, such as both being expansionary during recession, rather than contradicting each other and reducing overall effectiveness.

pick.summary: The Phillips Curve illustrates the short-run trade-off between unemployment and inflation, forcing policymakers to prioritize objectives, while fiscal policy offers precise targeting of specific sectors but creates larger budget deficits and takes longer to implement than monetary policy.

runnersUp.summary: Fiscal policy works through government spending increases or tax cuts that directly inject purchasing power into the economy, which then circulates multiple times as recipients spend their additional income on other goods and services.

cells.bigIdea: Two levers: what the government spends, and what money costs. Everything else is timing and side effects.

cells.subject: Economics

members.title: Economic Inequality: Causes, Dimensions and Policy Responses
members.exam: Students often list policies without explaining the causal link—examiners want you to connect specific causes like skill-biased technological change to targeted responses like education subsidies or retraining programs.
members.summary: Economic inequality arises from different sources like education gaps and technology changes, shows up in wage and access differences across groups, and governments respond using progressive tax, welfare payments and services.

members.title: Measuring Inequality: Lorenz, Gini and Palma
members.exam: Students confuse interpretation—a Gini of 0.35 versus 0.45 means more inequality at 0.45, and they forget that Palma isolates extremes while Gini captures the whole distribution including the middle class.
members.summary: The Lorenz curve plots cumulative income share against population share, the Gini coefficient measures the area between this curve and perfect equality as a ratio, and the Palma ratio divides the top 10 percent's share by the bottom 40 percent's share.

pick.title: Economic Inequality: Causes, Dimensions and Policy Responses
pick.exam: Students often list policies without explaining the causal link—examiners want you to connect specific causes like skill-biased technological change to targeted responses like education subsidies or retraining programs.
pick.summary: Economic inequality arises from different sources like education gaps and technology changes, shows up in wage and access differences across groups, and governments respond using progressive tax, welfare payments and services.

runnersUp.title: Measuring Inequality: Lorenz, Gini and Palma
runnersUp.exam: Students confuse interpretation—a Gini of 0.35 versus 0.45 means more inequality at 0.45, and they forget that Palma isolates extremes while Gini captures the whole distribution including the middle class.
runnersUp.summary: The Lorenz curve plots cumulative income share against population share, the Gini coefficient measures the area between this curve and perfect equality as a ratio, and the Palma ratio divides the top 10 percent's share by the bottom 40 percent's share.

cells.bigIdea: Inequality only becomes an economic problem once you can measure it — and the Gini, Lorenz curve and Palma ratio each pick a different slice of the same gap. The number you choose decides the fight you're having.

cells.subject: Economics

members.dotPoint: measuring the labour market: participation rate, unemployment rate, underemployment
members.title: The Labour Force, Participation and Underutilisation
members.exam: Students mistakenly include discouraged workers in unemployment figures when they should be excluded from the labour force entirely, or forget that underemployment measures hours worked below desired levels.
members.summary: The labour force includes only employed and actively seeking work, while participation rate shows the proportion of working-age population in the labour force, and underutilisation captures both unemployment and underemployment.

members.dotPoint: the meaning and importance of aggregate demand and the factors that may affect the level of aggregate demand in the economy, including disposable income, interest rates, consumer confidence, business confidence, the exchange rate and rates of economic growth overseas
members.title: Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply Factors
members.exam: Students commonly confuse movements along the curves with shifts of entire curves, or fail to distinguish short-run aggregate supply (flexible prices) from long-run aggregate supply (fixed by productive capacity).
members.summary: Aggregate demand represents total expenditure by households, firms, government and net exports, while aggregate supply shows the economy's total output capacity determined by resources, technology and productivity levels.

members.title: Aggregate Demand Curve
members.exam: Students incorrectly explain the downward slope using individual demand theory rather than the wealth effect, interest rate effect, and international trade effect at the macroeconomic level.
members.summary: The aggregate demand curve shows the inverse relationship between the price level and real GDP demanded, shifting right with increased consumption, investment, government spending or net exports.

members.dotPoint: the meaning of the goal of low and stable inflation (price stability)
members.title: Low and Stable Inflation
members.exam: Students often confuse the causes of inflation types or incorrectly claim that cost-push inflation can be solved by contractionary demand management when supply-side policies are actually needed.
members.summary: The Reserve Bank targets 2-3% inflation measured by the Consumer Price Index, using monetary policy to manage demand-pull inflation from excess spending and cost-push inflation from supply-side shocks like oil prices.

members.title: Strong and Sustainable Economic Growth
members.exam: A common trap is calculating nominal GDP growth instead of real GDP growth, forgetting to remove inflation when measuring actual economic expansion.
members.summary: Strong and sustainable economic growth means increasing real GDP at steady rates over time, improving material living standards while avoiding resource depletion or inflationary pressures that cause recessions.

members.title: Aggregate Demand Components and Determinants
members.exam: Students often confuse movement along the AD curve (caused by price level changes) with shifts of the entire AD curve (caused by changes in consumption, investment, government spending, or net exports).
members.summary: Aggregate demand slopes downward due to wealth effects, interest rate effects, and international trade effects that reduce purchasing power and competitiveness as prices rise.

members.title: Price Stability
members.exam: Students often confuse price stability with zero inflation, but examiners test understanding that mild positive inflation is the target, not completely stable prices.
members.summary: Price stability means maintaining low and predictable inflation rates, typically 2-3% annually in Australia, to protect purchasing power and support confident business and consumer decisions.

members.title: Macroeconomic Equilibrium
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between short-run equilibrium (which may occur below full employment) and long-run equilibrium (at potential GDP on the vertical LRAS curve).
members.summary: Macroeconomic equilibrium occurs where aggregate demand intersects aggregate supply, determining both the price level and real GDP with no inherent tendency to change.

members.title: Aggregate Supply
members.exam: Students confuse movements along AS curves with shifts of AS curves, or fail to distinguish that SRAS shifts become irrelevant in the long run when the economy self-corrects to LRAS.
members.summary: Short-run aggregate supply curves upward due to sticky wages and prices, while long-run aggregate supply is vertical at potential GDP because all input prices fully adjust to price level changes.

members.dotPoint: the meaning of the goal of full employment, including the NAIRU (natural rate of unemployment)
members.title: Full Employment
members.exam: Examiners test whether students incorrectly define full employment as zero unemployment, or whether they can explain why each unemployment type requires different policy responses like training programs versus demand stimulus.
members.summary: Full employment occurs at the natural rate of unemployment or NAIRU, typically 4-5% in Australia, where only frictional and structural unemployment exist without cyclical unemployment accelerating wage inflation.

members.title: The Business Cycle, Actual and Potential Output
members.exam: Students often confuse cyclical unemployment with structural unemployment, or fail to explain that negative output gaps create downward pressure on inflation while positive gaps create upward pressure.
members.summary: The business cycle tracks the economy's fluctuations between growth and recession, while the output gap measures the difference between what we actually produce and our full capacity.

pick.summary: The labour force includes only employed and actively seeking work, while participation rate shows the proportion of working-age population in the labour force, and underutilisation captures both unemployment and underemployment.

runnersUp.title: Low and Stable Inflation
runnersUp.exam: Students often confuse the causes of inflation types or incorrectly claim that cost-push inflation can be solved by contractionary demand management when supply-side policies are actually needed.
runnersUp.summary: The Reserve Bank targets 2-3% inflation measured by the Consumer Price Index, using monetary policy to manage demand-pull inflation from excess spending and cost-push inflation from supply-side shocks like oil prices.

cells.bigIdea: A government wants growth, jobs and steady prices all at once, and chasing any one hard enough damages the others. Every policy argument is about that trade.

cells.subject: Economics

members.title: Information Asymmetry and Adverse Selection
members.exam: Students often confuse adverse selection with moral hazard; adverse selection occurs before the transaction due to hidden information, while moral hazard occurs after due to hidden actions.
members.summary: When one party has more information than another in transactions, markets can collapse as buyers lower prices to protect themselves and sellers of quality products withdraw.

members.title: Public Goods and Free-Rider Problem
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between pure public goods and merit goods, with the trap being that merit goods like education are excludable and therefore not true public goods.
members.summary: Public goods are non-excludable and non-rivalrous, meaning everyone benefits once provided and one person's use doesn't reduce availability for others, causing markets to underprovide them.

members.dotPoint: types of market failure, including public goods, externalities, asymmetric information and common access resources
members.title: Externalities and Allocative Inefficiency
members.exam: Examiners give you a negative externality diagram and expect you to shade the deadweight loss and identify the socially optimal quantity where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost — the classic trap is labelling the tax at the wrong size instead of the exact gap between marginal private cost and marginal social cost at the optimal output.
members.summary: An externality is a cost or benefit that lands on someone outside the transaction, so the market's equilibrium quantity is not the socially best one and resources are allocated inefficiently.

members.dotPoint: the role and effect of indirect taxation, subsidies, regulations, advertising and direct provision as forms of government intervention in the market to address market failure
members.title: Government Intervention Methods
members.exam: A common trap is setting the Pigouvian tax equal to total external cost rather than per-unit external cost at the socially optimal quantity.
members.summary: Governments use indirect taxes, subsidies, regulation or tradeable permits to correct market failures by forcing producers to internalise external costs or benefits.

members.dotPoint: types of market failure, including public goods, externalities, asymmetric information and common access resources
members.title: When Markets Fail
members.exam: The key trap is asserting government intervention always improves outcomes without acknowledging government failure through poor information, regulatory capture, unintended consequences, or implementation costs exceeding benefits.
members.summary: Market failure occurs when competitive markets fail to achieve allocative efficiency due to externalities, information asymmetry, public goods, or market power, justifying potential government intervention to improve social welfare.

cells.bigIdea: Markets work until they don't, and economists have named every way they break. Spot which break you're looking at and the fix picks itself.

cells.subject: Economics

members.dotPoint: the effects of changes in demand and supply on equilibrium prices and quantities
members.title: Market Equilibrium and Price Mechanism
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain the self-correcting mechanism by describing how excess supply leads to downward price pressure and excess demand leads to upward price pressure, not just identifying whether a surplus or shortage exists.
members.summary: Market equilibrium is the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, and any deviation from this price triggers automatic market forces that push price back toward equilibrium through buyer and seller responses to shortages or surpluses.

members.dotPoint: the role of relative prices in the allocation of resources
members.title: Relative Prices and Resource Allocation
members.exam: Students incorrectly treat absolute price changes as resource signals when only relative price changes matter—a ten percent rise in all prices simultaneously changes nothing about resource allocation across sectors.
members.summary: Relative prices act as information signals that redirect resources between industries, so when wheat prices rise relative to barley, farmers shift land and labour toward wheat production because profit opportunities have changed.

members.title: Wage Determination and the Australian Labour Market
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between the different wage-setting mechanisms and explain how Fair Work Commission's annual minimum wage review affects low-income workers while enterprise bargaining primarily influences middle-income earners.
members.summary: Wages in Australia are determined through a multi-tiered system including the national minimum wage floor, awards setting industry-specific minimums, enterprise agreements negotiated above awards, and individual contracts at the top level.

members.dotPoint: the concept of relative scarcity, including needs, wants, resources, opportunity cost and the production possibility frontier (PPF) model, and the three basic economic questions
members.title: The Economic Problem
members.exam: Students mistakenly define scarcity as shortage or poverty when scarcity is actually the permanent condition that necessitates choice because even wealthy societies face resource constraints relative to wants.
members.summary: Scarcity means unlimited human wants clash with finite resources, forcing societies to make choices about what goods to produce, which production methods to use, and how to distribute output among competing claimants.

members.dotPoint: non-price factors likely to affect demand and the position of the demand curve, including changes in disposable income, the prices of substitutes and complements, preferences and tastes, interest rates, population demographics and consumer confidence
members.title: The Law of Demand
members.exam: Examiners test whether students distinguish between a change in quantity demanded shown by movement along the curve versus a change in demand shown by the entire curve shifting due to income, tastes, or related good prices.
members.summary: The law of demand states that as price falls, quantity demanded increases because consumers experience increased purchasing power with their fixed income and because the good becomes relatively cheaper compared to substitute products.

members.dotPoint: non-price factors likely to affect supply and the position of the supply curve, including changes in the costs of production, number of suppliers, technology, productivity and climatic conditions
members.title: Supply
members.exam: Students commonly confuse movements along the supply curve caused by price changes with shifts of the entire supply curve caused by non-price factors like input costs, technology, or weather conditions.
members.summary: The law of supply describes the positive relationship between price and quantity supplied because higher prices make production more profitable, incentivizing firms to increase output and attracting new suppliers into the market.

pick.dotPoint: the effects of changes in demand and supply on equilibrium prices and quantities
pick.title: Market Equilibrium and Price Mechanism
pick.exam: Examiners test whether students can explain the self-correcting mechanism by describing how excess supply leads to downward price pressure and excess demand leads to upward price pressure, not just identifying whether a surplus or shortage exists.
pick.summary: Market equilibrium is the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, and any deviation from this price triggers automatic market forces that push price back toward equilibrium through buyer and seller responses to shortages or surpluses.

runnersUp.dotPoint: the role of relative prices in the allocation of resources
runnersUp.title: Relative Prices and Resource Allocation
runnersUp.exam: Students incorrectly treat absolute price changes as resource signals when only relative price changes matter—a ten percent rise in all prices simultaneously changes nothing about resource allocation across sectors.
runnersUp.summary: Relative prices act as information signals that redirect resources between industries, so when wheat prices rise relative to barley, farmers shift land and labour toward wheat production because profit opportunities have changed.

runnersUp.title: Wage Determination and the Australian Labour Market
runnersUp.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between the different wage-setting mechanisms and explain how Fair Work Commission's annual minimum wage review affects low-income workers while enterprise bargaining primarily influences middle-income earners.
runnersUp.summary: Wages in Australia are determined through a multi-tiered system including the national minimum wage floor, awards setting industry-specific minimums, enterprise agreements negotiated above awards, and individual contracts at the top level.

runnersUp.dotPoint: the concept of relative scarcity, including needs, wants, resources, opportunity cost and the production possibility frontier (PPF) model, and the three basic economic questions
runnersUp.title: The Economic Problem
runnersUp.exam: Students mistakenly define scarcity as shortage or poverty when scarcity is actually the permanent condition that necessitates choice because even wealthy societies face resource constraints relative to wants.
runnersUp.summary: Scarcity means unlimited human wants clash with finite resources, forcing societies to make choices about what goods to produce, which production methods to use, and how to distribute output among competing claimants.

cells.bigIdea: Nobody sets the price. It's what falls out when what buyers want meets what sellers will part with — and almost all of economics is that meeting under different conditions.

cells.subject: English

members.title: Analysing Rhetorical Strategies and Persuasive Techniques
members.exam: Students often identify techniques like rhetorical questions or emotive language without explaining their persuasive effect on the specific audience, failing to connect how the technique advances the argument's purpose.
members.summary: Writers deploy logical appeals, emotional appeals, and credibility appeals through specific techniques like inclusive pronouns, metaphors, and tonal shifts to persuade audiences beyond the strength of their logical reasoning alone.

members.dotPoint: the ways authors employ arguments to position intended audiences
members.title: How Persuasive Texts Are Built
members.exam: Examiners reward students who explain why arguments appear in a particular sequence and how placement affects cumulative persuasive impact, not just what each paragraph contains.
members.summary: Persuasive texts follow deliberate structural patterns with strategic placement of arguments, often beginning with accessible appeals, escalating through stronger claims, and concluding with calls to action or emotional reinforcement.

members.dotPoint: supporting evidence
members.title: Analysing Evidence and Examples
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between anecdotal evidence that merely illustrates a point and statistical or expert evidence that substantiates it, with many students incorrectly treating all cited evidence as equally credible.
members.summary: Effective deconstruction requires evaluating whether evidence is relevant, sufficient, representative, and recent, rather than accepting every example as equally valid proof of the argument's claim.

members.dotPoint: sequence and structure
members.title: Identifying the Argument's Core Structure
members.exam: Examiners penalise students who summarise content chronologically rather than identifying the structural relationship between contention, supporting claims, and how each paragraph functions to build the overall case.
members.summary: The argument's skeleton consists of a thesis statement supported by a logical chain of major claims, each backed by reasoning and evidence arranged in a deliberate hierarchy of importance.

members.dotPoint: the role of visuals in supporting and augmenting argument
members.title: Analysing Visual Argument
members.exam: Examiners commonly include visual texts where the image contradicts or adds nuance to the written argument, testing whether students can analyse this interplay rather than treating them separately.
members.summary: Visual elements such as images, graphs, colour schemes, and layout choices construct meaning independently and in conjunction with written text to reinforce or complicate the argument.

members.dotPoint: Use of contention and supporting arguments including:
members.title: Finding the Contention
members.exam: Students frequently confuse the contention with the first argument or the topic itself, so examiners assess whether the identified contention encompasses the entire persuasive intent.
members.summary: The contention is the singular overarching position the writer wants the audience to accept, which must be separated from topic, tone, and individual supporting arguments.

cells.bigIdea: Every persuasive text wants something from you and has a plan for getting it. Find the want and the plan, and it stops working on you.

cells.subject: English

members.dotPoint: strategies to generate and develop ideas
members.title: The Framework of Ideas
members.exam: Students frequently write to a narrow prompt interpretation rather than developing a genuine idea, producing work that feels generic because it lacks a clear conceptual core driving decisions.
members.summary: Strong creative work begins with exploring broad conceptual questions through studying how published writers solve similar problems, then applying those craft lessons to your own original response.

members.dotPoint: the ways the purpose of the author hones the use of language
members.title: Voice, Form and Craft
members.exam: Students lose marks by treating creative writing as self-expression without craft awareness, failing to demonstrate that technical choices like tense, distance, or imagery patterns were deliberate meaning-making tools.
members.summary: Effective writing results from conscious choices about narrative voice, structural form, pacing, imagery and revelation sequence that together create deliberate effects on readers.

cells.subject: English

members.dotPoint: Use of contention and supporting arguments including:
members.title: Building Your Own Argument
members.exam: Students frequently present disconnected arguments without a unifying contention or fail to link evidence back to their main claim, resulting in fragmented rather than cumulative persuasion.
members.summary: Constructing persuasive writing involves establishing a clear contention upfront, ordering supporting arguments in a logical sequence that escalates impact, and selecting evidence that resonates with your identified audience.

members.title: Audience Analysis and Contextual Positioning
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify how a writer adjusts tone, formality and argument complexity for different audiences rather than simply labelling the audience as "general public" or "readers.
members.summary: Effective persuasion requires identifying the target audience's values, beliefs, knowledge level and the specific context in which they will encounter the argument to strategically tailor language, evidence and appeals.

members.title: Rhetorical Appeals as Persuasive Mechanisms
members.exam: Students often trap themselves by simply identifying appeals without explaining how they function persuasively in context or by mislabelling emotional language as pathos when it serves a logical purpose.
members.summary: The three rhetorical appeals—ethos (credibility and character), pathos (emotional engagement), and logos (logical reasoning and evidence)—operate as distinct persuasive strategies that writers combine to influence different aspects of audience psychology.

members.title: Structural Architecture of Persuasive Texts
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify how structural choices like delayed thesis or climactic ordering create specific persuasive effects rather than just labelling structures without explaining their rhetorical impact.
members.summary: Persuasive texts use deliberate structural patterns like problem-solution, comparative, or circular frameworks to guide readers toward predetermined conclusions through strategic sequencing of claims and evidence.

members.dotPoint: the structures and conventions appropriate for spoken texts that present an argument
members.title: Writing for an Audience
members.exam: Students typically write in their own comfortable register regardless of task specifications, using colloquial language for formal audiences or overly complex syntax when simplicity would persuade better.
members.summary: Effective persuasion adjusts vocabulary choice, sentence structure, formality level, and rhetorical devices based on whether the audience is specialist or general, sympathetic or hostile, empowered or disenfranchised.

cells.bigIdea: Writing to persuade is writing for one specific person you've thought hard about. Everything else follows from knowing who's reading.

members.dotPoint: the features of analytical responses to texts that position audiences, including relevant metalanguage
members.title: Why Listing Techniques Isn't Analysis
members.exam: The most common zero-mark response is spotting techniques like rhetorical questions without showing how they compel agreement, create urgency, or shift audience assumptions.
members.summary: Naming a technique without explaining its persuasive impact is not analysis; examiners reward students who connect the device to reader positioning, emotional effect, or argumentative purpose.

members.dotPoint: techniques and strategies
members.title: Appeals and Their Effect
members.exam: Examiners expect students to explain how a specific appeal manipulates the reader's response, not merely identify that an appeal to fear or authority exists in the text.
members.summary: Appeals such as fear, authority, or fairness function as psychological levers that position readers to accept an argument by triggering emotional or ethical responses alongside logical reasoning.

members.title: Figurative Language as Cognitive Manipulation
members.exam: Students wrongly label the device without explaining its persuasive effect on the audience; examiners want analysis of how the comparison shapes reader perception, not just identification.
members.summary: Figurative language rewires thought by linking concrete images to abstract ideas, making complex concepts feel intuitive by borrowing emotional weight and sensory detail from familiar experience.

members.dotPoint: techniques and strategies
members.title: Rhetorical Techniques
members.exam: The trap is cataloguing devices without analysing effect; examiners penalise identification-only responses and reward explanations of how the technique positions or influences the audience.
members.summary: Rhetorical techniques like repetition or loaded words are tools designed to embed ideas emotionally or emphasise key points, but their value lies in understanding their deliberate persuasive function.

members.title: Syntactic and Structural Devices for Emphasis
members.exam: Students identify the balanced structure but neglect to explain what ideas are being contrasted or unified; examiners demand analysis of how the parallelism clarifies argument or intensifies opposition.
members.summary: Parallelism and antithesis create cognitive satisfaction through balanced syntax, making contrasting or related ideas appear logically connected and authoritative because symmetry signals careful thought.

members.dotPoint: the features of analytical writing in response to a text, including the use of appropriate metalanguage
members.title: Building an Analytical Essay
members.exam: Examiners penalise essays that summarise or describe without a sustained argument, or where paragraphs feel disconnected from a central thesis.
members.summary: Every analytical essay needs a clear contention that answers the prompt directly, with each paragraph's topic sentence and evidence selection working to prove that overarching argument.

members.title: Analytical Framework for Literary Devices
members.exam: Examiners penalize students who identify devices without explaining their function, such as stating "the author uses a metaphor" without analyzing what it reveals about character or theme.
members.summary: Literary devices function as tools authors use to shape reader response, requiring analysis that connects the technique to its purpose and effect within the text's broader meaning.

members.dotPoint: vocabulary, text structures and language features in a text used to construct meaning
members.title: How Authors Construct Character
members.exam: Students frequently treat characters as real people and retell their actions instead of analysing how the author constructs them to generate meaning.
members.summary: Characters are authorial constructs built through dialogue, action, description, and narrative perspective to serve thematic purposes rather than realistic representations of people.

members.title: Structural Analysis and Narrative Architecture
members.exam: Examiners watch for students who discuss plot chronologically instead of analyzing deliberate structural choices like flashbacks, frame narratives, or non-linear sequencing and their effects.
members.summary: Analyzing structure means examining how texts are organized across all levels—from syntax and paragraph construction to chapter arrangement and narrative chronology—to understand how form creates meaning.

members.dotPoint: ideas, concerns and conflicts in a text
members.title: Tracing a Text's Central Ideas
members.exam: Examiners penalise essays that jump between disconnected observations instead of developing a coherent exploration of central textual ideas.
members.summary: Strong essays identify and track a text's recurring preoccupations and thematic concerns, showing how these ideas evolve and connect across the whole work.

members.dotPoint: reading and viewing strategies to draw out meanings in a text
members.title: Close Reading
members.exam: Students often skip over the actual text and make broad claims without grounding analysis in specific quotations or examining the language itself.
members.summary: Close reading means examining specific word choices, punctuation, syntax, and imagery at the micro level to uncover how meaning is created through precise authorial decisions.

members.title: Contextual Integration and Interpretive Frameworks
members.exam: Students often force-fit context as separate paragraphs rather than weaving it organically into their argument, or they assume context automatically explains meaning without showing the connection.
members.summary: Effective analysis connects textual features to their historical, cultural, biographical, or theoretical contexts, demonstrating how these external frames shape interpretation and meaning-making.

members.dotPoint: the language of chance: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain
members.title: Evaluative Language and Metalanguage
members.exam: Students commonly fall into the trap of labelling techniques without evaluating their effect, writing that a text uses metaphor without explaining whether that metaphor succeeds or how it shapes meaning.
members.summary: Metalanguage names the technical features of texts like narrative voice or imagery, while evaluative language assesses their effectiveness, and skilled analysis requires both identifying what exists and judging its impact.

members.dotPoint: the dynamics of a text including characters’ motivations, the tensions in relationships, the function of settings, the complexities of plot and the role of point of view
members.title: Structure and Point of View
members.exam: Students often ignore perspective entirely or confuse author with narrator, missing how restricted or unreliable viewpoints shape interpretation.
members.summary: Narrative perspective and structural choices about what information appears when and through whose viewpoint fundamentally control reader access to meaning and emotional response.

members.title: Comparative Textual Study: Texts in Conversation
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can move beyond listing similarities and differences to explaining how the comparison itself generates new insight that neither text alone provides.
members.summary: Comparative study involves reading two texts together to reveal how they speak to each other through shared themes, contrasting perspectives, or direct response, where each text deepens understanding of the other.

members.title: Literary Value and Textual Integrity
members.exam: Examiners look for students to argue why a text has value rather than assume it, testing whether candidates can defend textual integrity by showing how form and content genuinely work together.
members.summary: Textual integrity refers to how well a text's elements cohere into a unified whole, while literary value describes the cultural judgement that certain texts merit study, both concepts being debatable rather than fixed.

cells.bigIdea: A text is built, and every choice the writer made was a choice. Reading closely means seeing the construction, not just the story.

cells.subject: English

members.title: Imaginative, Discursive, Persuasive and Reflective Writing
members.exam: Examiners penalise students who confuse modes by inserting persuasive arguments into reflective pieces or failing to maintain the imaginative contract by breaking into direct opinion statements.
members.summary: The four writing modes each establish a different relationship with readers through distinct purposes—imaginative creates fictional worlds, discursive explores ideas analytically, persuasive argues a viewpoint, and reflective examines personal growth or understanding.

members.title: Intertextuality and Deliberate Allusion
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify specific intertextual references and explain their purpose rather than simply noting that a reference exists without analysing its transformative effect.
members.summary: Intertextuality involves deliberately referencing other texts through allusions, quotations, or structural echoes to create layers of meaning and establish dialogue between works across time and culture.

members.title: Perspective Shift and Narrative Reframing
members.exam: Students often fail to explain how the perspective shift creates new meaning, instead merely retelling events from a different viewpoint without analysing changed reader positioning or thematic implications.
members.summary: Shifting narrative perspective from one character to another reveals how point of view controls reader sympathy, exposes bias, and fundamentally alters which themes are foregrounded or silenced in a story.

members.title: Textual Transformation Through Genre Shift
members.exam: Examiners watch for students who change surface features like format without recognising that core elements must adapt to new genre conventions while maintaining deliberate connection to the original text.
members.summary: Transforming a text across genres requires understanding that genre conventions like structure, tone, and audience expectations are not superficial but fundamentally shape how content is interpreted and valued.

members.dotPoint: the ways purpose, context (including mode) and audience shape writing
members.title: Transforming a Text
members.exam: Examiners expect reflections that analyse specific craft decisions made during transformation, not plot summaries or vague claims that the new version explores the same themes differently.
members.summary: Transformation requires reconstructing a text in a new form, perspective or context, then reflecting analytically on which meanings remained stable and which emerged from your deliberate formal choices.

cells.subject: Foundation Maths

members.title: Solving Linear Equations
members.exam: Students commonly fail when they only apply operations to one side, or when they incorrectly handle negative coefficients by forgetting to flip signs when dividing by negatives.
members.summary: Solving linear equations requires performing inverse operations in reverse order on both sides to isolate the variable while maintaining the equality balance.

members.dotPoint: symbolic expressions, equations and formulas
members.title: Patterns and Linear Relationships
members.exam: Students often fail to identify the fixed cost versus the variable cost in worded problems, or incorrectly read values from a table without checking the pattern holds throughout.
members.summary: Linear patterns appear in real-world contexts where a fixed starting amount increases or decreases by a constant rate, modelled by rules like C = 5n + 20.

members.dotPoint: linear relationships and their use in modelling practical situations
members.title: Graphs and Models of Practical Situations
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can match context to shape—especially distinguishing constant rate (straight line) from increasing/decreasing rate (curve), and identifying sections where a quantity stays constant (horizontal segment).
members.summary: A graph translates a real-world story into a visual relationship between two variables, where the shape (linear, curved, steep, flat) reveals how one quantity changes as the other increases.

members.title: Linear Sequences
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can find the correct value of b by using T(1) = a + b, not mistakenly using the first term as b directly.
members.summary: Linear sequences have a constant common difference between consecutive terms, and the nth term formula is T(n) = an + b where a equals the common difference and b is found by substituting n = 1.

members.dotPoint: graphical and algebraic analysis of relations including transposition of formulas and finding a break-even point using simultaneous equations
members.title: Using Formulas
members.exam: Students lose marks by substituting before rearranging when the unknown appears multiple times or in a denominator, creating unnecessarily complex equations to solve.
members.summary: A formula is an equation showing relationships between quantities; substitute known values to find unknowns, or rearrange algebraically to make your target variable the subject first.

members.title: Substitution into Formulas
members.exam: The most common trap is incorrectly squaring negative numbers, such as calculating (-3)² as -9 instead of 9, or confusing it with -3².
members.summary: Substitution requires replacing variables with given values then carefully following BIDMAS order, with particular attention to squaring negatives and operations involving brackets.

cells.bigIdea: Every rule here is one steady relationship: change one thing by a step, the other moves by the same step, every time. Formula, sequence, equation, line — four ways of writing that relationship.

members.dotPoint: time and duration including time and date specifications, conventions, schedules and timetables.
members.title: Scheduling and Timetables
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify the critical path in a project network or calculate minimum completion time, with common errors including forgetting that some tasks can run simultaneously or miscounting parallel task durations.
members.summary: Scheduling involves arranging tasks in a feasible order while respecting prerequisites and resource constraints, often using tools like Gantt charts or critical path analysis to minimise total completion time.

members.dotPoint: shortest path problems in travel and delivery contexts
members.title: Networks and Shortest Paths
members.exam: Students commonly make errors by adding edge weights incorrectly when finding paths or forgetting to check all possible routes systematically, leading to a suboptimal answer that looks plausible but isn't actually shortest.
members.summary: A network is a collection of vertices connected by weighted edges, and shortest path algorithms like Dijkstra's find the minimum total weight route between two points in the network.

members.dotPoint: algorithmic, algebraic and computational strategies
members.title: Algorithms and Flowcharts
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly trace through a flowchart with given inputs or identify errors in loop conditions and decision branches that cause infinite loops or incorrect outputs.
members.summary: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure to solve a problem, and a flowchart is a visual diagram using shapes like rectangles for processes and diamonds for decisions to represent that algorithm clearly.

runnersUp.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly trace through a flowchart with given inputs or identify errors in loop conditions and decision branches that cause infinite loops or incorrect outputs.
runnersUp.summary: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure to solve a problem, and a flowchart is a visual diagram using shapes like rectangles for processes and diamonds for decisions to represent that algorithm clearly.

cells.bigIdea: Every problem is the same move: turn a messy situation into a map of steps and connections, then follow fixed rules to the cheapest path. Flowcharts, networks, timetables — different maps, same hunt.

members.title: Measures of Spread
members.exam: Examiners test calculation of IQR using correct quartile positions and trap students who confuse sample standard deviation formula with population formula or who forget to square root after finding variance.
members.summary: Range is the difference between maximum and minimum values, interquartile range captures the spread of the middle fifty percent of data, and standard deviation measures average distance of values from the mean.

members.title: Correlation and Scatterplots
members.exam: Examiners commonly test whether students can identify correlation strength from scatterplot patterns and trap students who confuse correlation with causation or who incorrectly claim weak scattered data shows strong correlation.
members.summary: Scatterplots display paired data as points on a graph, revealing positive correlation when both variables increase together, negative correlation when one increases as the other decreases, or no correlation when points appear randomly scattered.

members.dotPoint: development and specification of data collection requirements and methods, including consideration of audience and purpose of data collection, errors and misrepresentations in statistics
members.title: Reading Data Critically
members.exam: Examiners ask students to identify misleading features in graphs such as non-zero baselines on bar charts that exaggerate differences between values.
members.summary: Statistical graphs can be manipulated through axis scaling, truncation, cherry-picked intervals, or inappropriate graph types to exaggerate or hide patterns in data.

members.dotPoint: interpolation and extrapolation of data, predictions, limitations, inferences and conclusions comparing and interpreting data sets and graphs, including using measures of central tendency and spread (percentiles and standard deviation) and cumulative frequency.
members.title: Averages in Context
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify when the mean is inappropriate due to extreme values and justify using the median instead for skewed datasets.
members.summary: The choice of mean, median or mode depends on the data's distribution and the presence of outliers that can distort the mean away from a typical value.

members.title: Measures of Central Tendency
members.exam: Examiners test whether students choose the appropriate measure for skewed data and trap students who always use mean without recognizing that median better represents center when outliers are present.
members.summary: Mean is calculated by summing all values and dividing by the count, median is the middle value when data is ordered, and mode is the value that appears most frequently in the dataset.

cells.subject: Foundation Maths

members.title: Rates and Unit Conversions
members.exam: Students forget to convert both parts of a rate when changing units, commonly multiplying speed in km/h by 1000 instead of dividing by 3.6 to get m/s, or failing to convert hours to minutes when calculating drip rates.
members.summary: Rates express one quantity per unit of another, and converting units requires changing both numerator and denominator separately, like converting 72 km/h to 20 m/s by dividing distance units by 1000 and time units by 3600.

members.dotPoint: metric and other related quantity measures including derived and routine non-metric measures
members.title: Units and Converting Between Them
members.exam: Students move the decimal point the wrong direction or wrong number of places, particularly confusing conversions between square or cubic units which require squaring or cubing the linear conversion factor.
members.summary: The metric system uses powers of ten with prefixes like kilo, centi and milli, requiring movement of decimal points when converting between units of length, mass or capacity.

members.dotPoint: similarity, scale factor and scale drawings
members.title: Similarity, Scale Drawings and Plans
members.exam: Examiners test whether students confuse linear and area scale factors, expecting candidates to square the scale factor when finding area ratios or to recognise that a 1:50 scale drawing means 1 cm represents 50 cm in reality.
members.summary: Similar figures have identical angles and corresponding sides in constant ratio, meaning if you know the scale factor you can find any unknown length by multiplying, and areas scale by the square of the linear scale factor.

members.dotPoint: conventions, properties and measurement of perimeter, area, surface area and volume of compound shapes and objects
members.title: Perimeter, Area, and Composite Shapes
members.exam: Students commonly forget to subtract overlapping regions or incorrectly add areas when a shape has been removed, particularly in problems involving shaded regions within larger shapes.
members.summary: Composite shapes are decomposed into familiar components like rectangles and triangles, with areas calculated separately then combined using addition for joined regions or subtraction for cut-out sections.

members.title: Volume and Surface Area of Solids
members.exam: Students often confuse volume and surface area formulas or fail to recognize that doubling all dimensions multiplies volume by eight but surface area only by four.
members.summary: Volume measures three-dimensional space in cubic units and scales with the cube of linear dimensions, while surface area measures the total exterior covering and scales with the square of linear dimensions.

members.title: Pythagoras Theorem and Trigonometric Ratios
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can identify which side is the hypotenuse correctly, as many incorrectly apply the theorem by placing a non-hypotenuse value as c in the equation.
members.summary: Pythagoras theorem relates the three sides of right-angled triangles through the equation a² + b² = c², while trigonometric ratios connect angles to side ratios using sine, cosine, and tangent.

members.dotPoint: time and duration including time and date specifications, conventions, schedules and timetables.
members.title: Time and Timetables
members.exam: Crossing midnight trips students up when calculating duration, and they add time zones in the wrong direction when travelling east versus west.
members.summary: Time calculations involve converting between 12-hour and 24-hour formats, finding elapsed time across noon or midnight boundaries, and adjusting for time zone differences.

members.dotPoint: formal language, symbols and labelling and drawing conventions for diagrams, maps, plans, models, transformations, symmetry, similarity, perspective and common angle properties
members.title: Maps, Plans and Scale
members.exam: Students commonly multiply when they should divide or confuse the order when converting from map to real distance or real to map distance.
members.summary: Scale drawings use ratios to represent large real-world distances on manageable paper, requiring conversion between map measurements and actual distances using the scale factor.

members.title: Perimeter and Area Calculations
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can derive or explain why the area of a triangle is half base times height, not just apply the formula blindly to numerical problems.
members.summary: Perimeter and area formulas emerge from the fundamental properties of each shape, such as a rectangle's area being base times height because it contains that many unit squares arranged in rows and columns.

cells.subject: Foundation Maths

members.dotPoint: money management including investments and loans, credit and debit, comparing mortgages versus rental costs and debt consolidation
members.title: Budgeting and the Cost of Borrowing
members.exam: Students often forget to include all fees and charges when calculating total loan cost, or fail to compare different credit options using total repayment amounts.
members.summary: A budget tracks income versus expenses to avoid overspending, while borrowing costs extra through interest charges that add significantly to what you repay.

members.title: Compound Interest
members.exam: Students often forget to convert percentage rates to decimals or mismatch time periods with compounding frequency, such as using years when interest compounds monthly.
members.summary: Compound interest means interest earns interest because the balance grows each period, calculated using A = P(1 + r)^n where the exponent n makes growth exponential rather than linear.

members.title: Depreciation
members.exam: Students confuse which method to apply or incorrectly use the original purchase price instead of the current value when calculating reducing balance depreciation.
members.summary: Flat rate depreciation subtracts the same dollar amount each period using V = P - DN, while reducing balance depreciation applies a fixed percentage decrease each period to the remaining value.

members.title: Simple Interest
members.exam: Students mix up simple and compound interest formulas or fail to align time units with the rate period, such as using months when the rate is annual.
members.summary: Simple interest calculates interest only on the original principal using I = PRT, producing linear growth because the same dollar amount is added each period regardless of accumulated interest.

members.dotPoint: income calculations including rates of pay and payslips
members.title: Earning and Understanding Your Pay
members.exam: Students confuse gross and net pay in calculations, or miscalculate overtime rates by forgetting to apply penalty rate multipliers like time-and-a-half correctly.
members.summary: Gross pay is your total earnings before deductions, while net pay is what reaches your bank after tax, superannuation, and other deductions are removed.

members.dotPoint: ratios, proportions and percentages, direct and indirect variation
members.title: Percentages in Real Life
members.exam: Students calculate percentage discounts but forget to subtract from the original price, or add GST incorrectly by finding 10% instead of multiplying by 1.1.
members.summary: Converting between percentages, decimals and dollar amounts requires multiplying or dividing by 100, then applying the decimal multiplier to find the actual value.
