cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: investigate and compare theoretically and practically gravitational, magnetic and electric fields, including directions and shapes of fields, attractive and repulsive effects, and the existence of dipoles and monopoles
members.title: Comparing the Three Fields
members.exam: Students forget that magnetic fields do no work because force is always perpendicular to displacement, while gravitational and electric fields can do work.
members.summary: Gravitational fields only attract, electric fields attract or repel depending on charge sign, and magnetic fields only act on moving charges or currents.

members.dotPoint: electric field and electric force concepts: E=kQr2 and F=kq1q2r2
members.title: Electric Field Strength
members.exam: Students confuse the source charge Q that creates the field with the test charge q that experiences the force.
members.summary: Electric field strength E equals force per unit positive charge, calculated either from E equals F over q or E equals kQ over r squared depending on context.

members.dotPoint: the magnitude of the force on a charged particle due to a uniform electric field: *F* = *qE*
members.title: Uniform Fields Between Parallel Plates
members.exam: Students forget that uniform field means constant acceleration, so they can use kinematic equations directly for electron motion between plates.
members.summary: Parallel charged plates create a uniform electric field E equals V over d between them, meaning constant force and constant acceleration for any charge placed inside.

members.dotPoint: electric field and electric force concepts: E=kQr2 and F=kq1q2r2
members.title: Electric Fields and Coulomb's Law
members.exam: Students forget to check whether the calculated force is attraction or repulsion by examining whether the product q₁q₂ is positive or negative.
members.summary: Coulomb's law F equals kq₁q₂ over r squared mirrors gravitational law but charge signs determine attraction or repulsion, unlike gravity which only attracts.

members.title: Electromagnetic Induction
members.exam: Students write induced EMF equals N times change in flux without dividing by time, forgetting that EMF equals rate of change.
members.summary: Changing magnetic flux through a coil induces an EMF equal to the negative rate of flux change, with the negative sign representing Lenz's law opposition.

members.dotPoint: the magnitude and direction of the force applied to an electron beam by a magnetic field: *F* = *qvB*, in cases where the directions of *v* and *B* are perpendicular or parallel
members.title: Force on a Moving Charge
members.exam: Students incorrectly claim the magnetic force does work or changes kinetic energy, forgetting that perpendicular forces never change speed.
members.summary: A charge moving through a magnetic field experiences force F equals qvB sine theta perpendicular to both velocity and field, causing circular motion at constant speed.

members.dotPoint: investigate and apply theoretically and practically a field model to magnetic phenomena, including shapes and directions of fields produced by bar magnets, and by current-carrying wires, loops and solenoids
members.title: Magnetic Fields Around Currents
members.exam: Students apply the right-hand grip rule incorrectly, confusing which way the thumb points for conventional current direction versus field direction.
members.summary: A current-carrying straight wire creates concentric circular magnetic field lines around it, while a solenoid concentrates field lines inside producing a strong uniform field.

members.title: Maxwell and Electromagnetic Waves
members.exam: Students often forget that electromagnetic waves require both fields perpendicular to each other AND to the direction of propagation, or incorrectly assume they need a medium like sound waves do.
members.summary: Maxwell showed that a changing electric field creates a magnetic field and vice versa, allowing electromagnetic waves to self-propagate through space at the speed of light without requiring a medium.

members.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically the force on a current carrying conductor due to an external magnetic field, *F = nIlB*, where the directions of *I* and *B* are either perpendicular or parallel to each other
members.title: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor
members.exam: Students incorrectly use the angle between current and field instead of finding the perpendicular component, or forget force is zero when wire is parallel to field.
members.summary: A wire carrying current in a magnetic field experiences a force perpendicular to both current direction and field direction, calculated using F = BIL sinθ.

members.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically the operation of simple DC motors consisting of one coil, containing a number of loops of wire, which is free to rotate about an axis in a uniform magnetic field and including the use of a split ring commutator
members.title: How a DC Motor Works
members.exam: Students cannot explain why the commutator is necessary or what happens without it, missing that continuous rotation requires force direction to flip.
members.summary: Opposite sides of a current loop in a magnetic field experience opposite forces creating torque, with a commutator reversing current every half turn to maintain rotation.

members.title: Magnetic Flux Density and the Motor Effect
members.exam: Students forget to use the sine theta factor or misidentify the angle, especially when the conductor is not perpendicular to the field.
members.summary: The motor effect force F equals BIL sin theta acts on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, maximum when perpendicular and zero when parallel.

members.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically the generation of electromotive force (emf) including AC voltage and calculations using induced emf: ε=-N∆ΦB∆t, with reference to:
members.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
members.exam: Students frequently forget to include the number of turns N in calculations or misapply the rate of change by using final flux instead of the change per unit time.
members.summary: Faraday's Law quantifies that induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux multiplied by the number of turns, with the negative sign from Lenz's Law indicating the induced emf opposes the flux change.

members.dotPoint: explain the production of DC voltage in DC generators and AC voltage in alternators, including the use of split ring commutators and slip rings respectively
members.title: AC Generators and Transformers
members.exam: Students often incorrectly assume transformers work with DC current or forget that maximum emf occurs when the coil is parallel to the field (maximum rate of flux change), not perpendicular.
members.summary: AC generators convert mechanical energy to electrical energy through electromagnetic induction as a rotating coil experiences continuous flux changes, while transformers transfer AC power between circuits using mutual induction with different numbers of turns to step voltage up or down.

members.dotPoint: analyse the supply of power by considering transmission losses across transmission lines.
members.title: Power Transmission and Losses
members.exam: Students commonly fail to recognize that halving current reduces loss by a factor of four, or they incorrectly think voltage level directly affects power loss instead of understanding the current-squared relationship.
members.summary: Since power loss equals current squared times resistance, transmitting at high voltage with low current dramatically reduces energy wasted as heat in power lines.

members.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically the generation of electromotive force (emf) including AC voltage and calculations using induced emf: ε=-N∆ΦB∆t, with reference to:
members.title: Lenz's Law and Energy Conservation
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly predict current direction using the right-hand rule after identifying whether flux is increasing or decreasing through a loop.
members.summary: Lenz's Law states that induced currents always flow in a direction to create magnetic fields opposing the change in flux that produced them, which is necessary to conserve energy in the system.

members.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically the generation of electromotive force (emf) including AC voltage and calculations using induced emf: ε=-N∆ΦB∆t, with reference to:
members.title: Motional EMF in a Conductor
members.exam: Students often forget that the conductor must cut across field lines, not move parallel to them, or they miss that emf equals BLv only when motion is perpendicular to the field.
members.summary: A conductor cutting through field lines experiences charge separation as the magnetic force pushes electrons to one end, producing emf equal to the product of field strength, length, and velocity.

members.dotPoint: calculate magnetic flux when the magnetic field is perpendicular to the area, and describe the qualitative effect of differing angles between the area and the field: ΦB=B⊥A
members.title: Magnetic Flux and Flux Linkage
members.exam: Students commonly use the wrong angle, forgetting that θ is measured between the field and the normal to the surface, not between the field and the plane itself.
members.summary: Magnetic flux measures the total magnetic field passing through a surface and equals Φ = BAcosθ, while flux linkage is the total flux through all turns of a coil calculated as NΦ.

members.dotPoint: compare alternating voltage expressed as the root-mean-square (rms) to a constant DC voltage developing the same power in a resistive component
members.title: Peak, Peak-to-Peak and RMS in AC
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students know to use RMS values in power calculations, not peak values, and whether they can convert between peak and RMS correctly using the factor of 1.414.
members.summary: RMS voltage equals peak voltage divided by root two, representing the equivalent DC voltage that delivers identical average power to a resistive load over a complete cycle.

members.title: Transformers: Ideal Models and Real Losses
members.exam: Students commonly forget that step-up transformers increase voltage but decrease current proportionally, or fail to account for energy losses in real transformers through heat in resistance and eddy currents.
members.summary: Transformers use electromagnetic induction between primary and secondary coils to change voltage levels, with the ratio Vp/Vs = Np/Ns, and in ideal transformers power is conserved so VpIp = VsIs.

pick.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically the generation of electromotive force (emf) including AC voltage and calculations using induced emf: ε=-N∆ΦB∆t, with reference to:
pick.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
pick.exam: Students frequently forget to include the number of turns N in calculations or misapply the rate of change by using final flux instead of the change per unit time.
pick.summary: Faraday's Law quantifies that induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux multiplied by the number of turns, with the negative sign from Lenz's Law indicating the induced emf opposes the flux change.

members.dotPoint: analyse the change in gravitational potential energy from area under a force vs distance graph and area under a field vs distance graph multiplied by mass
members.title: Gravitational Potential Energy and Potential
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students can distinguish between potential V (energy per kilogram, J/kg) and potential energy E (total energy, J), particularly when calculating escape velocities or orbital energies.
members.summary: Gravitational potential energy is negative because work must be done against gravity to separate masses to infinity where potential energy is defined as zero, with the system naturally moving toward lower (more negative) energy states.

members.dotPoint: gravitational field and gravitational force concepts: g=GMr2 and Fg=Gm1m2r2
members.title: Gravitational Field Strength
members.exam: Students often forget that g is a vector pointing toward the mass creating the field, or incorrectly use surface gravity values when calculating field strength at orbital altitudes above Earth.
members.summary: Gravitational field strength describes the force per unit mass at any location in a gravitational field, which decreases with distance from the source mass following an inverse square relationship.

members.dotPoint: the use of the inverse square law to determine the magnitude of the field
members.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
members.exam: Students commonly make errors using the distance value, forgetting that r must be measured from center to center of the masses, not from surfaces, especially when dealing with planets or satellites.
members.summary: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation distance.

members.dotPoint: Newton's three laws of motion in one and two dimensions
members.title: Orbital Motion and Kepler's Laws
members.exam: Students often incorrectly think gravity decreases to zero in orbit, but examiners test whether you know orbital motion requires centripetal force provided by gravity at that altitude.
members.summary: Satellites in orbit are constantly falling toward Earth but moving forward fast enough that Earth's surface curves away beneath them at the same rate they fall.

members.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically the uniform circular motion of an object moving in a horizontal plane: Fnet=mv2r, including:
members.title: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force
members.exam: Students wrongly add centripetal force as an extra force on free body diagrams instead of identifying tension, friction, gravity components or normal force as the actual source.
members.summary: Centripetal force is not a new force but the name for whichever real force or force component points toward the centre of the circular path.

members.dotPoint: kinetic energy at low speeds: Ek=12mv2; elastic and inelastic collisions with reference to conservation of kinetic energy
members.title: Elastic vs Inelastic Collisions
members.exam: Students often incorrectly assume kinetic energy is conserved in all collisions or fail to check whether a collision is elastic before using energy equations.
members.summary: Momentum is always conserved in collisions but kinetic energy is only conserved in perfectly elastic collisions, not in inelastic ones.

members.title: Free Body Diagrams and Equilibrium
members.exam: Students commonly include forces the object exerts on other things instead of only forces acting on the object, or they forget to resolve angled forces into components.
members.summary: A free body diagram shows all forces acting on a single object with arrows indicating direction and relative size, essential for applying Newton's second law correctly.

members.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically the motion of projectiles near Earth’s surface, including a qualitative description of the effects of air resistance
members.title: Projectile Motion
members.exam: Students commonly use the wrong velocity component when calculating time of flight or range, or forget that initial vertical velocity is zero only when launched horizontally.
members.summary: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent—horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical motion undergoes constant downward acceleration due to gravity.

members.dotPoint: a vehicle moving around a banked track
members.title: Vertical Circles and Inclined Planes
members.exam: Examiners test minimum speed at the top of a loop where tension can drop to zero, or ask about normal force on inclines where students forget to resolve weight perpendicular and parallel.
members.summary: In vertical circles the required centripetal force changes with position because gravity adds or subtracts from other forces depending on whether the object is at the top or bottom.

members.title: Displacement, Velocity and Acceleration
members.exam: Examiners test whether students confuse distance with displacement or speed with velocity, especially in problems where an object returns to its starting point.
members.summary: Displacement is a vector from start to finish, velocity is displacement per unit time, and acceleration is velocity change per unit time—all directional quantities.

members.dotPoint: elastic potential energy: area under force-distance graph including ideal springs obeying Hooke’s Law: Es=12kx2
members.title: Hooke's Law and Elastic Potential Energy
members.exam: Examiners test whether students remember the one-half factor in elastic potential energy or wrongly assume energy is directly proportional to extension instead of its square.
members.summary: Hooke's law states force is proportional to extension, and elastic potential energy equals one-half k x-squared, meaning energy scales with the square of displacement.

members.dotPoint: investigate and apply theoretically and practically the laws of energy and momentum conservation in isolated systems in one dimension
members.title: Momentum and Impulse
members.exam: Students often forget impulse is a vector or fail to recognise that increasing collision time reduces the average force for the same momentum change.
members.summary: Momentum equals mass times velocity and impulse equals force times time, which equals the change in momentum—the principle behind crumple zones and airbags.

members.dotPoint: investigate and apply theoretically and practically Newton’s three laws of motion in situations where two or more coplanar forces act along a straight line and in two dimensions
members.title: Newton's Three Laws in Two Dimensions
members.exam: Examiners test whether students correctly resolve forces into components before summing them or mistakenly add magnitudes of angled forces directly without vector addition.
members.summary: Newton's laws apply in any direction so when forces act at angles you resolve them into perpendicular components and apply F equals ma separately in each direction.

members.dotPoint: analyse transformations of energy between kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, gravitational potential energy and energy dissipated to the environment (considered as a combination of heat, sound and deformation of material):
members.title: Work, Energy and the Conservation Principle
members.exam: Students forget to account for all energy types in the system or incorrectly apply conservation when friction or air resistance is present and energy is dissipated as heat.
members.summary: Total mechanical energy is conserved in the absence of non-conservative forces like friction, allowing you to equate initial and final energy without analysing forces at every point.

members.title: Torque and Rotational Systems
members.exam: Students commonly forget to use only the perpendicular component of force when calculating torque, or they incorrectly add torques without considering clockwise versus anticlockwise direction signs.
members.summary: Torque is the rotational equivalent of force, calculated as the product of force and perpendicular distance from the pivot point, and it determines whether objects rotate or remain in rotational equilibrium.

members.title: Equations of Motion (SUVAT)
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify which equation to use when specific variables are unknown, and students often fall into the trap of using SUVAT equations when acceleration is not constant.
members.summary: The SUVAT equations are your safety net because if you know any three variables you can always calculate the other two with certainty when an object moves in a straight line with constant acceleration.

members.title: Nuclear Fission
members.exam: Examiners frequently test whether students understand that energy is released because products have higher binding energy per nucleon, not lower, and students must correctly identify that the mass of products is less than reactants despite having more binding energy.
members.summary: Fission releases energy because the total binding energy of the products exceeds that of uranium-235, with the released neutrons capable of triggering chain reactions in surrounding nuclei.

members.title: Nuclear Structure and the Strong Nuclear Force
members.exam: Students commonly confuse the relative strengths of forces or incorrectly state that the strong force operates at long ranges, and examiners test understanding that beyond the short range the electromagnetic repulsion dominates causing instability in large nuclei.
members.summary: The strong nuclear force overcomes electrostatic repulsion between protons but only operates at distances less than about 3 femtometers, being approximately 100 times stronger than electromagnetic force at this range.

members.title: Mass-Energy Equivalence and Binding Energy Calculations
members.exam: Students often forget to convert mass defect from atomic mass units to kilograms using the conversion factor 1u equals 1.66 times 10 to the negative 27 kilograms before applying E equals mc squared, or they incorrectly calculate mass defect by subtracting in the wrong direction.
members.summary: The mass defect is converted to binding energy according to Einstein's equation E equals mc squared, representing the energy needed to completely separate all nucleons in a nucleus.

members.title: Radioactive Decay and Half-Life Mathematics
members.exam: Students frequently confuse the number of half-lives with the fraction remaining, calculating 1 divided by n instead of 1 divided by 2 to the power of n, or they incorrectly manipulate the exponential decay equation when solving for time or initial quantity.
members.summary: Half-life represents the time for half the nuclei to decay and relates to the decay constant by the equation t half equals natural log of 2 divided by lambda, allowing prediction of activity or remaining quantity at any time.

cells.bigIdea: The nucleus is held together by a force that only reaches a tiny distance. Everything nuclear comes from that force competing with electrical repulsion.

members.dotPoint: explain the production of atomic absorption and emission line spectra, including those from metal vapour lamps
members.title: Energy Level Transitions in Atoms
members.exam: Students incorrectly apply continuous energy formulas or forget that absorption requires photon energy to exactly match the gap, not exceed it.
members.summary: Atoms absorb or emit photons only when the photon energy matches the exact energy gap between discrete electron energy levels, producing unique spectral fingerprints for each element.

members.dotPoint: interpret the single photon and the electron double slit experiment as evidence for the dual nature of light and matter
members.title: Wave-Particle Duality and Matter Waves
members.exam: Students forget that larger momentum means shorter wavelength, or fail to explain why wave effects are unobservable for macroscopic objects.
members.summary: All matter has an associated wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum, given by lambda equals h divided by p, making particles exhibit interference and diffraction.

members.dotPoint: atomic energy levels, absorption and emission spectra
members.title: Spectroscopy and Spectra
members.exam: Students frequently reverse emission and absorption spectra visually (bright lines versus dark lines on continuous background), or they fail to calculate photon energy correctly using E = hf = hc/λ when given wavelength data from spectral lines.
members.summary: Each element produces unique sharp lines in emission or absorption spectra because electrons jump between fixed energy levels, releasing or absorbing photons with energies exactly matching the energy difference between levels.

members.title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
members.exam: Students mistakenly attribute uncertainty to poor equipment rather than recognizing it as an intrinsic quantum property independent of measurement technology.
members.summary: The product of uncertainties in position and momentum must always exceed a fundamental limit, meaning you cannot simultaneously know both values with arbitrary precision.

members.dotPoint: describe the limitation of the wave model of light in explaining experimental results related to the photoelectric effect
members.title: The Photoelectric Effect
members.exam: Students wrongly predict that brighter low-frequency light will eventually eject electrons, missing that frequency determines whether ejection occurs at all.
members.summary: Light ejects electrons from metal surfaces instantaneously when photon energy exceeds the work function, with excess energy becoming the electron's kinetic energy.

members.title: Photon Model of Light
members.exam: Students fail to connect photon energy to frequency rather than intensity, or confuse the conditions needed for electron ejection in the photoelectric effect.
members.summary: Light is composed of discrete packets called photons, each carrying energy directly proportional to its frequency through the relationship E equals h f.

members.dotPoint: interpret spectra and calculate the energy of absorbed or emitted photons: *E* = *hf*
members.title: Quantisation of Energy and Photons
members.exam: Students incorrectly assume partial photons can exist or that increasing light intensity alone can compensate for insufficient photon energy.
members.summary: Energy can only be absorbed or emitted in discrete packets called quanta, not in continuous amounts as classical physics predicted.

members.title: From Bohr to Schrodinger: The Quantum Atom
members.exam: Students often incorrectly claim Bohr's model works for multi-electron atoms, or they confuse orbits (fixed paths) with orbitals (probability regions); examiners test whether you know the Heisenberg uncertainty principle emerged from wave-particle duality.
members.summary: Bohr's fixed circular orbits worked only for hydrogen, so de Broglie proposed electrons behave as waves, leading Schrödinger to model electrons as three-dimensional probability clouds called orbitals where exact position and momentum cannot both be known.

members.dotPoint: Analyse and evaluate data and investigation methods: process quantitative data using appropriate mathematical relationships and units use appropriate numbers of significant figures in calculations construct graphs that show the relationship between variables extrapolate to determine graph intercepts of significance construct linearised graphs and identify the significance of the gradient (using relationships relevant to the key knowledge outlined in the areas of study) identify and analyse experimental data qualitatively, handling, where appropriate, concepts of: accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility, resolution and validity of measurements; and errors (random and systematic) identify outliers, and contradictory, provisional or incomplete data repeat experiments to evaluate the precision of data evaluate investigation methods and possible causes of error and uncertainty, and suggest how precision can be improved, and how uncertainty can be reduced
members.title: Blind Procedures and Bias
members.exam: Students incorrectly claim double-blind eliminates placebo effect rather than experimenter bias, or fail to identify that the experimenter still knows the study hypothesis.
members.summary: Single-blind procedures prevent participant expectations from influencing results, while double-blind also prevents experimenter bias by keeping researchers unaware of group allocation.

members.dotPoint: Analyse and evaluate data and investigation methods: process quantitative data using appropriate mathematical relationships and units use appropriate numbers of significant figures in calculations construct graphs that show the relationship between variables extrapolate to determine graph intercepts of significance construct linearised graphs and identify the significance of the gradient (using relationships relevant to the key knowledge outlined in the areas of study) identify and analyse experimental data qualitatively, handling, where appropriate, concepts of: accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility, resolution and validity of measurements; and errors (random and systematic) identify outliers, and contradictory, provisional or incomplete data repeat experiments to evaluate the precision of data evaluate investigation methods and possible causes of error and uncertainty, and suggest how precision can be improved, and how uncertainty can be reduced
members.title: Validity and Reliability
members.exam: Students commonly fail to recognise that high reliability does not guarantee validity, or cannot distinguish between internal validity and external validity in applied scenarios.
members.summary: Validity refers to whether a study measures what it claims to measure, while reliability refers to whether results are consistent across repeated measurements or trials.

members.dotPoint: Comply with safety and ethical guidelines: demonstrate safe laboratory practices when planning and conducting investigations by using risk assessments that are informed by safety data sheets (SDS), and accounting for risks apply relevant occupational health and safety guidelines while undertaking practical investigations demonstrate ethical conduct when undertaking and reporting investigations
members.title: Ethics: Concepts and Guidelines
members.exam: Students list concepts when asked for guidelines or vice versa, or claim a study violated 'ethics' without naming the specific guideline breached.
members.summary: The five ethical concepts are beneficence, integrity, justice, non-maleficence and respect, while the six ethical guidelines are confidentiality, debriefing, informed consent procedures, use of deception in research, voluntary participation and withdrawal rights.

members.dotPoint: Plan and conduct investigations: determine appropriate investigation methodology: case study; classification and identification; experiment; fieldwork; literature review; modelling; product, process or system development; simulation design and conduct investigations: select and use methods appropriate to the selected investigation methodology, including consideration of equipment and procedures, taking into account potential sources of error and causes of uncertainty; determine the type and amount of qualitative and/or quantitative data to be generated or collated work independently and collaboratively as appropriate and within identified research constraints, adapting or extending processes as required and recording such modifications in a logbook
members.title: Experimental Method and Variables
members.exam: Students often confuse extraneous variables with confounding variables, or fail to identify how poor control of variables weakens the ability to establish causation.
members.summary: The experimental method involves manipulating one variable to measure its effect on another while holding all other factors constant to establish cause-and-effect relationships.

members.dotPoint: Plan and conduct investigations: determine appropriate investigation methodology: case study; classification and identification; experiment; fieldwork; literature review; modelling; product, process or system development; simulation design and conduct investigations: select and use methods appropriate to the selected investigation methodology, including consideration of equipment and procedures, taking into account potential sources of error and causes of uncertainty; determine the type and amount of qualitative and/or quantitative data to be generated or collated work independently and collaboratively as appropriate and within identified research constraints, adapting or extending processes as required and recording such modifications in a logbook
members.title: Sampling Techniques
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify sampling bias in scenarios and explain how specific sampling methods limit the generalisability of research findings.
members.summary: Sampling techniques determine how participants are selected from a population, with different methods trading off between representativeness and practical feasibility.

members.dotPoint: Plan and conduct investigations: determine appropriate investigation methodology: case study; classification and identification; experiment; fieldwork; literature review; modelling; product, process or system development; simulation design and conduct investigations: select and use methods appropriate to the selected investigation methodology, including consideration of equipment and procedures, taking into account potential sources of error and causes of uncertainty; determine the type and amount of qualitative and/or quantitative data to be generated or collated work independently and collaboratively as appropriate and within identified research constraints, adapting or extending processes as required and recording such modifications in a logbook
members.title: Variables: The Four That Matter
members.exam: Students label every potential extraneous variable as a confounding variable without evidence it actually varied systematically with the IV, inflating their analysis incorrectly.
members.summary: The independent variable is manipulated, the dependent variable is measured, controlled variables are held constant, extraneous variables could affect the DV, and a confounding variable is an extraneous variable that has systematically varied with the IV, so its effect cannot be separated from the IV's.

members.title: Statistics and Significance
members.exam: Students interpret p less than 0.05 as proving the hypothesis true rather than indicating results are statistically significant, or confuse statistical with practical significance.
members.summary: Descriptive statistics like means and standard deviations summarise data patterns, while inferential statistics like p-values indicate whether results are likely due to chance.

members.title: Accuracy, Precision and Validity
members.exam: Students lose marks by calling a measure accurate when it is only precise, or by conflating internal validity with measurement validity in evaluation questions.
members.summary: Accuracy means hitting the true value, precision means consistency across trials, and validity means your measure actually captures the construct you claim it does.

members.title: Sampling and Allocation
members.exam: Students claim random sampling ensures groups are equivalent when this is actually the function of random allocation, confusing generalisability with internal validity.

members.dotPoint: model mathematically time dilation and length contraction at speeds approaching *c* using the equations: t=γt0 and L=L0γ where γ=1√1-v2c2
members.title: Length Contraction and Relativistic Momentum
members.exam: Students often forget that length contraction only occurs in the direction parallel to motion, not perpendicular, or they incorrectly apply the formula by multiplying L_0 by gamma instead of dividing.
members.summary: Length contraction describes how objects moving at relativistic speeds appear shorter in the direction of motion, while momentum increases beyond classical predictions due to the gamma factor.

members.dotPoint: describe Einstein’s two postulates for his special theory of relativity that:
members.title: The Two Postulates of Special Relativity
members.exam: Examiners test whether students understand that the constancy of light speed contradicts everyday intuition about relative velocities, particularly in questions asking why speeds don't simply add when approaching c.
members.summary: Special relativity rests on two postulates: all inertial frames are equivalent for physical laws, and light speed in vacuum is constant at c for all observers regardless of their motion or the source's motion.

members.dotPoint: model mathematically time dilation and length contraction at speeds approaching *c* using the equations: t=γt0 and L=L0γ where γ=1√1-v2c2
members.title: Time Dilation and the Lorentz Factor
members.exam: Students commonly confuse proper time with dilated time, applying the gamma factor incorrectly by multiplying when they should divide, or failing to identify which observer measures proper time in the rest frame.
members.summary: Time dilation means moving clocks run slower as measured by stationary observers, with the effect quantified by the Lorentz factor gamma equals one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared.

cells.topic: Stars & the Origins of the Elements

members.dotPoint: fuels required for the synthesis of ATP
members.title: Nucleosynthesis in Stars
members.exam: Students often wrongly state that iron is produced in supernovae rather than recognizing that iron is the endpoint of fusion and only elements heavier than iron require supernova conditions.
members.summary: Stars fuse light nuclei into heavier elements up to iron through nucleosynthesis, while elements heavier than iron form during supernova explosions, and all these materials are dispersed into space to form new stars and planets.

members.title: Nuclear Fusion and Stellar Energy
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can calculate energy released using mass defect and E=mc², and commonly trap students who forget to convert atomic mass units to kilograms before calculation.
members.summary: Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei under extreme temperature and pressure, converting a small amount of mass into enormous energy according to Einstein's mass-energy equivalence equation.

members.title: Stellar Spectra and Star Classification
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can link spectral class to temperature correctly, with a common error being to think M-type stars are hotter than O-type stars by reversing the sequence.
members.summary: Each chemical element absorbs specific wavelengths of light, creating dark absorption lines in a star's spectrum that identify both composition and temperature, allowing classification into spectral types O-B-A-F-G-K-M from hottest to coolest.

members.title: The Big Bang and the Expanding Universe (Hubble)
members.exam: Students commonly confuse the expansion of space itself with galaxies moving through space, or fail to apply Hubble's Law correctly by mixing up velocity, distance and the Hubble constant in calculations.
members.summary: Hubble discovered that galaxies are receding with velocities proportional to their distance, proving the universe is expanding uniformly from an initial hot dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago.

members.title: The Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) Diagram
members.exam: A frequent mistake is placing stars incorrectly on the axes, especially confusing which axis represents temperature and forgetting that temperature increases leftward, or not recognizing that main sequence position correlates with stellar mass.
members.summary: The HR diagram plots luminosity versus temperature and reveals that stars occupy distinct regions—main sequence where most stars fuse hydrogen, red giants, supergiants and white dwarfs—with position indicating mass, age and evolutionary stage.

members.title: Complementarity and Measurement
members.exam: Examiners test whether students understand that the mere act of measurement or detection collapses the wave function, not just looking at results afterward, and students often incorrectly claim both patterns can coexist simultaneously.
members.summary: Observing which path a particle takes in the double-slit experiment forces it to behave as a particle, destroying the wave interference pattern, demonstrating that measurement determines the observed nature.

members.dotPoint: compare the momentum of photons and of matter of the same wavelength including calculations using: p=hλ
members.title: De Broglie Wavelength
members.exam: Students commonly make calculation errors by forgetting to convert units (especially electron volts to joules or mass to kilograms) or incorrectly using kinetic energy formulas when given voltage instead of velocity directly.
members.summary: All matter particles have an associated wavelength inversely proportional to their momentum, given by lambda equals h divided by mv, explaining why electrons diffract through slits like light waves do.

members.dotPoint: constructive and destructive interference of coherent waves in terms of path differences: *nλ* and n+12λ respectively, where n = 0,1, 2,…
members.title: Interference and Path Difference
members.exam: Students confuse path difference with distance from slits, or incorrectly apply the conditions by mixing up when to use n-lambda versus (n+0.5)lambda for maxima and minima.
members.summary: Constructive interference occurs when path difference equals whole number multiples of wavelength, while destructive interference occurs at odd multiples of half wavelengths, creating alternating bright and dark regions.

members.title: Diffraction and Polarisation (Malus' Law)
members.exam: Students often forget that Malus' Law requires the incident light to already be polarised, or they incorrectly apply it when light passes through the first polariser which simply halves the intensity.
members.summary: Diffraction shows light spreads through gaps and around edges while polarisation filters light by orientation, with Malus' Law stating transmitted intensity equals incident intensity times cosine-squared of the angle between polariser axes.

members.title: Newton vs Huygens: Competing Models of Light
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify which specific phenomena each historical model successfully explained versus failed to explain, particularly that Newton's model incorrectly predicted light speeds up in denser media while Huygens predicted it slows down.
members.summary: Newton's corpuscular theory explained reflection and rectilinear propagation but failed at diffraction, while Huygens' wave theory explained diffraction and refraction but couldn't explain why light travels in straight lines or casts sharp shadows.

members.dotPoint: explain the results of Young’s double slit experiment with reference to:
members.title: Young's Double-Slit Experiment
members.exam: Students misapply the formula x equals L-lambda over d by confusing which variable is which, or forget that this only works for small angles and requires coherent sources.
members.summary: Coherent light passing through two slits produces an interference pattern of bright and dark fringes on a screen, with fringe spacing proportional to wavelength and distance to screen but inversely proportional to slit separation.

members.dotPoint: behaviourist approaches to learning, as illustrated by classical conditioning as a three-phase process (before conditioning, during conditioning and after conditioning) that results in the involuntary association between a neutral stimulus and unconditioned stimulus to produce a conditioned response, and operant conditioning as a three-phase process (antecedent, behaviour and consequence) involving reinforcement (positive and negative) and punishment (positive and negative)
members.title: Classical Conditioning
members.exam: Students forget that the learner is passive or confuse the order of pairing, mixing up which stimulus comes first or which is neutral versus unconditioned.
members.summary: Learning occurs when a neutral stimulus acquires the power to trigger a reflex by being repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus that naturally triggers that reflex.

members.dotPoint: approaches to learning that situate the learner within a system, as illustrated by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ways of knowing where learning is viewed as being embedded in relationships where the learner is part of a multimodal system of knowledge patterned on Country
members.title: Multimodal Systems of Knowledge
members.exam: Students treat it as storytelling rather than recognising it as a multimodal encoding system with neurological advantages for deep processing and retrieval.
members.summary: Indigenous knowledge systems encode information across multiple sensory and contextual channels simultaneously, integrating place, performance, narrative and social practice into a unified learning framework.

members.dotPoint: social-cognitive approaches to learning, as illustrated by observational learning as a process involving attention, retention, reproduction, motivation and reinforcement
members.title: Observational Learning
members.exam: Students forget that learning and performance are separate, or they miss that vicarious reinforcement or punishment affects whether the observer will imitate the behaviour.
members.summary: Learning occurs through watching a model, requiring attention, retention, reproduction and motivation, with learned behaviour potentially stored without ever being performed.

members.exam: Students confuse it with classical conditioning or mislabel punishment as negative reinforcement, forgetting that reinforcement always increases behaviour.
members.summary: Consequences following a behaviour determine whether that behaviour increases or decreases in frequency, with the learner actively operating on the environment.

members.title: Reinforcement and Punishment

members.summary: Positive means stimulus added, negative means stimulus removed, reinforcement strengthens behaviour, punishment weakens it—creating four distinct combinations that shape operant responses.

cells.subject: Psychology

members.dotPoint: the roles of the hippocampus, amygdala, neocortex, basal ganglia and cerebellum in long-term implicit and explicit memories
members.title: Explicit and Implicit Memory
members.exam: Students mislabel procedural memory as explicit because they can talk about the activity, forgetting that being unable to fully articulate the process makes it implicit.
members.summary: Explicit memory requires conscious recall of facts or events, while implicit memory influences behaviour without conscious awareness, like procedural skills or priming.

members.dotPoint: the roles of the hippocampus, amygdala, neocortex, basal ganglia and cerebellum in long-term implicit and explicit memories
members.title: Where Memory Lives in the Brain
members.exam: Students claim one structure like hippocampus stores all memory, or they forget that hippocampal damage spares procedural memory because basal ganglia and cerebellum are intact.
members.summary: Memory is distributed across brain regions with hippocampus encoding explicit memories, amygdala adding emotional weight, neocortex storing long-term traces, and subcortical structures handling procedural memory.

members.dotPoint: the explanatory power of the Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model of memory in the encoding, storage and retrieval of stored information in sensory, short-term and long-term memory stores
members.title: Atkinson-Shiffrin Multi-Store Model
members.exam: Students often confuse the capacity limits, forgetting that sensory memory has unlimited capacity but extremely brief duration, or they fail to explain that rehearsal is required to transfer information between stores.
members.summary: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model proposes three separate memory stores with different capacities and durations, where information flows sequentially from sensory to short-term to long-term memory through attention and rehearsal processes.

members.dotPoint: the role of episodic and semantic memory in retrieving autobiographical events and in constructing possible imagined futures, including evidence from brain imaging and post-mortem studies of brain lesions in people with Alzheimer’s disease and aphantasia as an example of individual differences in the experience of mental imagery
members.title: Memory and Imagining the Future
members.exam: Students treat memory and imagination as separate systems or fail to explain why hippocampal damage impairs both past recall and future thinking.
members.summary: The hippocampus and associated episodic memory systems that reconstruct past experiences are also engaged when mentally simulating future scenarios or planning ahead.

members.title: Retrieval Failure and Cue-Dependent Forgetting
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can distinguish between cue-dependent forgetting and actual memory loss, and students often confuse context-dependent cues with state-dependent cues or fail to apply encoding specificity correctly.
members.summary: Retrieval failure occurs when memory traces exist but cannot be accessed due to absent or mismatched cues present during encoding, including environmental context and internal physiological states.

members.dotPoint: the role of episodic and semantic memory in retrieving autobiographical events and in constructing possible imagined futures, including evidence from brain imaging and post-mortem studies of brain lesions in people with Alzheimer’s disease and aphantasia as an example of individual differences in the experience of mental imagery
members.title: When Memory Systems Fail
members.exam: Students confuse aphantasia with amnesia or forget that Alzheimer's follows a temporal gradient with recent memories lost first due to hippocampal degeneration.
members.summary: Alzheimer's destroys the hippocampus progressively so recent memories disappear before remote ones, while aphantasia shows absent visual imagery without memory loss.

members.title: Reconstructive Memory and Schema Theory
members.exam: Students commonly fail to explain that schemas cause both helpful organization and systematic errors, or they cannot provide specific examples of how schemas alter memory during reconstruction.
members.summary: Schemas are mental frameworks that organize knowledge and expectations, influencing how we interpret and remember events but also causing memory distortions through filling gaps with schema-consistent information.

members.dotPoint: the explanatory power of the Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model of memory in the encoding, storage and retrieval of stored information in sensory, short-term and long-term memory stores
members.title: Iconic and Echoic Memory
members.exam: Students reverse the durations or forget the functional reason echoic lasts longer, which explains everyday phenomena like delayed auditory processing.
members.summary: Iconic memory stores visual information for approximately 0.3 seconds while echoic memory stores auditory information for 3-4 seconds, both operating as sensory registers.

members.title: Mnemonics: Written and Oral
members.exam: Students dismiss oral methods as primitive or fail to recognise that songlines can encode complex spatial and ecological information more durably than written lists.
members.summary: Memory techniques encode information through structure—acronyms and method of loci in literate traditions, songlines and narrative in oral traditions—with different retrieval strengths.

members.dotPoint: the relative influences of factors that contribute to the development of specific phobia, with reference to gamma-amino butyric acid (GABA) dysfunction and long-term potentiation (biological); behavioural models involving precipitation by classical conditioning and perpetuation by operant conditioning, and cognitive biases including memory bias and catastrophic thinking (psychological); and specific environmental triggers and stigma around seeking treatment (social)
members.title: Biological Contributors to Phobia
members.exam: Students confuse correlation with causation or fail to link GABA dysfunction specifically to reduced inhibition rather than increased fear signals.
members.summary: GABA dysfunction removes inhibition on fear circuits while long-term potentiation strengthens neural pathways through repeated activation, embedding phobic responses biologically.

members.dotPoint: Application of a biopsychosocial approach to explain specific phobia
members.title: Specific Phobia Through a Biopsychosocial Lens
members.exam: Students treat the three domains as competing explanations rather than complementary perspectives that explain different aspects of the same condition.
members.summary: Specific phobia demonstrates how biological, psychological and social factors operate simultaneously and interact rather than competing as alternative explanations for a single disorder.

members.dotPoint: stress, phobia and anxiety distinguished
members.title: Stress, Anxiety and Phobia
members.exam: Students use these terms interchangeably or fail to identify that only phobia involves a specific identifiable stimulus and diagnostic-level impairment.
members.summary: Stress responds to present demands, anxiety involves apprehension about future threats, and phobia is persistent irrational fear of specific stimuli causing significant impairment.

members.dotPoint: the application of a biopsychosocial approach to maintaining mental wellbeing, with reference to protective factors including adequate nutritional intake and hydration and sleep (biological), cognitive behavioural strategies and mindfulness meditation (psychological) and support from family, friends and community that is authentic and energising (social)
members.title: Protective Factors
members.exam: Students describe protective factors as passive conditions rather than active practices or omit cultural determinants for First Nations populations.
members.summary: Protective factors actively maintain mental wellbeing across biological (sleep, nutrition), psychological (CBT strategies, mindfulness) and social domains, with culturally-specific factors for First Nations peoples.

members.title: Stress Response and Cortisol
members.exam: Students confuse acute adaptive stress response with chronic maladaptive effects; examiners test whether you can distinguish helpful short-term versus harmful long-term cortisol elevation.
members.summary: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis releases cortisol during stress to redirect bodily resources, but chronic activation impairs immune function, memory, and increases mental illness risk.

members.title: The 4Ps Model of Mental Health
members.exam: Students commonly mislabel factors, especially confusing precipitating with perpetuating factors; examiners specifically test correct temporal classification with scenario-based questions.
members.summary: The 4Ps framework categorizes influences as predisposing factors (existing vulnerabilities), precipitating factors (immediate triggers), perpetuating factors (maintaining conditions), and protective factors (reducing severity or preventing onset).

members.dotPoint: ways of considering mental wellbeing, including levels of functioning; resilience, as the ability to cope with and manage change and uncertainty; and social and emotional wellbeing (SEWB), as a multidimensional and holistic framework for wellbeing that encapsulates all elements of being (body, mind and emotions, family and kinship, community, culture, country, spirituality and ancestors) for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
members.title: Three Indicators of Wellbeing
members.exam: Students equate high functioning alone with mental health without recognizing that someone can appear functional while experiencing low resilience or poor emotional wellbeing.
members.summary: Mental wellbeing is assessed through levels of functioning in daily tasks, resilience to cope with adversity, and social-emotional wellbeing in relationships and self-perception.

members.title: Biopsychosocial Framework
members.exam: Students often list factors separately instead of explaining how they interact; examiners want to see analysis of combined effects, not isolated descriptions.
members.summary: Mental health emerges from the interaction of biological factors (genetics, neurochemistry), psychological factors (cognition, emotion regulation), and social factors (relationships, culture) rather than any single cause.

members.dotPoint: evidence-based interventions and their use for specific phobia, with reference to the use of short-acting anti-anxiety benzodiazepine agents (GABA agonists) in the management of phobic anxiety and breathing retraining (biological); the use of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and systematic desensitisation as psychotherapeutic treatments of phobia (psychological); and psychoeducation for families/supporters with reference to challenging unrealistic or anxious thoughts and not encouraging avoidance behaviours (social)
members.title: Evidence-Based Interventions
members.exam: Students mismatch intervention types with domains or fail to justify why a specific intervention addresses a particular contributing factor.
members.summary: Interventions target specific domains—biological treatments address neurochemistry and physiology, psychological interventions modify cognition and behaviour, social approaches address environmental and interpersonal contexts.

members.dotPoint: the relative influences of factors that contribute to the development of specific phobia, with reference to gamma-amino butyric acid (GABA) dysfunction and long-term potentiation (biological); behavioural models involving precipitation by classical conditioning and perpetuation by operant conditioning, and cognitive biases including memory bias and catastrophic thinking (psychological); and specific environmental triggers and stigma around seeking treatment (social)
members.title: Psychological Contributors to Phobia
members.exam: Students confuse classical and operant conditioning processes or incorrectly label the relief from avoidance as positive rather than negative reinforcement.
members.summary: Classical conditioning establishes the phobic association while operant conditioning maintains it through negative reinforcement when avoidance behaviours reduce anxiety.

members.dotPoint: the relative influences of factors that contribute to the development of specific phobia, with reference to gamma-amino butyric acid (GABA) dysfunction and long-term potentiation (biological); behavioural models involving precipitation by classical conditioning and perpetuation by operant conditioning, and cognitive biases including memory bias and catastrophic thinking (psychological); and specific environmental triggers and stigma around seeking treatment (social)
members.title: Social Contributors and Stigma
members.exam: Students incorrectly claim stigma causes phobia directly rather than understanding it as a maintaining factor that prevents treatment access.
members.summary: Environmental triggers precipitate phobic responses while stigma acts as a barrier preventing help-seeking behaviour, perpetuating rather than causing the disorder.

members.dotPoint: mental wellbeing as a continuum, with an individual’s mental wellbeing influenced by the interaction of internal and external factors and fluctuating over time, as illustrated by variations for individuals experiencing stress, anxiety and phobia
members.title: The Mental Wellbeing Continuum
members.exam: Students treat the three levels as discrete diagnostic categories rather than recognizing them as points on a fluid spectrum with movement possible.
members.summary: Mental wellbeing exists on a continuum from mentally healthy through mental health problems to mental disorders, with individuals moving along it rather than occupying fixed categories.

members.dotPoint: ways of considering mental wellbeing, including levels of functioning; resilience, as the ability to cope with and manage change and uncertainty; and social and emotional wellbeing (SEWB), as a multidimensional and holistic framework for wellbeing that encapsulates all elements of being (body, mind and emotions, family and kinship, community, culture, country, spirituality and ancestors) for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
members.title: The SEWB Framework
members.exam: Students incorrectly describe SEWB as equivalent to the biopsychosocial model or reduce it to cultural factors added onto Western frameworks.
members.summary: Social and Emotional Wellbeing extends beyond individual psychology to encompass connections to family, community, culture, Country and spirituality as equally essential interdependent domains for First Nations peoples.

pick.dotPoint: the relative influences of factors that contribute to the development of specific phobia, with reference to gamma-amino butyric acid (GABA) dysfunction and long-term potentiation (biological); behavioural models involving precipitation by classical conditioning and perpetuation by operant conditioning, and cognitive biases including memory bias and catastrophic thinking (psychological); and specific environmental triggers and stigma around seeking treatment (social)
pick.title: Biological Contributors to Phobia
pick.exam: Students confuse correlation with causation or fail to link GABA dysfunction specifically to reduced inhibition rather than increased fear signals.
pick.summary: GABA dysfunction removes inhibition on fear circuits while long-term potentiation strengthens neural pathways through repeated activation, embedding phobic responses biologically.

runnersUp.dotPoint: Application of a biopsychosocial approach to explain specific phobia
runnersUp.title: Specific Phobia Through a Biopsychosocial Lens
runnersUp.exam: Students treat the three domains as competing explanations rather than complementary perspectives that explain different aspects of the same condition.
runnersUp.summary: Specific phobia demonstrates how biological, psychological and social factors operate simultaneously and interact rather than competing as alternative explanations for a single disorder.

runnersUp.dotPoint: stress, phobia and anxiety distinguished
runnersUp.title: Stress, Anxiety and Phobia
runnersUp.exam: Students use these terms interchangeably or fail to identify that only phobia involves a specific identifiable stimulus and diagnostic-level impairment.
runnersUp.summary: Stress responds to present demands, anxiety involves apprehension about future threats, and phobia is persistent irrational fear of specific stimuli causing significant impairment.

runnersUp.exam: Students describe protective factors as passive conditions rather than active practices or omit cultural determinants for First Nations populations.
runnersUp.summary: Protective factors actively maintain mental wellbeing across biological (sleep, nutrition), psychological (CBT strategies, mindfulness) and social domains, with culturally-specific factors for First Nations peoples.

cells.bigIdea: Mental health isn't a switch between well and unwell — it's a position on a line that moves. What moves it is biological, psychological and social at once.

cells.subject: Psychology

members.dotPoint: the roles of different subdivisions of the central and peripheral nervous systems in responding to, and processing and coordinating with, sensory stimuli received by the body to enable conscious and unconscious responses, including spinal reflexes
members.title: Conscious and Unconscious Responses
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can correctly identify that reflex arcs are unconscious because they are initiated in the spinal cord before reaching the brain, not simply because they are fast.
members.summary: Conscious responses involve deliberate cortical processing and awareness, while unconscious responses bypass conscious centres and execute automatically without awareness of the stimulus.

members.dotPoint: the role of neurotransmitters in the transmission of neural information across a neural synapse to produce excitatory effects (as with glutamate) or inhibitory effects (as with gamma-amino butyric acid [GABA]) as compared to neuromodulators (such as dopamine and serotonin) that have a range of effects on brain activity
members.title: Glutamate and GABA
members.exam: Students must distinguish between excitatory meaning increasing firing likelihood versus simply transmitting signals, as all neurotransmitters transmit but only some excite.
members.summary: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter increasing likelihood of postsynaptic firing, while GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter decreasing likelihood of firing.

members.dotPoint: the role of neurotransmitters in the transmission of neural information across a neural synapse to produce excitatory effects (as with glutamate) or inhibitory effects (as with gamma-amino butyric acid [GABA]) as compared to neuromodulators (such as dopamine and serotonin) that have a range of effects on brain activity
members.title: Neuromodulators: Dopamine and Serotonin
members.exam: Examiners expect students to explain that the same molecule can function as both neurotransmitter and neuromodulator depending on receptor type and location, not that they are entirely different chemical classes.
members.summary: Neuromodulators like dopamine and serotonin act broadly and slowly across neural regions to alter general excitability, unlike neurotransmitters which act rapidly at single synapses.

members.dotPoint: synaptic plasticity – resulting from long-term potentiation and long-term depression, which together act to modify connections between neurons (sprouting, rerouting and pruning) – as the fundamental mechanism of memory formation that leads to learning
members.title: Synaptic Plasticity
members.exam: Examiners test whether students understand LTP and LTD are opposites occurring at the same synapse based on activity patterns, not different processes in different brain regions.
members.summary: Synaptic connections physically strengthen through long-term potentiation when repeatedly co-activated, weaken through long-term depression when underused, and the brain forms new synapses or prunes existing ones.

members.title: Synaptic Transmission
members.exam: Students forget that neurotransmitters must be removed from the synapse through reuptake or enzymatic breakdown, or they incorrectly state that electrical signals cross the synapse directly.
members.summary: Synaptic transmission converts electrical signals to chemical messages when calcium influx triggers neurotransmitter release from vesicles into the synaptic cleft, where they bind to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron.

members.dotPoint: the role of neurotransmitters in the transmission of neural information across a neural synapse to produce excitatory effects (as with glutamate) or inhibitory effects (as with gamma-amino butyric acid [GABA]) as compared to neuromodulators (such as dopamine and serotonin) that have a range of effects on brain activity
members.title: Synaptic Transmission and the Lock and Key
members.exam: Students incorrectly assume one neurotransmitter type binds to only one receptor type, when actually each neurotransmitter has multiple receptor subtypes causing different postsynaptic effects.
members.summary: Neurotransmitters cross the synaptic gap and bind only to receptors with complementary shapes in a lock-and-key mechanism, ensuring specificity despite many molecules being present simultaneously.

members.title: Structure of Neurons
members.exam: Students often confuse the direction of signal flow, incorrectly stating signals travel from axon to dendrites rather than dendrites to soma to axon to terminal buttons.
members.summary: Neurons have specialized structures including dendrites receiving signals, soma integrating them, axon transmitting them, and myelin sheath insulating the axon to speed saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.

members.dotPoint: the roles of different subdivisions of the central and peripheral nervous systems in responding to, and processing and coordinating with, sensory stimuli received by the body to enable conscious and unconscious responses, including spinal reflexes
members.title: The Nervous System's Command Structure
members.exam: Students wrongly categorize spinal reflexes as PNS when the spinal cord is CNS, or claim autonomic only includes sympathetic and forget parasympathetic.
members.summary: The central nervous system processes information while the peripheral nervous system transmits it, with somatic division controlling voluntary movement and autonomic division regulating involuntary functions via sympathetic and parasympathetic branches.

members.dotPoint: neuron structure and function: dendrites, axon, myelin, terminal buttons
members.title: Inside the Neuron
members.exam: Students confuse the direction of information flow or fail to explain that demyelination in diseases like multiple sclerosis slows neural transmission because signals must propagate continuously rather than jumping between nodes.
members.summary: Neurons have specialized structures where dendrites receive incoming signals, the cell body integrates them, the axon conducts the action potential, and myelin sheath speeds transmission by allowing saltatory conduction between nodes.

members.title: Action Potential Mechanism
members.exam: Students incorrectly describe action potentials as graded or proportional to stimulus strength, rather than understanding they always reach the same peak voltage once threshold is exceeded.
members.summary: Action potential is an all-or-nothing electrical signal where sodium rushes into the neuron causing rapid depolarization to +40mV, followed by potassium rushing out to restore the negative resting potential of -70mV.

members.dotPoint: the roles of different subdivisions of the central and peripheral nervous systems in responding to, and processing and coordinating with, sensory stimuli received by the body to enable conscious and unconscious responses, including spinal reflexes
members.title: The Spinal Reflex
members.exam: Examiners test whether students recognize the brain still receives sensory information during reflexes but receives it after the motor response has already been initiated by the spinal cord.
members.summary: Spinal reflexes occur when sensory neurons synapse with interneurons in the spinal cord that immediately activate motor neurons, producing movement before the brain receives or processes the signal.

members.title: Validity and Reliability
members.exam: Students commonly fail to recognise that high reliability does not guarantee validity, or cannot distinguish between internal validity and external validity in applied scenarios.
members.summary: Validity refers to whether a study measures what it claims to measure, while reliability refers to whether results are consistent across repeated measurements or trials.

members.dotPoint: Comply with safety and ethical guidelines: demonstrate ethical conduct and apply ethical guidelines when undertaking and reporting investigations demonstrate safe laboratory practices when planning and conducting investigations by using risk assessments that are informed by safety data sheets (SDS), and accounting for risks apply relevant occupational health and safety guidelines while undertaking practical investigations
members.title: Ethics: Concepts and Guidelines
members.exam: Students list concepts when asked for guidelines or vice versa, or claim a study violated 'ethics' without naming the specific guideline breached.
members.summary: The five ethical concepts are beneficence, integrity, justice, non-maleficence and respect, while the six ethical guidelines are confidentiality, debriefing, informed consent procedures, use of deception in research, voluntary participation and withdrawal rights.

members.dotPoint: Plan and conduct investigations: determine appropriate investigation methodology: case study; classification and identification; controlled experiment (within-subjects design, between-subjects design, mixed design); correlational study; fieldwork; literature review; modelling; product, process or system development; simulation design and conduct investigations; select and use methods appropriate to the investigation, including consideration of sampling technique (random and stratified) and size to achieve representativeness, and consideration of equipment and procedures, taking into account potential sources of error and uncertainty; determine the type and amount of qualitative and/or quantitative data to be generated or collated work independently and collaboratively as appropriate and within identified research constraints, adapting or extending processes as required and recording such modifications
members.title: Experimental Method and Variables
members.exam: Students often confuse extraneous variables with confounding variables, or fail to identify how poor control of variables weakens the ability to establish causation.
members.summary: The experimental method involves manipulating one variable to measure its effect on another while holding all other factors constant to establish cause-and-effect relationships.

members.title: Sampling Techniques
members.exam: Examiners test whether students can identify sampling bias in scenarios and explain how specific sampling methods limit the generalisability of research findings.
members.summary: Sampling techniques determine how participants are selected from a population, with different methods trading off between representativeness and practical feasibility.

members.dotPoint: characteristics of the selected scientific methodology and method, and appropriateness of the use of independent, dependent and controlled variables in the selected scientific investigation
members.title: Variables: The Four That Matter
members.exam: Students label every potential extraneous variable as a confounding variable without evidence it actually varied systematically with the IV, inflating their analysis incorrectly.
members.summary: The independent variable is manipulated, the dependent variable is measured, controlled variables are held constant, extraneous variables could affect the DV, and a confounding variable is an extraneous variable that has systematically varied with the IV, so its effect cannot be separated from the IV's.

members.dotPoint: placebo, single-blind and double-blind procedures; experimenter and participant effects
members.title: Blind Procedures and Bias
members.exam: Students incorrectly claim double-blind eliminates placebo effect rather than experimenter bias, or fail to identify that the experimenter still knows the study hypothesis.
members.summary: Single-blind procedures prevent participant expectations from influencing results, while double-blind also prevents experimenter bias by keeping researchers unaware of group allocation.

members.dotPoint: p-values, statistical significance and the p<0.05 convention
members.title: Statistics and Significance
members.exam: Students interpret p less than 0.05 as proving the hypothesis true rather than indicating results are statistically significant, or confuse statistical with practical significance.
members.summary: Descriptive statistics like means and standard deviations summarise data patterns, while inferential statistics like p-values indicate whether results are likely due to chance.

members.dotPoint: the accuracy, precision, repeatability, reproducibility and validity of measurements
members.title: Accuracy, Precision and Validity
members.exam: Students lose marks by calling a measure accurate when it is only precise, or by conflating internal validity with measurement validity in evaluation questions.
members.summary: Accuracy means hitting the true value, precision means consistency across trials, and validity means your measure actually captures the construct you claim it does.

members.dotPoint: Plan and conduct investigations: determine appropriate investigation methodology: case study; classification and identification; controlled experiment (within-subjects design, between-subjects design, mixed design); correlational study; fieldwork; literature review; modelling; product, process or system development; simulation design and conduct investigations; select and use methods appropriate to the investigation, including consideration of sampling technique (random and stratified) and size to achieve representativeness, and consideration of equipment and procedures, taking into account potential sources of error and uncertainty; determine the type and amount of qualitative and/or quantitative data to be generated or collated work independently and collaboratively as appropriate and within identified research constraints, adapting or extending processes as required and recording such modifications
members.title: Sampling and Allocation
members.exam: Students claim random sampling ensures groups are equivalent when this is actually the function of random allocation, confusing generalisability with internal validity.
members.summary: Sampling selects participants from the population to join the study, while allocation distributes those participants into experimental conditions or groups.

members.dotPoint: Plan and conduct investigations: determine appropriate investigation methodology: case study; classification and identification; controlled experiment (within-subjects design, between-subjects design, mixed design); correlational study; fieldwork; literature review; modelling; product, process or system development; simulation design and conduct investigations; select and use methods appropriate to the investigation, including consideration of sampling technique (random and stratified) and size to achieve representativeness, and consideration of equipment and procedures, taking into account potential sources of error and uncertainty; determine the type and amount of qualitative and/or quantitative data to be generated or collated work independently and collaboratively as appropriate and within identified research constraints, adapting or extending processes as required and recording such modifications
members.title: Choosing an Investigation Methodology
members.exam: Students write that correlation proves causation or fail to justify why a particular methodology was appropriate for the research question posed.
members.summary: Controlled experiments manipulate an IV to establish causation, correlational studies identify relationships without manipulation, and case studies provide rich detail on individual instances.
